articles.title: The government must reach an agreement with the EU on postponing the CBAM for Ukraine — FRU - ЭкоПолитика
articles.summary: The government must reach an agreement with the EU on postponing the CBAM for Ukraine — FRU  ЭкоПолитика
articles.full_text:
Ukraine has every reason to expect the European Union to exempt it from the CBAM and to defer the introduction of the carbon levy. According to the business community, the full-scale war constitutes such an insurmountable circumstance, as it prevents the eco-modernisation of assets.
This was reported by RBC-Ukraine, citing a statement by Ruslan Illichov, Director-General of the Federation of Employers of Ukraine.
War constitutes a force majeure event
Under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the European Union requires importing countries to pay for embedded carbon emissions. For Ukrainian businesses, this pressure is insurmountable.
"We believe there are sufficient grounds for a force majeure to enable us to defer this payment," said Illichov during the United by Mining forum.
In his view, the full-scale war is preventing Ukrainian industry from meeting the European Union’s environmental requirements. These relate to reducing emissions in the production of metals and cement, and in the extraction of minerals.
In addition to the challenging military situation, steelmakers and cement producers will face further financial pressure following the introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) on 1 January 2026, due to the need to pay a carbon duty when exporting their products to the EU.
What should I do?
The CEO of the FSU maintains that the Ukrainian government must now take proactive action. The task is to conduct productive negotiations with the European Commission.
A separate issue is that of default emission values. Where it is not possible to verify actual greenhouse gas emission levels, the EU applies default values to importers. According to Ruslan Illichov, these are too high for Ukrainian companies.
As a reminder, to verify emissions accreditors within the framework of the CBAM, Ukraine has agreed to receive assistance from the Swedish accreditation body SWEDAC.
In his first major interview, the new head of government mentioned that negotiations with the European Union regarding the CBAM for Ukraine are ongoing. The European Parliament has provisionally agreed to the possibility of applying special measures.
The European Parliament recently supported the extension of the scope of the CBAM to cover derivative goods manufactured from the main products, including fastenings and household items.

articles.title: France and Germany warned against protectionist measures after EU letter - China Daily Global Edition
articles.summary: France and Germany warned against protectionist measures after EU letter  China Daily Global Edition
articles.full_text:
By XING YI in London | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-10-07 22:56
Ahead of high-level trade talks between China and the European Union later this week, Chinese officials and experts have warned France and Germany against resorting to protectionist measures, politicizing economic issues and framing them in terms of security.
The warning came after a letter jointly signed by French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to bolster the EU with a new trade diversification instrument and a new trade defense measure.
Reuters reported on Monday that the letter, together with an unofficial proposal paper, had been welcomed by the commission, which said it was a valuable contribution to the debate on geoeconomic risks and global imbalances, and aligned with Von der Leyen's stance on competitiveness and her approach to EU trading partners.
Though the letter did not mention China, analysts said China was the most likely focus of the proposal as it was sent out before possible China-EU trade talks on Thursday.
A spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday that the ministry had taken note of the report and expressed hope that France and Germany, as major global economies, would uphold openness, cooperation and free trade, abide by World Trade Organization rules, and refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures at every turn. Still less should they politicize economic and trade issues under the garb of security concerns.
"They should avoid taking the wrong approach down the wrong path, which could ultimately backfire on themselves," the spokesperson said.
The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU also issued a response opposing the reported proposal in its current form and calling for continued dialogue, consultation and a balanced approach to addressing trade concerns.
"At a particularly critical stage of the ongoing China-EU trade negotiations, we believe that introducing such a mechanism could increase uncertainty, undermine mutual trust and complicate efforts to achieve constructive and tangible outcomes," said a spokesperson for the CCCEU.
In June, China and the EU held the first round of trade talks and established four workstreams covering trade and investment balancing, export controls, intellectual property rights and WTO reform.
The progress came against the backdrop of deep economic ties between the two sides, with bilateral trade exceeding $828 billion in 2025.
Michael Schumann, chairman of the board of the Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade of Germany, said German businesses are increasingly concerned about the political uncertainty surrounding the economic relationship between the two sides and expect a credible political signal that the EU and China want to manage their differences rather than escalate them.
"Companies need predictability," said Schumann. They want fair competition and better market access, and want to preserve the enormous opportunities that continue to exist in China, he added.
"At the same time, Europe should avoid creating the impression that new economic instruments are an end in themselves. Strong instruments can have a role as a safeguard and as leverage in negotiations, but the objective must always be to create better and more balanced conditions for trade."
He said the logic that every dispute must be answered with another restriction should be avoided. "Once retaliation becomes the dominant dynamic, businesses and consumers on both sides lose."
Schumann regarded the talk of a "kill switch" in the current debate and reporting surrounding the Franco-German paper as irresponsible rhetoric.
"I have said repeatedly that language matters in international relations. Words can open doors, but they can also close them. Europe should defend its legitimate economic interests firmly, but we should not talk ourselves into a confrontation that neither side can benefit from," he added.
Mark Logan, a London-based political risk consultant and former member of the British Parliament, said Europe should pay close attention to signs of greater engagement displayed at the recent China-United States summit and pursue more cooperation with China rather than engage in protectionist measures.
"European leaders must find a way to work with China and the new emerging centers of economic power by learning the most important ingredients for their success: technological innovation and entrepreneurialism," said Logan.

articles.title: France fires upgraded nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time - Defense News
articles.summary: France fires upgraded nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time  Defense NewsFrance completes test of new nuclear-capable missile  Le Monde.frKremlin Says France's Test Nuclear Launch Is Part of 'Dead End' Anti-Russia Strategy  The Moscow TimesFrance tests upgraded nuclear missile against backdrop of Russia tensions  ReutersUkraine war live: Kremlin responds to France testing upgraded nuclear weapon  The Independent
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday, a capability demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron called “very important” for the country’s strategic credibility and which he said would be monitored by allies and adversaries alike.
The nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine Le Vigilant fired an M51.3 missile in an acceptance test following the boat’s overhaul, the Ministry of the Armed Forces said in a statement. The missile, which didn’t carry a nuclear warhead, was launched off Finistère in western France and splashed down in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometers from any coastline, the ministry said.
France’s work to upgrade the M51 missile, manufactured by ArianeGroup, is part of a broader modernization of the country’s nuclear deterrence apparatus that also includes the construction of new ballistic-missile submarines and a future upgrade of the Rafale fighter jet that would carry a hypersonic nuclear cruise missile.
“This is a very important moment for our strategic credibility,” Macron told troops onboard a French Navy vessel from which he observed the launch. “Everything that has happened recently and what is happening today will be closely scrutinized by both our allies and our competitors alike, and it already is. Along the course we have set, this is a step forward.”
The modernization of France’s nuclear arsenal comes as the country works with several European allies on what Macron has called “forward deterrence,” a proposal that could involve extending the reach of French nuclear deterrence to those allies, although the details of what that would look like remain vague for now.
Every major overhaul of a French nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine is followed by an acceptance test firing of the M51, the ministry told Defense News in an emailed response to questions.
ArianeGroup and France’s Directorate General for Armament completed a first flight test of the modernized M51 from a launch site in Biscarrosse in southwest France in 2023, and the new missile entered operational service in October last year.
The latest M51.3 variant is estimated to have a range of more than 9,500 kilometers, from more than 9,000 kilometers for the previous version, according to the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The missile carries four to six multiple independently-targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs, according to the Bulletin.
While the official range of the missile is undisclosed, ArianeGroup says the M51 reaches an altitude of more than 2,000 kilometers before reentering the atmosphere at a speed of Mach 20.
The missile is equipped with the new TNO-2 oceanic nuclear warhead, and offers better performance in terms of range, accuracy and penetration capability, according to the ministry. The solid-propellant three-stage missile weighs more than 50 metric tons, and each of France’s four ballistic missile submarines can carry 16 of them.
“The M51.3 ensures the long-term credibility of the ocean-based component in the face of evolving adversary missile defenses,” the ministry said. “It reflects the commitment of the President of the Republic to maintaining operational credibility of the nuclear forces over the long term, at the level required by the international environment.”
The first version of the M51 was fired from the Biscarrosse launch site in 2006, with the first submarine launch from the SSBN Le Terrible in January 2010. Today’s launch was the seventh time a variant of the M51 was fired from a French submarine, and the 13th launch of the missile overall, all of them “of course, conducted without a nuclear warhead,” according to the ministry.
Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

articles.title: The nuts and bolts of CBAM - Irish Farmers Journal
articles.summary: The nuts and bolts of CBAM  Irish Farmers Journal
articles.full_text:
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has quickly become one of the biggest talking points in the fertiliser trade, but exactly how the new system works and how the costs eventually find their way back to farmers, is far from straightforward.
CBAM came into force at the beginning of 2026 and, while its scope stretches beyond agriculture, fertiliser is one of the key products covered by the mechanism.
At its simplest, CBAM is designed to put a carbon cost on certain goods imported into the EU, similar to the carbon costs already faced by European manufacturers.
Speaking on the Irish Farmers Journal’s Down to Agribusiness podcast, Kieran Holden, fertiliser technical lead with Goulding Soil Nutrition and president of the Fertiliser Association of Ireland, explained that to understand CBAM, it is first necessary to understand the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).
The ETS dates back to 2005 and requires carbon-intensive industries operating in Europe to account for and ultimately pay for their emissions. This creates a potential problem for European manufacturers.
If a European fertiliser plant has to pay a carbon price while a manufacturer outside Europe does not, the imported product can have a significant cost advantage. This is known as “carbon leakage”.
CBAM is intended to level that playing field by attaching a comparable carbon cost to imported products.
Why fertiliser matters
CBAM covers a range of carbon-intensive products, including fertiliser, cement, aluminium, steel and electricity. However, fertiliser presents a particular challenge, because Europe is reliant on imports to meet its requirements.
Holden said that, on average, Europe imports 6.9 million tonnes of urea annually, equivalent to around 59% of its total urea consumption of 11.7 million tonnes.
At the same time, natural gas, the key feedstock and energy source for conventional nitrogen fertiliser production, remains considerably more expensive than it was before the energy crisis.
That means CBAM is being introduced into a fertiliser market that is already dealing with elevated production costs.
Who actually pays CBAM?
For fertiliser entering Ireland from outside the EU, the CBAM obligation ultimately falls on the importer. The amount due depends on the carbon emissions associated with producing the fertiliser.
There are two main ways of establishing those emissions: an EU-set default emissions value, or a verified emissions figure from the individual production facility. The latter could prove difficult in practice.
Holden said that as of late September 2026, the first verification body capable of carrying out CBAM verification had only just been approved.
Verification also requires an in-person visit to the production facility. With potentially tens of thousands of installations around the world exporting CBAM-covered products into Europe, Holden said the practical difficulties involved could result in importers relying heavily on the EU’s default values.
Those default values are important because, in some cases, they can result in substantial CBAM liabilities.
How is the bill calculated?
The calculation involves more than simply applying a flat carbon tax to every tonne of fertiliser.
Broadly, the embedded emissions associated with the imported product are established first.
Allowances are then made for the free carbon allocation available to comparable European production and for qualifying carbon prices already paid in the country where the product was manufactured.
The level of free allocation is particularly important. During 2026, a large proportion of the relevant benchmark remains covered by free allocations. However, these are due to be progressively reduced between now and 2034.
This mirrors what is happening to European manufacturers under the ETS.
Once the relevant emissions exposure has been established, the importer must secure the corresponding number of CBAM certificates.
The price of those certificates is linked to the carbon price under the EU ETS.
For 2026, certificate prices are being calculated quarterly and retrospectively. From 2027, Holden said the system is due to move to weekly pricing.
For example, the CBAM certificate price for both the first and second quarters of 2026 was around €75. The third-quarter figure, published just this week, is €82.32. However, that does not mean €82.32 is simply added to every tonne of fertiliser.
What does it mean per tonne?
Holden provided the example of urea imported from Egypt. For 2026, he said Egyptian urea carries a chargeable CO2 element, requiring approximately 0.525 CBAM certificates per tonne. At an estimated certificate price of €82, this translates into a CBAM cost of approximately €43/t.
Algerian urea has a slightly higher default value, producing an estimated CBAM cost of approximately €44/t under the same assumptions.
The impact on calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN) can be considerably greater. Holden said CAN imported from Egypt could face a CBAM cost of around €115/t in the third quarter of 2026 using the applicable default values.
For importers, costs of that magnitude can determine whether sourcing fertiliser from a particular country remains commercially viable. The consequence could therefore extend beyond higher fertiliser prices. It could also affect where Irish importers can source fertiliser and, potentially, product availability.
This is particularly significant for Ireland because the country has no domestic nitrogen fertiliser production and consequently depends on imported supplies.
Buying the certificates
Although CBAM has applied since 1 January 2026, importers cannot yet simply log on and buy certificates. A Common Central Platform is due to become operational in 2027, through which importers will purchase the certificates required to meet their obligations.
Importers will have until September 2027 to deal with their 2026 CBAM liability. In Ireland, the Environmental Protection Agency is the national competent authority responsible for the rollout of CBAM, while Revenue also has a role in the system.
Unlike conventional carbon credits, there is not a limited supply of CBAM certificates.
Instead, certificates are available as required, with their value linked back to the EU carbon market. Under current proposals, around 25% of the revenue raised through the sale of CBAM certificates would go into a Temporary Decarbonisation Fund between 2027 and 2029, while the remaining 75% is expected to flow back to the European Commission to support the EU budget. This has yet to be fully decided however.
Opportunities
Looking further ahead, the gradual removal of free allocations could also change the economics of lower-carbon fertiliser production.
Holden estimated that by 2034, urea could carry around €210/t in CBAM costs and CAN around €310/t. At that point, lower-carbon alternatives such as fertiliser produced from green ammonia could become increasingly competitive with conventional production.
For now, however, green ammonia remains significantly more expensive, meaning the transition to lower-carbon fertiliser is likely to be a gradual one.
In brief
CBAM adds a carbon cost to fertiliser imported into the EU.
Importers meet their obligations by purchasing CBAM certificates.
Costs vary significantly depending on fertiliser type and country of origin.
CBAM costs are set to increase as free allocations are phased out.

articles.title: The UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism - Commonwealth Secretariat
articles.summary: The UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism  Commonwealth Secretariat
articles.full_text:
Download full text (PDF)
Global temperatures are projected to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels within the next decade. The industrial sector, encompassing steel, cement, chemicals and aluminium, accounts for 25–30 per cent of total global carbon emissions, making its decarbonisation critical. In response, developed economies have adopted carbon pricing
instruments, including Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms to prevent carbon leakage and align domestic and import costs.
The United Kingdom’s CBAM, effective from1 January 2027, imposes a carbon tax, administered by His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC), on imports of aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, and iron and steel. Unlike the European Union’s (EU’s) certificate-trading approach, the UK CBAM calculates liability by multiplying embodied
emissions by the effective UK carbon price, with deductions for overseas carbon pricing already paid.
This paper finds that, while the UK CBAM has a defensible rationale in preventing carbon leakage, its effectiveness is constrained by design limitations including widespread use of default emission values, vulnerability to ‘resource reshuffling’, and weak alignment with principles of international equity enshrined in the UN Framework Convention on
Climate Change (UNFCCC) and Paris Agreement.

articles.title: Global Market: Eurozone energy inflation has yet to spread to broader prices, ECB's Rehn says - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Global Market: Eurozone energy inflation has yet to spread to broader prices, ECB's Rehn says  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Eurozone inflation is currently running well above the ECB's 2% target, prompting policymakers to debate how much further interest rates may need to rise following two rate increases over the summer.
Several ECB policymakers have warned that inflation risks are tilted to the upside, but Rehn highlighted opposing forces within the economy that could limit further price pressures.
Also Read | Global Market: Nikkei rises as Wall Street gains, oil prices fall
He said the recent increase in long-term interest rates was contributing to slower economic growth and reducing the extent to which higher energy costs were being passed through to consumer prices and wages.
ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane has also pointed to the potential impact of tighter financial conditions on inflation. ECB board member Isabel Schnabel, one of the central bank's more hawkish policymakers, has similarly warned that the economy could react more strongly to higher borrowing costs than previously expected, potentially reducing medium-term inflation pressures.
Financial markets currently expect another two to three rate increases during the current tightening cycle, with an around 80% probability of a hike by December.
Also Read |Global Market | Central banks face tougher crisis-management role as public debt rises: BIS chief
At the same time, Rehn acknowledged that energy prices remain elevated and that the euro zone economy has shown considerable resilience. Strong investment in artificial intelligence has been one factor supporting economic activity.
The report stated that this resilience has raised concerns among some ECB policymakers that underlying price pressures could prove stronger than previously anticipated, complicating the central bank's efforts to bring inflation sustainably back to its 2% target.

articles.title: MEPs call for tougher action against China - Euronews.com
articles.summary: MEPs call for tougher action against China  Euronews.comEU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars  The GuardianEU’s top trade envoy in China for tense talks over cars  Financial TimesGermany and France Are Proposing a New Weapon to Counter Flood of Chinese Goods  WSJEU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
The resolution calls China “a decisive enabler” of Russia’s war in Ukraine and says the EU should take action against China’s weaponisation of the rare eath minerals that Europe depends on.
The European Parliament has called for tougher action against China’s economic coercion and support for Russia, warning that relations with Beijing have reached a “critical point”.
MEPs backed the resolution by a landslide on Wednesday, urging the EU to consider deploying its powerful Anti-Coercion Instrument if Beijing weaponises Europe’s dependence on critical raw materials.
The vote came as EU Trade Chief Maroš Šefčovič was flying to Beijing for crunch talks aimed at rebalancing the increasingly strained trade relationship.
October is shaping up to be a crucial month for EU-China relations. EU leaders, whose countries now all run trade deficits with China, are pressing the European Commission to deliver concrete results from negotiations with Beijing.
Tensions also extend well beyond trade. The EU has become increasingly alarmed by Beijing’s close relationship with Moscow and its role in sustaining Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“The relations have now reached a critical point, mostly due to China’s unfair economic practices such as dumping and spying and its position on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine,” the resolution adopted by EU lawmakers reads.
The text was backed by 454 MEPs, with 86 voting against and 110 abstaining.
Lawmakers described China’s role in the Ukraine war as that of “a decisive enabler”, pointing to “Chinese diplomatic backing and material assistance that sustains the Russian military-industrial complex”.
Pressure to use anti-coercion tool
They also call on EU countries and the Commission to “urgently” take action on “the weaponisation of critical dependencies by China.”
Europe felt the vulnerability of those dependencies in 2025, when China restricted exports of rare earths, which are vital to the EU’s automotive, defence and clean-tech industries, amid its escalating trade war with the United States.
The MEPs said the EU should consider using the Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI) when China instrumentalises such EU dependencies.
The ACI is an EU mechanism that allows the bloc to adopt radical measures – up to restrictions on licences and intellectual property rights – against a third country that uses economic coercion against the EU.
China’s dominance of the production and processing of strategic raw materials has become a major sticking point in trade negotiations, giving Beijing considerable leverage as Brussels seeks to curb its dependence on Chinese imports.
A Commission proposal pushing companies to diversify their suppliers in strategic sectors is in the making and should be presented by the end of the year.
The resolution comes two days after Germany and France harden their stancetowards Beijing, calling for a new trade tool that could allow the Commission to impose measures leading to “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed”.

articles.title: European Commissioner Kubilius calls for a military Schengen — Anadolu Agency - UA.NEWS
articles.summary: European Commissioner Kubilius calls for a military Schengen — Anadolu Agency  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, speaking at the Military Schengen 2026 conference in Hamburg, Germany, called on EU countries to accelerate military mobility and create a unified mechanism for moving troops and equipment. This was reported by Anadolu Agency.
Assessment of Russia’s spending
According to Kubilius, Russia, an aggressor state, could allocate €180 billion to its military budget in 2027, approximately 3% more than this year’s spending. He said that, taking purchasing power parity into account, this expenditure could equal or slightly exceed the combined defence spending of all EU member states.
The European commissioner also said that Russia is outpacing Europe in defence industrial output and is rapidly developing new military technologies, including drones. In his assessment, in the event of possible Russian aggression, Europe would have to confront a Russian army capable of using 10 million drones per year, or about 30,000 per day.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
A single permit for transport
Kubilius stressed that deterring aggression depends not only on defence spending and procurement, but also on the ability to rapidly move troops and equipment across Europe. He proposed replacing the current system of 27 national systems with a single European rulebook for military transport.
Under the proposed package, a single European permit for military transport would be valid throughout the EU and issued no later than within three days. For emergencies, the EU proposes creating a European Enhanced Response System for Military Mobility, which could be activated by the Council of the EU.

articles.title: EUDR Compliance Gaps Persist for Smallholders, New Report Finds - Daily Coffee News by Roast Magazine
articles.summary: EUDR Compliance Gaps Persist for Smallholders, New Report Finds  Daily Coffee News by Roast Magazine

source_detail.name: Daily Coffee News by Roast Magazine

articles.full_text:
As the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) heads toward its Dec. 30 application date, a new report from the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) suggests many smallholders still lack the resources needed to meet EUDR-related buyer requirements.
The report from the sustainability-focused think tank involved interviews and surveys with 333 farmers and producer groups behind numerous agricultural products in 16 countries, including coffee farmers. The authors did note that the sample was uneven and should not be treated as statistically representative.
Market Leakage
The research did find that while awareness of EUDR was widespread, many still faced barriers involving land documentation, compliance costs, traceability and technical capacity.
Notably, 74% of all respondents said they believed stricter compliance requirements could push farmers toward less-regulated markets. Among coffee respondents, that figure was 79%.
“This finding highlights a critical challenge for policy-makers and supply chain actors: ensuring that the EUDR reduces deforestation without excluding the smallholders who play a vital role in global agricultural production,” the authors of the new IISD report wrote.
The regulation, adopted in 2023, is designed to prevent products linked to deforestation or forest degradation from entering or leaving the EU market. It covers coffee alongside cattle, cocoa, palm oil, rubber, soy and wood. Under the current schedule, the law begins applying to large and medium-sized operators on Dec. 30, 2026, and to most micro and small operators on June 30, 2027.
In their replies to IISD, some farmers said they may sell to buyers offering higher prices or faster payments rather than remain in EUDR-oriented channels. Others could lose access to EUDR-compliant buyers because they cannot afford mapping, traceability or other compliance costs.
The authors warn that such “leakage” could undermine the regulation itself, promoting trade in markets with weaker environmental requirements.
The Importance of Networks
The report also identified a growing divide between smallholders already connected to cooperatives, third-party certification programs and organized international supply chains and those working independently. Connected farmers generally reported better documentation, traceability, training and institutional support.
Recent DCN reports have noted different levels of farmer preparation in the coffee lands of Colombia, Costa Rica and Honduras.
Across all commodities within the IISD report, 84% of respondents identified government policies and programs as a needed form of assistance. That was followed by financial assistance (78%), training and capacity building (74%) and better information and awareness (71%).
“The report argues that achieving the objectives of the EUDR will require a shared-responsibility approach involving governments, private sector actors, voluntary sustainability standards organizations and sustainability initiatives, and development partners,” the authors wrote. “Supporting smallholder inclusion is not only a matter of equity, but also fundamental to the effectiveness and credibility of the regulation itself.”
IISD is a Canada-based think tank focused on sustainable development. The report was produced through IISD’s State of Sustainability Initiatives program, which conducts research and advises governments, sustainability-standard organizations and supply-chain actors.

articles.title: EU Data Act Guidance Sets New SaaS Export and Switching Rules - SaasRise
articles.summary: EU Data Act Guidance Sets New SaaS Export and Switching Rules  SaasRise
articles.full_text:
On 6 October 2026 the European Commission released guidance that clarifies how the Data Act applies to SaaS subscriptions. The guidance spells out exportable data categories, open‑API requirements and contractual disclosures, forcing providers to rethink exit‑strategy clauses and GTM playbooks.
Why It Matters
The clarified obligations reshape the SaaS value chain by turning data portability from a legal afterthought into a core product feature. For operators, this means re‑engineering onboarding, support and engineering processes to ensure that every data element—attachments, relational links and change history—can be exported on demand. From a GTM perspective, the ability to promise frictionless switching becomes a differentiator that can lower sales cycles and improve net‑retention, especially in vertical SaaS markets where data lock‑in has traditionally been a barrier to entry.
Investors will also watch how quickly providers adapt, as compliance costs and potential revenue erosion from free export services could impact margins. Companies that embed export‑ready architecture early can protect gross margin and maintain strong net‑retention, while those that lag may face contract renegotiations, legal exposure, or loss of enterprise accounts to more compliant rivals.
Key Points
- EU Commission guidance released 6 Oct 2026 clarifies SaaS data‑export obligations under the Data Act
- Providers must offer a structured, machine‑readable export of all customer‑owned data and open APIs at no charge
- Contracts must list exportable data categories, including attachments, identifiers and change history
- Exemptions for IP and trade secrets cannot be used to delay switching
- Guidance mandates a two‑month notice period before export is delivered
Analysis
The Data Act guidance marks a shift from abstract regulatory language to actionable compliance checklists, forcing SaaS firms to treat data portability as a product feature rather than a legal footnote. Historically, SaaS contracts have leveraged data lock‑in to boost net‑retention, but the EU’s insistence on open interfaces erodes that moat. Companies that can automate export pipelines—turning ticket histories, attachment blobs and relational graphs into ready‑to‑import packages—will create a new competitive advantage, especially in high‑touch verticals like healthcare and finance where migration risk is a major procurement hurdle.
From a market dynamics standpoint, the guidance could accelerate consolidation among European SaaS providers. Smaller players lacking the engineering bandwidth to build compliant APIs may become acquisition targets for larger, export‑ready platforms. Meanwhile, US‑headquartered SaaS firms serving EU customers must internalize the cross‑border compliance burden, potentially prompting regional data‑processing subsidiaries or partnerships with EU‑based firms to meet the open‑interface requirement without exposing proprietary code.
Looking forward, the pending committee decision could tighten timelines or introduce sector‑specific exemptions, adding another layer of uncertainty. Operators should therefore adopt a modular architecture that decouples core business logic from data storage, enabling swift compliance updates. Investors will likely factor a provider’s export‑readiness into due‑diligence scoring, rewarding firms that demonstrate low‑friction switching as lower‑risk bets in a regulatory environment that increasingly favors customer sovereignty.

articles.title: Russia threatens ‘necessary measures’ as Lithuania prepares NATO build-up - London Business News
articles.summary: Russia threatens ‘necessary measures’ as Lithuania prepares NATO build-up  London Business News
articles.full_text:
Lithuania’s decision to consider removing its constitutional prohibition on nuclear weapons and offer to finance a permanent US military base has triggered a sharp warning from Moscow, exposing the growing risks of military escalation along NATO’s eastern flank.
The Kremlin said the moves represented a significant deterioration in the security environment around Russia, as Vilnius seeks deeper American military involvement to deter potential aggression.
Dmitry Peskov, Vladimir Putin’s spokesman, warned that Moscow would be “forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security” if NATO military capabilities continued to expand close to Russian territory.
“A build-up of NATO forces on Russia’s doorstep cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighbouring country cannot,” Peskov said.
“This marks yet another significant escalation of tensions.”
The confrontation centres on two developments in Lithuania. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has confirmed that Vilnius is prepared to fund a dedicated American military facility, shortly after Donald Trump said Washington would “certainly look” at establishing a permanent US presence in the Baltic state.
Read more related news:
Lithuania’s parliament has also advanced a constitutional amendment that would remove the country’s longstanding prohibition on hosting weapons of mass destruction. A final vote is scheduled for January.
If approved, the change would remove a legal barrier to the possible deployment of NATO nuclear weapons on Lithuanian territory, although no decision has been announced to station US nuclear weapons there.
The geographic implications are nevertheless stark. Lithuania borders Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave and sits alongside Belarus, Moscow’s closest military ally in the region.
Lithuania does not possess its own nuclear arsenal. Several European NATO members already participate in arrangements under which US nuclear weapons are stationed on their territory while remaining under American control.
For Vilnius, the issue is less about acquiring nuclear weapons than strengthening deterrence.
Around 1,000 US troops are already stationed in Lithuania on a rotational basis, alongside American Abrams tanks and other armoured forces. Germany is also preparing to establish a permanent brigade of about 5,000 troops in the country by the end of next year.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas welcomed Trump’s comments on a permanent American presence, saying they showed the US president “knows Lithuania, knows our investments, knows our determination to build security and appreciates it.”
Lithuania has increasingly positioned itself as one of Europe’s most heavily armed frontline states. Defence spending is expected to reach 5.38 per cent of gross domestic product this year, reflecting the perceived threat from Russia and the country’s proximity to Kaliningrad and Belarus.
The military build-up comes against an increasingly volatile backdrop. The Baltic region has experienced a series of airspace incidents, including a drone crossing from Belarus that was shot down by Italian fighter jets and reported incursions by Russian aircraft.
The latest dispute also follows a warning from Putin over Kaliningrad. Russian officials have threatened to deploy nuclear weapons if NATO attempts to attack or blockade the Russian exclave, an isolated but heavily militarised territory between Poland and Lithuania.
Russian officials in London have separately warned against British media simulations of a potential Baltic conflict, telling those contemplating action against Kaliningrad to “have no illusions about the consequences.”
The danger is not that Lithuania’s constitutional change automatically produces a nuclear deployment. It is that each side increasingly interprets the other’s defensive preparations as evidence of offensive intent.
That dynamic is reshaping the Baltic security environment: more troops produce demands for more deterrence, which prompts Moscow to threaten countermeasures, which in turn strengthens the argument for further NATO reinforcement.
For Europe, the central risk is that this cycle continues without either side deliberately choosing a wider confrontation.
But with American forces, German troops and potentially a new legal framework for nuclear weapons converging on a state bordering Russia’s most militarised Baltic territory, the margin for miscalculation is becoming increasingly narrow.

articles.title: Why Europe Must Fund Ukraine Now: War Could Stretch to 2028 as Kyiv Faces $32B Gap in 2027 - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: Why Europe Must Fund Ukraine Now: War Could Stretch to 2028 as Kyiv Faces $32B Gap in 2027  Kyiv Post
articles.full_text:
Reviewing the Ukraine war watchers I think there had been a general assumption, or fear, that after the State Duma elections in Russia, last month, that Putin would launch a new mobilization campaign as a prelude to yet another big offensive in Donbas. The consensus was also that this would be pretty futile – just providing more bodies to the Russian meat grinder, which has been running at tens of thousands of Russian casualties per month for much of 2026.
Actually Putin appears to have held back from the mobilization track – perhaps fearful of the domestic political consequences of the war being brought home to the elites of Moscow and St Petersburg, finally losing their sons, brothers, uncles and fathers to this futile war to massage Putin’s ego.
Instead, Russia appears to have been pushed back along the front lines: September was the first month since Ukraine’s ill-fated counteroffensive in autumn 2023 that Russia suffered a net loss of territory in Ukraine.
Putin seems to have changed strategy to one of being content to maintain the frontlines in Donbas, while moving to an all-out campaign against the Ukrainian economy.
Herein we have seen a step up in Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian industrial assets, energy infrastructure, transport, retail and logical hubs and supply chains.
We have seen attacks on Ukraine’s steel industry - with five blast furnaces taken out of service and rendering its once export leading steel industry dormant.
There have been attacks on key bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv – again to sap moral but also to undermine the functioning of the capital’s economy.
And in the Black Sea, Russia has spurned efforts by Turkiye, the US, et al to agree a ceasefire covering grains, and Ukrainian grain exports have slowed to a trickle.
A similar ceasefire effort to cover energy assets has also been rejected by Russia. The aim seems to be to wear down Ukraine’s economy, erode its military industrial capability and sap the moral of Ukrainians.
I think the aim is also to push the economy into recession, create large budget and balance of payments shortfalls which will impose larger funding asks on Europe at a time when public finances are already under strain across the continent and playing out in market worries about the sustainability of public finances in France, the UK, et al.
I think there have been opportunities for a serious peace process, and a peace under the Trump presidency. But Trump has so mismanaged this process, that he has given heart to Putin that under Trump’s leadership the NATO alliance will fracture, and with that its willingness to support Ukraine.
And in Trump’s backing for far-right parties in Europe - the AfD in Germany, FN in France, and Reform in the UK, I think he has presented light at the end of the tunnel for Putin, that elections will inevitably usher in new governments in Europe which will pull the plug on European funding for Ukraine.
Key I think in this respect are French elections in May where I think Putin thinks a victory by Le Pen will see not only French support to Ukraine ended but a spanner put in the works of EU funding and support for Ukraine.
So I think Putin now sees advantage in fighting on and through the winter to get to next May and the prospect then of a collapse in European support for Ukraine. And thru the winter the strategy is to maximize destruction on Ukraine to increase the bill on Europe for supporting Ukraine.
All this just seems obvious to seasoned Ukraine watchers like me (40-year track record there) – it is possible to read Putin, and unfortunately Trump, like a book.
Putin is not difficult to read. He is a bully, a Russian style mafia like character forged from his KGB background. He respects strength and power and pushes on when he sees weakness. In Europe and in Trump he sees weakness and a lack of leadership.
Trump has imposed few costs on Putin, or Russia, for the war in Ukraine. Rather Trump seems to suggest he wants to reward Putin for his land grab in Ukraine, by his show of strength by trying to get US – Russia business back to normal.
Putin sees no penalty or sanction in continuing to test NATO borders in Europe through cyberattacks, attacks on NATO munition dumps, assassination attempts on European industrialists, drone forays against targets in Europe, and lately by attacks on shipping in NATO members waters.
Each effort that Putin gets away with just reveals the weakness of NATO, its lack of a response, and the lack of assurance on the US backstop. So he will continue.
And by heightening fears of Russia in Europe, he will hope to gift his far-right allies in Europe electoral ammunition as they will offer their electorates the offer of appeasement with Russia to secure a peace. Or that’s what they think they will achieve. But knowing Putin he will take whatever gifts are offered by the AfD, RN, and Reform and ask, and take more.
Leadership is needed in Europe but is in short supply.
On the Ukraine financing piste, the war is costing Ukraine more, and the war looks set to extend longer into 2028. This means that the €90 billion EU USL agreed at the EU Council meeting in December 2025 is not enough.
Ukraine has spoken about a $27 billion military financing gap in 2026, and a $32 billion financing gap in 2027, and that’s even without thinking of the tens of billions of extra funds needed if the war extends to 2028.
The right approach for Europe is to get ahead of the game, and the risks from French elections. To insulate Ukraine’s financing from those elections with potentially new facilities, and even finally tapping the $300 billion in immobilized CBR assets in Western jurisdictions.
But when leadership and vision is required from European leaders, we are seeing dithering and penny, or Euro cent pinching.
And the argument to our taxpayers should be that a $100 billion investment in Ukraine’s defense, to stop Russia, could save 1-2% per year in European defense spending over the longer term, that’s potentially a €250-500 billion saving per year.
It all looks a no brainier. But Europe so often has no brains, and invariably only acts when actually hit by crisis – in this case it would be a Russian victory in Ukraine.
Imagine that, it would mean tens of millions of Ukrainians moving West, straining the social, economic and political fabric of Europe and Russia moving further up on NATO’s borders but augmented by the capture of Ukraine’s substantive military capability. Europe would be facing the combined military capabilities of Russia, and subsumed Ukraine, and without a US backstop.
That would be a simply disastrous scenario for Europe – hence the cheapest option is to fund Ukraine NOW.

articles.title: McEntee 'very clear' increase in defence spending will not lead to NATO membership - Newstalk
articles.summary: McEntee 'very clear' increase in defence spending will not lead to NATO membership  Newstalk
articles.full_text:
Despite increasing the budget for the Defence Forces, the Government remains “very clear” that Ireland will not join a European military alliance, Helen McEntee has said.
In Budget 2027, the Department of Defence was allocated just over €1.6 billion, which Minister McEntee described as “the largest budget” in recent history, adding that this year’s “significant increase” follows a large one in Budget 2026.
Defence spending now represents 0.2% of GDP - which is still one of the lowest figures on the European continent.
“Our investment in key things like our radar programme, helicopters and equipment that our defence forces need [has increased] by about 13%,” Minister McEntee told Newstalk Breakfast.
“We've increased our current spending - which is not related to pay; we've increased that by about 15.5%.
“And then we've increased our pay by about 6.9%, so that brings us to the 10.5%.”
Members of the NATO military alliance have committed to spending 3.5% of their GDP on defence by 2035; with a further 1.5% earmarked for the protection of critical infrastructure and civilian preparedness for war.
However, Minister McEntee said Ireland does not have an overall target for defence spending in mind.
“What we've said is we want to continue to increase significantly our investment in the number of defence force personnel,” she said.
“And we've set a target of 11,500 and this is through a review that was done a couple of years ago.
“So, we did the Commission on the Defence Forces; it set out how many we should have, what type of capabilities, how we need to change and adapt to the types of changing security environment that we're in now.
“And that's exactly what we're doing.”
When questioned whether this means Ireland is inching towards joining a broader European military alliance, Minister McEntee replied “no” and said that remains the “very clear position” of the Government.
“When we talk about our neutrality, we're very clear we're not going to join,” she said.
“I don't think we should a military alliance, but that doesn't mean we don't talk to other people.
“People talk about wars and conflicts and we're going to be sending people off to Ukraine and we're going to be sending people off everywhere else.
“When you think of people's security and safety, it comes in many different forms - so, our economic security is extremely important.”
View this post on Instagram
In her State of the Union address to the European Parliament last month, Ursula von der Leyen warned that Europe should be “under no illusions” about the threat posed by Russia to member states.
“Hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats,” she said.
“Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions, they are ramping up every day.
“So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness.”
The Commission President has proposed a new Emergency Security Protocol, which member states could trigger if under threat.
Main image: Helen McEntee at Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, Dublin. Picture by: Eamonn Farrell/RollingNews.ie.

articles.title: Case Study: Apollo implements new EUDR compliance technology - European Rubber Journal
articles.summary: Case Study: Apollo implements new EUDR compliance technology  European Rubber Journal
articles.full_text:
"Implementation strengthens our ability to establish end-to-end visibility from source to finished product” 
Gurugram, India – Apollo Tyres has partnered with Emertech Innovations to establish an integrated compliance and traceability system for its natural rubber (NR) supply-chain under the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
The implementation covers 56,491 source plots spanning around 150,000 hectares across India and several international sourcing markets, according to an Emertech case-study published 5 Oct.
The plot data, said the technology partner, comprises 43,932 point-based plots and 12,559 polygon-based plots within Apollo's NR supplier network.
The process involves five stages – engage; validate; assess; trace and file – each building on the one before, with an administrative portal that gives Apollo’s teams one view across all of them.
Under the system, NR suppliers submit GeoJSON files, sourcing information, risk evidence and supporting documents through a dedicated supplier portal.
The platform checks submissions for file structure, coordinates, geometry and mandatory plot information, as well as the correct use of points or polygons.
Using a satellite-based deforestation analysis tool, Emertech examines land within the submitted plot boundaries, comparing historical satellite imagery with current forest-cover and land-use information.
The analysis, it said, assesses evidence of changes after the EUDR regulatory cut-off date of 31 Dec 2020 and assigns a risk result to each plot.
The system also flags potentially risky plots which will be “held for review” before being allowed into the compliant supply-chain.
Emertech has “integrated” the compliance platform with Apollo's existing ERP and operational systems, allowing validated supplier and plot information to be linked to all supply-chain documents.
These include purchase-orders, incoming consignment notes, goods receipts, material and batch records, production transactions, finished products and export shipments.
As described by Emertech, the process maintains the connection “from the land where the NR originated to the product eventually placed on the European market.”
For EU-bound shipments, the system consolidates the applicable source-plot information and prepares the relevant due diligence statement.
Furthermore, the platform is integrated with the EU Information System within the TRACES NT environment, allowing statements to be filed directly with the EU system.
Submission status and reference numbers are subsequently returned to Apollo's central “administrative portal,” which provides “one view across every stage for compliance, procurement and operational teams.”
The portal also maintains a record linking all declarations with the suppliers, source plots, risk evidence, production records and shipment concerned.
“EUDR requires a high degree of transparency and traceability across the NR supply chain,” said Shibu George, group head, advanced manufacturing & enterprise application, at Apollo Tyres.
The collaboration with Emertech, he added, had enabled Apollo to bring together “sourcing, traceability and geospatial validation capabilities at scale,” covering a significant NR sourcing footprint.
“This implementation strengthens our ability to establish end-to-end visibility from source to finished product,” concluded George.

articles.title: Commissioner Kos: EU enlargement now possible, in our interest, but issues need to be resolved - Interfax-Ukraine
articles.summary: Commissioner Kos: EU enlargement now possible, in our interest, but issues need to be resolved  Interfax-Ukraine
articles.full_text:
Facts
Commissioner Kos: EU enlargement now possible, in our interest, but issues need to be resolved
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that enlargement of the European Union was a long-term investment in peace, security and prosperity in Europe and was possible today, although certain issues still needed to be resolved.
She made the remarks on Tuesday in Strasbourg at a press conference where she presented a package of documents adopted by the European Commission concerning the European Union's preparations for future enlargement.
Kos said enlargement was in the EU's interest, as it was about protecting its interests and upholding its values. She said a larger Union represented a long-term investment in Europe's peace, security and prosperity, which was one of the reasons the European Union had been created. Enlargement also offered an opportunity to make Europe stronger, as a larger Union would increase its political and economic influence in a world marked by intense geopolitical competition.
According to Kos, enlargement would also bring tangible benefits to EU citizens by strengthening democracy, security and solidarity. She said it would benefit the European economy by strengthening the single market, creating more jobs and opening up more opportunities for people and businesses. She added that the package focused on what both candidate countries and EU member states needed to do to take the next steps in the enlargement process.
The commissioner outlined five groups of proposed measures. She said the first concerned practical solutions related to governance, the rule of law and policies. According to Kos, the EU could optimise the use of so-called passerelle clauses and expand the use of qualified majority voting where permitted by the treaties.
In particular, she said the proposal envisaged reducing the number of areas in which a single country could veto decisions supported by all other member states. She said this could apply, for example, to sanctions, the fight against tax fraud and the accession process, specifically the intermediate stages between the opening and closing of negotiations.
Kos said the second point concerned a more ambitious approach to gradual integration. She recalled that several months earlier the Commission had proposed possible changes to the enlargement methodology and presented three options: maintaining the status quo, enhanced gradual integration and a reverse membership model. She said member states had indicated that they did not support the reverse membership concept.
The commissioner said the current proposals on gradual integration were directly linked to that discussion and were aimed at substantially expanding opportunities to integrate candidate countries into specific areas of EU activity even before they obtained full membership.
At the same time, Kos stressed that gradual integration was not intended to replace full membership but rather to serve as a catalyst for the enlargement process. She said it would require two key components: progress on reforms by candidate countries and strategic alignment of positions, which she described as the novel element of the approach.
She said that once candidate countries met the required standards, they should be able to participate in strategic areas where cooperation brought mutual benefits to both current and future member states, including energy, transport, artificial intelligence, security and defence.
Kos identified the third point as the establishment of a common framework for accession and safeguards for the entire future enlargement process. She said countries seeking to join the EU had to meet very high rule-of-law standards and that the Union needed to be certain they would not deviate from those standards after accession, taking into account previous experience.
She said possible safeguard mechanisms included simplifying procedures for suspending financial support or restricting voting rights. She added that mechanisms were also being proposed to prevent new member states from blocking decisions on future enlargement because of bilateral disputes, describing this as another new element.
Kos identified the impact of accession on EU policies as the fourth point. She said the Commission's analysis showed that the EU was already prepared for enlargement in most policy areas, although certain sectors would require adjustments.
She said Ukraine's membership should not have a negative impact on EU farmers and that the Commission intended to support Ukraine in restoring access to its traditional export markets in third countries.
Kos said the fifth and final point concerned roadmaps for the four candidate countries that had made the greatest progress: Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.
She said the Commission planned to present indicative roadmaps for those countries in the enlargement reports due to be published on October 28. According to Kos, the aim was to help them maintain the pace of reforms, while the roadmaps would set out the next steps, preliminary timelines and clear expected outcomes, thereby increasing predictability in the accession process.
The commissioner stressed that no simplified procedures or shortcuts were envisaged.
The next step will be discussion of the proposed package in the European Parliament and the European Council.
Kos said the Commission's position was clear that EU enlargement was possible today, while acknowledging that a number of challenges still needed to be addressed.
She said one such challenge was the need to optimise EU institutions and ensure a more flexible and effective decision-making process. With regard to the rule of law and the principle of sincere cooperation, she said the Commission was proposing tools that would allow the EU to respond more decisively to serious violations, including by reducing funding or restricting voting rights.
On agriculture, Kos said the Commission proposed considering special mechanisms for Ukraine.
She added that the proposals would now be discussed with EU member states and that steps would be taken to ensure that an enlarged European Union would also become a stronger Union capable of determining its own future.

articles.title: Will the UK impose tariffs on Chinese EVs? Beijing signals possible response - Business Upturn
articles.summary: Will the UK impose tariffs on Chinese EVs? Beijing signals possible response  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
China will monitor the United Kingdom’s moves on tariffs targeting Chinese electric vehicles and respond accordingly, as London considers whether to introduce new trade measures against Chinese-made EVs. The issue has emerged amid growing concerns in Britain and other major economies over Chinese industrial capacity, government support and the competitive pressure facing domestic automakers.
Beijing’s position comes as the UK weighs possible tariffs on Chinese electric cars. British officials have been consulting industry representatives over potential measures, but the UK has not yet formally imposed a new China-specific tariff on electric vehicles. Any decision would therefore represent a shift in Britain’s current trade approach toward Chinese EV imports.
China has increasingly objected to what it regards as protectionist restrictions on its electric-vehicle exports. Its Commerce Ministry has previously said measures restricting Chinese EVs should comply with World Trade Organization rules and has opposed what it considers discriminatory trade barriers.
In January, China’s Commerce Ministry said Beijing and the European Union had made progress in consultations over the EU’s anti-subsidy case concerning Chinese battery-electric vehicles. The ministry said both sides had agreed that Chinese exporters could pursue price commitments as a way of addressing European concerns within the WTO framework.
China has also taken steps to regulate its own electric-vehicle exports. Since January 1, 2026, China has required export licences for pure-electric passenger vehicles, under rules introduced by the Commerce Ministry, Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, General Administration of Customs and State Administration for Market Regulation. Beijing said the system was intended to promote the healthy development of new-energy vehicle trade and regulate export activity.
The UK’s position is complicated by its broader industrial policy. London has been reviewing its zero-emission vehicle strategy while seeking to support domestic manufacturing and investment. The government said in August that more than one in four new cars sold in Britain were electric and that EV sales had risen 45% year-on-year in July. It also launched a review of the pathway toward its target for all new cars and vans to be zero-emission by 2035.
The potential tariff debate reflects a wider global argument over the competitivenes

articles.title: France debt crisis: why rising bond yields are raising fears of another euro crisis - Invezz
articles.summary: France debt crisis: why rising bond yields are raising fears of another euro crisis  Invezz
articles.full_text:
powered by
Long EURUSD via a tactical “ECB caps yields” bet: the article flags a likely ECB response if sovereign stress threatens the euro’s survival, and experts warn euro could slide toward $1.10. If the ECB pauses QT/reinvests flexibly or signals intervention, the euro should rebound as funding stress eases and rate expectations stabilize. Key risk: ECB stays hawkish (or inflation forces tightening) and doesn’t cap yields, so EUR keeps sliding despite any temporary bond-market relief.
Key Risk: ECB refuses to cap yields and stays hawkish, keeping EUR under pressure.
Buy German Bunds / sell French government bonds: the France–Germany 10Y spread is at the highest since 2012 and is still widening (0.55% mid-Sept → 1.45% now). The thesis is that fiscal credibility is breaking (missed targets, election risk, rising pension/defence/green costs) while 2027 issuance (€340bn) forces more supply into a market demanding higher risk premia. Key risk: France delivers credible, enforceable fiscal tightening fast enough to stop spread widening (credible political path post-election or ECB yield-capping that directly compresses French yields).
Key Risk: France regains fiscal credibility quickly enough to stop the France–Germany yield spread from widening.
- France's 10-year borrowing costs hit 5%, debt reached 119% of GDP.
- Paris aims to cut its deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027.
- Bond yields rise in Italy and Greece as ECB faces inflation-stability trade-off.
France was once viewed as one of Europe’s safest sovereign borrowers, with its bonds carrying little more risk than Germany’s.
That confidence is now being eroded as investors demand a growing premium to finance the country’s mounting debt.
French 10-year borrowing costs rose to 5% last week, their highest level since July 2002.
The premium investors demand to hold French government bonds rather than German debt has also climbed to its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011-2012.
For years, the premium on 10-year French bonds over German debt measured in mere basis points.
That spread has widened sharply, rising from 0.55 percentage points in mid-September to 1.45 points by Monday morning — its highest level since the 2012 eurozone debt crisis.
The selloff has begun spilling into other markets.
The euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on Monday, while borrowing costs in other heavily indebted European economies, including Italy, Belgium and Greece, have also started to rise.
At the heart of the problem is France's deteriorating fiscal position.
The government is spending substantially more than it collects in taxes, leaving it dependent on borrowing to finance the gap.
France's debt problem reaches a critical point
France's budget deficit is expected to reach 5.4% of GDP this year, far above the European Union's 3% limit.
The country has not balanced its budget in more than three decades and has failed to meet the EU deficit target since 2019.
Structural pressures have made the problem increasingly difficult to reverse.
An expensive pension system, rising defence spending and the costs of the green transition have all placed additional demands on government finances.
French public debt reached €3.6 trillion in the second quarter of 2026, equivalent to 119% of GDP, according to the national statistics agency INSEE.
That compares with 115.6% a year earlier.
The pressures were already mounting before the war in Iran.
The conflict has added to the strain by pushing up energy costs and weighing on economic growth.
The growing concern among investors is not simply that France has accumulated a large debt burden, but that its political system may make it increasingly difficult to implement the spending cuts and tax increases needed to stabilise it.
France faces a presidential election, while a hung parliament has made governing more difficult.
Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party is also gaining ground, potentially making politically unpopular fiscal consolidation even harder.
Paris offers a deficit-cutting plan but markets unconvinced
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's minority government presented its draft 2027 budget last Thursday, seeking to reassure markets that France can bring its finances under control.
The plan calls for roughly €54 billion in spending reductions and additional revenue and targets a deficit of 5% of GDP next year, compared with 5.4% in 2026.
About two-thirds of the adjustment would come from spending restraint, while the remainder would be raised through higher taxes and contributions.
The government has proposed around €6 billion of savings each from pensions and healthcare.
Government spending excluding interest payments and defence would also be frozen in cash terms, effectively squeezing budgets as prices continue to rise.
But investors remain unconvinced that the government can deliver the promised savings, particularly with elections approaching.
"It just seems to me like the market is rejecting this 2027 budget. There's an election coming up ... who's going to vote for fiscal austerity with elections coming up?" said Erik Bregar, director of FX and precious metals risk management at Silver Gold Bull in Toronto in a Reuters report.
Stéphane Colliac, an economist at BNP Paribas, noted that France had already missed its budget targets in three of the four years between 2023 and 2026.
The scale of the adjustment required is also growing.
With interest payments and defence spending both increasing, Colliac estimates that the government needs to find savings equivalent to about 1% of GDP simply to reduce the deficit by 0.4 percentage points.
More borrowing is coming
France's fiscal challenge is compounded by the amount of debt it must issue.
The French Treasury plans to sell €340 billion of debt in 2027, €20 billion more than this year, as pandemic-era borrowing comes due.
That increase means France will need to find substantial demand for its bonds at a time when investors are already demanding higher yields.
Even if the government's plans are fully implemented, Colliac expects French debt to rise to 121% of GDP in 2027 and eventually stabilise at around 124% in 2032.
That trajectory has intensified concerns about debt sustainability.
Higher yields mean the government must devote an increasing share of its budget to interest payments, leaving less room for public investment and other spending.
Interest payments are expected to rise from €79.2 billion in 2026 to €91.2 billion in 2027 under the government’s budget projections.
The dynamic can become self-reinforcing: larger debt increases borrowing costs, higher borrowing costs increase interest payments, and higher interest payments make it harder to bring down the deficit.
Fears of a wider European contagion
For now, France remains the biggest source of concern.
But markets are increasingly signalling that the problem may not remain confined to Paris.
Italian and Greek spreads over German Bunds widened by almost 15 basis points during the recent French turmoil, according to ING strategists Michiel Tukker and Benjamin Schroeder.
“Debt dynamics are no longer deemed only a French problem,” they wrote.
The move is significant because German government bonds are generally treated as the benchmark for eurozone sovereign debt.
When investors demand a greater premium from other governments, it signals a reassessment of the risk attached to their finances.
"Government bond yields in France are spiralling out of control. Contagion to the rest of high-debt Europe is unfolding rapidly," wrote Robin J Brooks, former chief economist at the IIF and former chief FX strategist at Goldman Sachs.
Currency markets are reflecting those concerns.
Experts warn that mounting French fiscal concerns could push the euro towards $1.10.
ECB faces a difficult choice
The deteriorating bond market presents the European Central Bank with an uncomfortable policy dilemma.
The ECB must balance concerns over inflation against the risk that rising sovereign yields could destabilise financial markets and further weaken the euro.
Eurozone inflation rose to 3.8% in September, strengthening the case for tighter monetary policy.
At the same time, the selloff in government bonds has increased calls for the central bank to pause its quantitative tightening programme or intervene if market stress becomes severe.
"There can be absolutely no suspense on how this ends. The ECB will intervene to cap yields. It’ll do so because it thinks sovereign debt defaults are an existential threat to the Euro and therefore its own survival," Brooks wrote.
ING global head of macro research Carsten Brzeski said the ECB could “pause quantitative tightening temporarily and reinvest maturing bonds in its portfolio ‘flexibly,’ sending a positive signal to bond markets.”
The idea was also raised in an opinion article by Lorenzo Bini Smaghi, a former ECB board member.
French far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has separately called for the ECB to put part of government debt “in the freezer.”
But intervention would carry its own risks.
A central bank response could ease pressure on bond markets while potentially weakening the ECB's credibility at a time when inflation remains above target.
Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist at Oxford Economics, said the ECB needs to act carefully.
"Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he told DW.
Amaro expects policymakers to continue monitoring developments in the euro-dollar exchange rate but stop short of trying to influence the currency market for now.
A leadership change at the ECB is also approaching, potentially complicating the central bank's response and raising the threshold for intervention.
2012 fears return, but not everyone is convinced
The market turmoil has revived memories of the sovereign debt crisis that threatened the survival of the eurozone roughly 15 years ago.
But some i

articles.title: Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze - The Guardian
articles.summary: Naval drone hits oil tanker off Russian resort city Sochi, triggering massive blaze  The GuardianShip ablaze near Sochi, huge plume of smoke rising over sea – photos  Українська правдаRussia says tanker crew rescued in Black Sea after attack set ship ablaze  ReutersTanker Catches Fire, Spills Oil off Russian Resort Town of Sochi  The Maritime ExecutiveUkraine Drone Attack Sets Fire On Oil Tanker With 23 Indian Crew Members  NDTV
articles.full_text:
An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said.
The transport ministry said a Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked and that “crude oil is burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”.
“Firefighting efforts will begin once the fire’s intensity has subsided and rescue vessels can safely approach the tanker,” the ministry said.
A crew of 23 – all Indian citizens – had been rescued, it added.
Russia and Ukraine have targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since the conflict began, and Russia has recently attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.
There was no comment from Kyiv on the attack.
Videos and photos circulated on social media from Sochi – a popular Black Sea resort city of almost 500,000 people – showed bright orange flames out at sea and a thick column of black smoke billowing into the sky.
Local officials restricted access to the coast and beaches.
Elsewhere on Tuesday, Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
Bulgarian authorities said that the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev condemned the attack.
After an emergency government meeting, Radev said: “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law.”
Sea and aerial drones attacked the ships about 80 miles (128km) off Bulgaria’s coast, he said.
Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that a “massive strike” from Russia was likely to come, and in the early hours of Wednesday Kyiv was attacked.
Russian strikes damaged buildings and warehouses across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram.
Agence France-Presse reported multiple explosions in Kyiv, and Reuters reported two people were killed by Russian strikes.
A separate Russian strike on Ukraine’s south-eastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, officials said, without giving details.
Kyiv has been under increased attack as winter approaches, with Russian airstrikes targeting energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro river. Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly day and night, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse
