articles.title: Amazon’s $3.9B UK Clean Energy Bet Pushes Renewable Portfolio Past 1 GW - CarbonCredits.com
articles.summary: Amazon’s $3.9B UK Clean Energy Bet Pushes Renewable Portfolio Past 1 GW  CarbonCredits.com
articles.full_text:
Amazon is expanding its renewable energy footprint in the UK as demand for low-carbon electricity grows across the economy. The company has now signed a new Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Statkraft for the 36-megawatt (MW) Mossy Hill wind farm near Lerwick in Scotland’s Shetland Islands. The project is expected to become operational in November 2030.
The deal adds to more than £3 billion (about US$3.9 billion) that Amazon says it invested in low-carbon technologies across the UK between 2021 and 2025. Its UK portfolio now spans more than 50 carbon-free energy projects with combined capacity of over 1 gigawatt (GW) once fully operational.
The investment comes as clean energy spending accelerates globally. The International Energy Agency (IEA) predicts global energy investment will hit $3.4 trillion by 2026. Of this, around $2.2 trillion will focus on clean energy technologies, grids, storage, nuclear, efficiency, and electrification.
Amazon’s UK Renewable Portfolio Passes 1 GW
The Mossy Hill agreement is Amazon’s latest addition to a rapidly growing UK portfolio.
The company has signed PPAs and developed renewable energy projects across England and Scotland. Its portfolio includes nine off-site wind and solar farms and 41 on-site solar installations at Amazon facilities. Once they start, the projects will produce over 1 GW of carbon-free energy. This is enough to power more than 1.3 million UK homes each year.
The earlier Chirmorie Wind Farm agreement in South Ayrshire was particularly significant. Its 90 MW project represented what Amazon described as the UK’s largest-ever onshore wind PPA at the time.
Mossy Hill adds another 36 MW to the pipeline. Together, these projects give Amazon a large, long-term position in Britain’s renewable power market while supporting new generation capacity for the wider grid.
John Boumphrey, Amazon UK and Ireland Country Manager, said:
“Our latest project in the Shetland Islands builds on years of investment in renewable energy across the UK… Last year we announced our plan to invest £40bn (US$53bn) in the UK by 2027 and the transition to a lower-carbon economy is a part of how we’re putting that commitment to work.”
The $3.9 Billion Figure Covers More Than Wind Power
Amazon’s roughly $3.9 billion UK clean energy investment is broader than its renewable electricity portfolio. The company reports over £3 billion in low-carbon investments from 2021 to 2025. This funding supports technologies and projects that help the UK shift to a lower-carbon economy.
Frontier Economics conducted an independent analysis for Amazon. They estimate that the investment supported 34,000 jobs and added up to £2 billion in gross value to the UK economy.
Amazon has also committed to invest £40 billion in the UK between 2025 and 2027. That broader investment includes new fulfillment centers, logistics infrastructure, cloud and AI capacity, transportation and other facilities.
Clean energy is therefore one part of a much larger expansion. The company claims its renewable projects can boost UK energy security. They add to local electricity generation and cut reliance on imported fuels.
Why Amazon Is Locking In Long-Term Renewable Power
Amazon’s renewable strategy relies heavily on PPAs. Under these agreements, the e-commerce giant commits to buying electricity from a renewable project for a specified period.
Such contracts can provide developers with predictable revenue and help them secure financing for new projects. This model has allowed large corporations to become major sources of demand for new renewable capacity.
Amazon says it has helped projects reach deployment by acting as an anchor offtaker. Its UK portfolio therefore does more than match electricity consumption. It can also support the construction of new generation capacity.
The strategy is becoming more relevant as electricity demand rises. The IEA expects global electricity investment to hit nearly $1.6 trillion by 2026. With end-use electrification added, it could rise to around $2 trillion. Grid investment alone could approach $550 billion, up nearly 20% year over year.
Renewable projects backed by long-term corporate demand can therefore play a growing role in meeting future electricity needs.
Amazon Has Already Matched 100% of Its Electricity
The renewable projects also support Amazon’s global climate strategy. Amazon reached its goal of using 100% renewable energy for its global operations in 2025. This is five years sooner than the original target of 2030. It achieved the same level for the third consecutive year.
Its carbon-free energy portfolio includes over 700 projects worldwide. This totals more than 42 GW of capacity in 30 countries, based on its 2025 sustainability report.
The company co-founded The Climate Pledge in 2019 and remains committed to achieving net-zero carbon emissions across its global operations by 2040. However, matching electricity consumption with renewable energy does not mean Amazon’s overall emissions have already fallen.
Amazon’s 2025 sustainability report reveals that its absolute carbon emissions rose 16% from 2024. However, carbon intensity dropped 38% from the 2019 baseline. Revenue increased 156% over the same period. That distinction is important as Amazon continues to expand.
AWS and AI Are Driving Amazon’s Power Needs
Amazon’s renewable energy strategy is also tied to the rapid expansion of AWS. It claims that AWS infrastructure added more data center capacity in 2025 than any other company worldwide. Data centers need a lot of reliable electricity to operate effectively.
At the same time, Amazon is working to improve energy efficiency. Its data centers recorded an average Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.14 in 2025, compared with an industry average of 1.25 cited by the company. Amazon also says its data centers are seven times more water-efficient than the industry average.
Globally, data center electricity demand is becoming a major driver of power investment. This makes securing additional low-carbon electricity increasingly important for technology companies.
Amazon is also investing beyond wind and solar. Its broader energy strategy includes advanced nuclear, geothermal, and long-duration energy storage. The goal is to provide cleaner electricity while also improving the reliability of power supplies.
Renewable Power Has Not Yet Stopped Emissions Growth
Amazon’s renewable investments are significant, but the company’s overall decarbonization challenge remains large. Its business continues to expand across e-commerce, transportation, and cloud computing.
The company’s 2025 sustainability report says it delivered 2.4 billion packages using electric vehicles during the year and operated more than 52,700 electric delivery vans globally. It is targeting 100,000 electric delivery vehicles by 2030.
- Amazon also reduced carbon emissions per shipped unit by 7% in 2025.
However, its absolute emissions increased as its operations grew. The company needs ongoing investment in electricity, transportation, buildings, packaging, and its supply chain to hit its 2040 target. This is where renewable energy can have a larger role.
Amazon Is Turning Renewable Power Into Infrastructure Strategy
Amazon’s latest UK wind agreement shows how corporate renewable energy buying is moving beyond a simple sustainability initiative. The 36 MW Mossy Hill project adds to more than 50 UK carbon-free energy projects and takes Amazon’s planned UK portfolio beyond 1 GW of capacity.
At the same time, the global energy market is moving in the same direction. The IEA expects $2.2 trillion to flow into clean energy areas in 2026, nearly twice the investment expected for fossil fuels.
For Amazon, the UK strategy provides long-term access to carbon-free electricity while supporting new renewable capacity. The challenge now is to keep that growth aligned with emissions reductions. Amazon has already matched 100% of its global electricity consumption with renewable energy, but its absolute carbon footprint increased in 2025.
The company’s ongoing investment in wind, solar, electric transport, efficient data centers, and new clean energy technologies will be key. This will determine if it can achieve net-zero emissions by 2040.

articles.title: At least 20 killed as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: At least 20 killed as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine  Al JazeeraChildren killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats  BBCUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment  The GuardianDeadly Russian strikes cut power in several Kyiv districts  Financial TimesRussia hits Ukraine with wave of attacks on Putin’s birthday  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
At least 20 people, including children, have been killed as Russia launched a barrage of drones and missiles across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Ukraine’s air force said on Wednesday that Russia launched 130 drones, 48 cruise missiles, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles in the overnight attack. It added air defence units downed 161 targets.
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, and Poltava in central Ukraine, the southeastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv in the northeast were the focus of the Russian attacks, authorities said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a social media post that Russia had fired 70 missiles and also drones in one of its biggest attacks since Moscow launched the war in 2022.
“One of the key targets was our energy infrastructure. The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” Zelenskyy said.
The attacks also damaged residential buildings, industrial facilities, and infrastructure, according to Ukrainian officials.
In Pryluki, in the northern Chernihiv region, a Russian missile slammed into a five-storey residential building, regional authorities said. At least 14 people, including four children, were killed and 50 others wounded, emergency services said.
Kyiv’s Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were killed in the densely populated Darnytskyi neighbourhood in a fire caused by an air attack.
Two people were killed when missiles hit high-rise buildings in Dnipro and Kremenchuk in central Ukraine, while two others died in Oleksandriya, Zelenskyy said.
‘Massive’ attack
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea-, and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.
Targets included sites where the company Fire Point makes and stores Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv, as well as in the regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava, and Kharkiv, it said.
The attacks also targeted port and ship-repair infrastructure in the Odesa region, as well as vessels it said were being used in the interests of Ukraine’s armed forces, the ministry added.
“Ukraine has once again been hit by Russian missiles throughout the night,” Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on Telegram.
“Another sleepless night, another act of terror, after which people still have to plan their working day despite everything,” he added.
Kyiv has come under relentless bombardment in recent weeks, with Russian air attacks on energy infrastructure, rail and road transport, including the bridges that connect the city over the Dnipro River.
Air raid sirens have sounded almost constantly, urging residents to take cover in basements, shelters and subway stations.
In a separate post, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces hit four Russian targets over the last 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions, as well as carrying out a response in the Black Sea.
He called the attacks a “just” response to Moscow’s strikes, and added that the facilities hit helped “Russia finance and wage its brutal war”.
Concerns over Black Sea navigation
As the war intensifies and expands, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has pressed Russian President Putin to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
A statement by the Turkish presidency said Erdogan reiterated his offer to help facilitate direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, saying that safe Black Sea access was important to Ankara.
The conversation between the Turkish and Russian leaders came after drones hit two commercial vessels early on Tuesday as attacks on Black Sea shipping increase amid an intensifying Russia-Ukraine war. One vessel caught fire, while the other sank.
Bulgarian authorities say they have ended search operations after confirming that no survivors were found from the ship that sank off the country’s coast.

articles.title: Ukraine’s secret operation is making Russia nervous – and reversing Putin’s gains - The i Paper
articles.summary: Ukraine’s secret operation is making Russia nervous – and reversing Putin’s gains  The i PaperUkraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push  The New York TimesThe War Room newsletter: Operation Vivaldi is wrong-footing Russia  The EconomistSilence, Delusion and Robots: Ukraine’s Eastern Advances  Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)Ukraine’s surprise robot offensive exposes a vulnerability in Putin’s war machine  CNBC
articles.full_text:
On an unremarkable day in May, in near-total secrecy, Ukraine quietly launched one of its most audacious fightbacks against Russia to date.
The first rumours came over summer. A few analysts and military bloggers noticed more movement than usual at a crucial point near Lyman, a city in Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Ukrainian forces seemed to be counter-attacking there, where over the past year, Russia had been making slow but steady gains.
Ukraine played it down as “limited in scope” and battlefield trackers logged little change in territory. But by the start of September, Russian milbloggers were nervous, describing a difficult situation on the front.
“It seems to me that the Ukrainians have been conducting a counteroffensive for 2.5 months, which our command is trying not to notice,” Anatoly Radov, a prominent pro-war commentator, said on 6 September.
It was only on 15 September that Ukraine finally acknowledged something large-scale had been taking place. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the 3rd Army Corps, announced that Ukrainian forces – under maximum operational secrecy – had been conducting a groundbreaking offensive called “Operation Vivaldi”.
“A devastating blow has been dealt to the combat effectiveness of the Russian 20th and 25th Armies,” Biletskyi said.
For months, Moscow had been pushing to encircle Ukraine’s fortress belt cities, including major targets Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, and in January its troops were at the outskirts of Lyman, a crucial logistics, road and rail hub. Its capture would have handed Moscow a staging base for an offensive against Sloviansk. Vivaldi has blunted the northern claw of that pincer movement.
“Vivaldi is critical for Ukraine’s war effort overall,” Mykola Bielieskov, a research fellow at the National Institute for Strategic Studies think-tank in Kyiv, told The i Paper.
The near-total secrecy of the offensive, not to mention its tactics
The Russian delusion factor
Under a media blackout, Ukraine has seized 147 square kilometres of territory during Operation Vivaldi, according to the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Ukraine’s real-time gains could be even higher. The announced advances are likely months-old and details are still being carefully controlled by Ukrainian officials. The ISW has said its own mapping methodology is “likely underestimating the extent of Ukrainian gains”.
It added that since March, Russia’s rate of seizing territory from
Ukraine’s information blackout appears to have played a major part in its success. “Often offensives are given away before they start, giving Russia time to move units around and get into a position to counter the advance. So, secrecy in the lead-up is really important,” said Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow in military science at the Royal United Services Institute. “In some cases, it has taken the Russians a while to realise that they were under attack or the scale of the advance.”
Biletskyi warned those watching events unfold not to
“Operational security is enormously important in warfare,” Scott Boston, a senior defence analyst at the Rand Corporation, told The i Paper. “The Russians in particular have a lot of reconnaissance capabilities, including drones, and the more they are fixated on Kostyantynivka or Kramatorsk or Dobropillia, the less they might be noticing and responding elsewhere where there’s
Bielieskov has claimed that maskirovka – a Soviet military doctrine of deception – helped Ukraine take advantage of poor communication within the Russian military.
“Russia has repeatedly shown an unwillingness to report bad news up the chain of command,” said Boston. “When that happens at multiple levels it really dilutes the effect of their potential advantages.”
The extent of that culture was demonstrated last month when Vladimir Putin claimed that Russia had captured the city of Svyatohirs’k, west of Lyman and far behind Ukrainian lines. Shortly afterwards, Biletskyi posted a video of himself in central
“I want to address the Russian military and military political leadership. Take off your clown noses and colourful wigs. Stop making fools of yourselves,” he said.
Russian military bloggers have shown their frustration over Moscow’s detachment from the reality on the ground. Radov published a recording – now deleted – which he said he sent to a Russian officer, asking: “Is there a guy among you – for f**k’s sake – who can tell Uncle Vova [Putin] that his picture isn’t actually all that pretty… we’re totally f**ked on the Lyman front.”
Tactics and technology are changing the game
During Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine has deployed innovative
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps said EW units had disrupted more than 20,000 Russian drone missions by detecting, jamming and suppressing their signals to conceal Ukrainian attacks.
“For a long time, Ukraine has been building up its EW capabilities, devolving them to the lowest echelons possible and connecting them to other systems as much as
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces have saturated Russian rear areas, using drones like the AI-enabled Hornet to enable 30-200-kilometre strikes against logistics, command posts, drone control centres and river crossings.
Ukraine has also sent in heavy bomber drones to air-drop ground robots equipped with grenade launchers miles behind Russian lines, and claims to have filled two Soviet-era armoured personnel carriers with explosives, converting them into giant robotic systems to slam into Russian positions.
“They have changed the game by developing a whole new approach that focuses on their
According to Bielieskov, Vivaldi has “proved that the same technology that led to stalemate in 2023-25” is useful for bringing more movement to the battlefield. “The trick is quality of training and leadership of officers,” he said.
What Vivaldi means for the war
Ukraine claims Russian losses, both dead and injured, across the three announced seasons have so far totaled 5,000, with hundreds taken prisoner. However, the latest offensive is unlikely to change the course of the war.
“In terms of the entire size of the occupied territories in Ukraine, it is fair to say this is a
By reversing months of Russian gains, Vivaldi also represents a setback for Putin’s war aims of seizing the Donbas.
“Oleksandrivka, Vivaldi and various others have successfully pushed Russian units back and frustrated some of their goals for the year,” said Cranny-Evans. However, he said it was important to balance this out. “Whilst it is good and encouraging to see Ukraine advancing, the Russians are still advancing in some areas, and their strikes against Ukraine’s power infrastructure and even its
Rose added that to alter the course of the war, “Ukraine will have to envision Vivaldi on a grander scale… only such a decisive Ukrainian battlefield victory will force Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian elites and the common Russian soldier to reappraise the war”.
Even so, as the Vivaldi offensive moves into its fourth season, Biletskyi warned that the “music continues”.

articles.title: EU Commission throws down the gauntlet to member states on reforming the bloc - Euronews.com
articles.summary: EU Commission throws down the gauntlet to member states on reforming the bloc  Euronews.com‘No more Viktor Orbán’: EU plans 15-year probation period for new member states  The GuardianPreparing for a wider European Union  European CommissionEU hopefuls fear new safeguard plans could create second-class members  Euronews.comEU enlargement: European Commission tables reforms to prepare bloc for new members  DW.com
articles.full_text:
The European Commission is proposing fewer commissioners and less unanimity to prepare the EU for 30 or more members. However, EU diplomats say capitals are unlikely to agree.
The European Commission has put forward far-reaching proposals, including cutting the number of commissioners and moving away from unanimity, testing member states' appetite for internal reforms that stop short of treaty change.
The proposals are part of a broader package to make the EU's structures and decision-making fit for a membership of 30 or more countries. They are bound to be controversial among European capitals.
"The main question has been: is the EU fit for another enlargement? And there is a clear yes, a future enlargement is possible. Our assessment shows that in most policy areas, the EU is already fit for enlargement," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told reporters.
Unanimity
The Commission proposes identifying areas where so-called passerelle clauses could be activated, allowing the Council to move from unanimity to qualified majority. Activating those clauses, however, itself requires unanimity.
The idea of extending qualified majority voting is not new, particularly in foreign and security policy, where a veto can undermine the EU's ability to project geopolitical weight abroad.
Last month, 11 countries including France and Germany circulated a joint letter calling for the bloc to explore curbing obstructive foreign policy vetoes on the basis of sincere cooperation, notably through greater use of constructive abstention.
Asked whether member states back the move, Kos acknowledged that positions differ widely among EU countries. "It will not be easy, but it is worth trying," she said. A specific area she identified where less unanimity could be used is precisely during accession processes.
"Our proposal is to make our decision-making process more effective. We suggest using more QMV [qualified majority voting], which is nothing new. What is new is that we are suggesting that we will reduce the number of unanimity decisions in the accession process," Kos said.
Unanimity is required to grant a country candidate status and to close negotiations. In between, however, the current methodology gives any member state a veto over 150 steps.
The Commission also wants to make more use of enhanced cooperation, which lets at least nine member states pursue deeper integration on matters of crucial or strategic interest where blockages persist.
The most recent examples are the Ukraine Support Loan, from which Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out, and the European Public Prosecutor's Office.
Here too, Brussels may meet resistance from some capitals, notably the so-called "Friends of the Western Balkans", a group that includes Italy and Austria. They have pushed back against differentiated membership and regulatory asymmetry.
Institutional changes
The Commission is also proposing to drop the principle that every EU country has a commissioner, which could prove problematic in a Union of 30 or more members.
Under the Lisbon Treaty, the Commission should have a number of members equal to two-thirds of the member states, chosen by "strictly equal rotation" that reflects the demographic and geographical range of all EU countries.
The system never took effect. In 2013, the European Council unanimously decided to keep one commissioner per member state, a concession to Ireland to secure a yes vote in its second referendum on the Lisbon Treaty.
Ireland was merely the most vocal opponent of losing a permanent presence in the Commission. Small member states widely fear their voice would be harder to hear in Brussels.
Rotation could also be hard to swallow for large countries such as France and Germany, which might find themselves left out of the College of Commissioners while the likes of Malta or Luxembourg are included.
"There are some candidates who say, no worries, this country can represent us. Other countries who say, yes, but not at the beginning. We would like to see how it [the Commission] works," Kos added.
The proposal for a leaner EU executive is well timed. The Commission is undergoing a so-called "large-scale review", and capitals are in intense talks on the bloc's next long-term budget, in which the EU administration is likely to face deep cuts.
Sceptical reception
Proposals that mainly affect candidate countries, such as safeguards against democratic backsliding and gradual integration, are likely to meet less resistance.
However, supporters of the reforms point out that, as candidates edge closer to joining the bloc, the question of how to keep an enlarged Union effective will be harder to dismiss.
Still, the suggestion is sure to raise eyebrows among European governments. Four EU diplomats who spoke to Euronews on condition of anonymity said these internal reforms are unlikely to fly.
The first test will come next week, when the enlargement reforms will land on the table of the EU leaders gathered for the European Council on 15-16 October.
"Some things are drafted to be killed," an EU diplomat said.

articles.title: Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed - BBC
articles.summary: Ex-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed  BBCEx-Barclays traders jailed for rigging interest rates have convictions quashed  The GuardianFormer City traders’ fraud convictions overturned  City AMBarclays traders’ convictions quashed after Supreme Court ruling  The TimesFive more UK rate-rigging convictions quashed as SFO prosecutions unravel  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Five former Barclays traders sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis have had their convictions overturned following a long-running legal battle.
Jay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon, Colin Bermingham were convicted following trials for manipulating the interest rates used for loans between banks.
But their convictions were quashed on Wednesday by the Court of Appeal. The ruling came after two other former City traders had their convictions overturned last year, which paved the way for others to appeal.
The traders were cast by prosecutors as a symbol of banker greed amid public backlash and anger during the 2008 financial crisis.
Merchant, Mathew, Pabon and Bermingham have all served various jail terms. Moryoussef was sentenced in his absence in 2018, never returned to the UK to serve time after France refused to extradite him.
The prosecutions were over the manipulation of two key interest rate mechanisms: Libor and Euribor, which at the time were used to set borrowing costs on a range of loans such as mortgages and car finance deals.
Mathew said the "strain" of what he had gone through had been a burden on him for the last 10 years.
"Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it's about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened," the 45-year-old said.
"I now have two children and this means a great deal to have the record corrected for their sake as well."
Merchant, 55, added that he looked forward to moving on with his life, but said part of that would be "ensuring that those responsible for what happened are held fully accountable".
Lord Justice Edis said full reasons behind the overturned convictions would be given later on Wednesday.
The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.
There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.
The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.
Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.
Each of the former Barclays traders in Wednesday's successful appeal had originally been convicted of a single count of conspiracy to defraud as result of alleged attempts to influence financial benchmark rates.
Two other bankers have already had their names cleared.
Tom Hayes, a former trader at Swiss bank UBS, was the first banker jailed. He won a 10-year legal battle last year to have his conviction overturned at the Supreme Court in July 2025.
His victory alongside that of fellow trader Carlo Palombo, who was jailed in 2019, paved the way for others to challenge their convictions.
Hayes and Palombo argued they were wrongly prosecuted for what were normal commercial practices in order to appease public anger towards the banks over the financial crisis.
Pabon, 48, who had his name cleared on Wednesday, hailed Hayes for his refusal to "let it go". He had "pushed this through" for the rest of them, he said.
The Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original case against the traders, has not opposed the appeals.
Barclays bank has been contacted for comment.
The latest ruling means just two traders still have convictions over interest rate rigging - former Deutsche Bank trader Christian Bittar and former Barclays trader Peter Johnson.
Bittar was jailed in 2018 after pleading guilty and served two years in prison. He will challenge his conviction on 9 October.
Johnson was the original whistleblower calling attention to the Libor scandal but pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance of winning at trial. He also hopes to appeal.

articles.title: EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic has arrived in Beijing for talks on the European Union’s (EU) growing trade deficit with China.
Sefcovic will meet Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday and Friday after months of discussions over the EU’s trade deficit of more than €1bn ($1.12bn) daily, as well as Chinese curbs on exports of rare earths and other critical minerals.
Meanwhile, Chinese companies are increasingly challenging Europe’s top car brands. China rejected the EU request for voluntary curbs on Chinese hybrid car exports as the two sides enter negotiations, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The European Commission now hopes to get Beijing to accept a unilateral EU measure to cap hybrid imports instead, the outlet said, citing two diplomats briefed on the plan.
The two days of discussions come just as a majority of EU lawmakers called for a more assertive trade policy towards Beijing in a non-binding resolution on Wednesday. China vowed a “resolute response” to safeguard its industries if the European Union goes ahead with restrictions against Chinese companies or products, according to its commerce ministry.
Germany and France propose rapid EU measure
French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leaders of the bloc’s two biggest powers, on Tuesday urged the EU to prepare a “credible instrument” that could be quickly activated to strike back against countries that harm the bloc economically.
The new measure would not target any specific country. German officials said the EU needed a tool as powerful as the Section 301 tariffs imposed by the United States or China’s restrictions on critical-mineral exports.
The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders’ summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days.
China responded to the letter by urging Paris and Berlin to steer clear of “protectionist” measures.
“We hope that France and Germany, as major economies in the world, will uphold openness, cooperation and free trade,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.
“They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves.”
G20 finance leaders, except China’s, agreed in September to act against “non-market” distortions that exacerbate imbalances. Beijing says that hyping up issues such as economic imbalances and overcapacity is a form of protectionism designed to exert pressure on and restrict China.
Ongoing trade talks
EU and Chinese officials have been discussing trade imbalances since June. Sefcovic said he wanted “tangible results by October” as well as some form of commitment that can be put to EU leaders meeting in Brussels.
Trade relations with China top the summit’s agenda next week, as ballooning debt has prompted auditors to warn about the next seven-year EU budget and has spurred protests in France.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament last month that the trade imbalance had reached a tipping point and that Europe would use every tool at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.

articles.title: Shell expects refineries to almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel made - The Guardian
articles.summary: Shell expects refineries to almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel made  The Guardianii view: Shell predicts record refining margin and surge in gas output  Interactive InvestorShell expects record refining margins as Iran war boosts fuel markets  ReutersShell’s Refining Margin Soars to Record High After Middle East Conflict Upends Fuel Markets  WSJShell's Refining Margin Jumps 75% as Fuel Supplies Dry Up  Crude Oil Prices Today | Oil...
articles.full_text:
Shell’s refineries are expected to make record profits on each barrel of fuel produced after shortages in the global market caused pump prices around the world to climb to all-time highs.
In a trading update on Wednesday, the energy supermajor forecast profit margins of $42 a barrel in the July to September period, far above the margins of $24 a barrel in the second quarter.
The forecast margins are also significantly higher than the previous record for petroleum products of about $28 a barrel, set in the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The margins reflect the steep increase in the price of refined fuels, including diesel, relative to the cost of the crude oil. A partial recovery of Gulf oil exports has allowed crude market prices to ease back to about $100 a barrel, while war damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia has caused fuel prices to continue to climb.
That gap should make larger profits possible for refineries, particularly those in the US and Europe. The Middle East crisis has already helped Shell to a profit of almost $10bn (£7.5bn) for the second quarter of 2026, more than double the figure for the same period last year and its second highest quarterly earnings on record.
The market value of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company, now the second largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index, climbed to a record high of £36.23 a share at the end of last month.
That share price was reached despite oil prices retreating from their 2026 peak of above $115 a barrel in spring to about $100. It was lifted by European gas prices, which doubled from the previous year over the summer, and record high diesel prices.
Global oil prices were slightly lower in the third quarter of the year. Brent crude averaged $85.60 a barrel, compared with $97.05 in the second quarter, but still well above the $68.14 recorded in the third quarter last year.
The diesel price premium over the global oil benchmark jumped above $100 a barrel for the first time, indicating record high profits from refining crude into fuels.
Shell operates some of Europe’s largest refineries alongside the French energy company TotalEnergies, which has the continent’s largest refining capacity.
TotalEnergies’ chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, welcomed the opportunities created by the global energy crisis. He told an industry conference in London this week: “We’re doing really well by being integrated. Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.”
Europe’s benchmark gas price index more than doubled to €70.50 (£60) in August. The price of gas reached an average of more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter before leaping to almost €64/MWh in the third quarter.
Shell’s gas production has been hard hit by the Middle East crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf, cutting its prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (BOED) by a third.
Shell said on Wednesday that it expected gas production to climb to about 740,000 to 780,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day after its acquisition of Canada’s ARC Resources, up sharply from its previous forecast of 570,000 to 630,000 BOED for the quarter. It produced about 631,000 BOED in the second quarter.
The deal, which is expected to add about 370,000 barrels a day to Shell’s production of oil and gas, was completed in early September to add a month’s worth of production to its estimates for the quarter.

articles.title: Merz’s conservatives in new crisis over alleged support for AfD - Financial Times
articles.summary: Merz’s conservatives in new crisis over alleged support for AfD  Financial TimesAfD candidate elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time  BBCGermany news: Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers  DW.comGermany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains  Al JazeeraGermany's far-right AfD struggles to form first state government after landmark win  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the German politics myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is embroiled in another crisis after four members of his party were accused of helping elect the first-ever parliamentary president from the far-right Alternative for Germany.
AfD’s Tobias Rausch on Tuesday was voted as Speaker of the regional assembly in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt — a post similar to the role of Speaker of the House of Commons — marking a watershed moment for the anti-immigration, pro-Russian party.
His vote tally was higher than expected, as he secured four mystery votes in the secret ballot, in addition to the expected support from a hard-left party. The result sent shockwaves through the German political establishment and triggered a frenzied search for the identity of those supporters.
Rausch has claimed that some or all of the four were members of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union. Asked if he was elected with support from members of the party, he said “yes”.
The suspicion of CDU support has piled fresh pressure on Merz, who remains committed to maintaining a “firewall” around the AfD but has faced calls from some members of his party to abandon it as the far right has surged to first place in the national polls.
The chancellor on Wednesday described the outcome of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt as a “historic rupture”, adding: “Anyone who lends their vote to the AfD is playing into the hands of extremists and destroying credibility. That is certainly incompatible with the values of my party, the CDU.”
The CDU plans to hold crisis meetings this weekend to discuss its heavy defeats in Saxony-Anhalt and in the small north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern — as well as the secret support for Rausch.
The drama in Magdeburg, the Saxony-Anhalt state capital, has also deepened the tensions in the chancellor’s coalition with the Social Democrats. Merz’s vice-chancellor Lars Klingbeil, who is the SPD’s co-leader, said the CDU needed to urgently “explain how this could have happened”.
Defence minister Boris Pistorius, who joined an SPD rally against the outcome on Tuesday night, said democrats had “served as the enablers of fascists”.
Merz warned, however, against “hasty conclusions” about who had voted for whom. He suggested that members of another party might have secretly voted for the AfD to create the impression of CDU support, deepening existing tensions within the German centre-right.
“False flag operations aren’t just military; they exist in politics too,” he said.
The chancellor said there were “at least two, perhaps even three” groups in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament that were “doing everything they can to undermine cohesion in our democracy”.
Beyond the AfD, the BSW and the CDU, the three other parties in the regional assembly are the anti-capitalist Die Linke, the Green party and SPD. Merz did not specify which one he meant.
The AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, said last week that he expected to be comfortably elected as premier of Saxony-Anhalt in December after his party’s landslide victory in the state of 2mn people last month.
He said he expected to win even though his party fell short of the 42 seats needed for a majority, enabling him to form the first AfD-led government in the party’s 13-year history.
Rausch described the vote for his election as a “trial balloon” for to see if an agreement made with a “loose group” within the CDU could be trusted. He said that he expected CDU members to help bring Siegmund to power.

articles.title: EU defense chief warns Russia ‘not being deterred’ - Türkiye Today
articles.summary: EU defense chief warns Russia ‘not being deterred’  Türkiye Today
articles.full_text:
European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius on Tuesday urged European countries to accelerate military mobility, warning that Russia’s rising defense spending, production capacity and development of new military technologies showed Moscow was still “not being deterred.”
Speaking at the Military Schengen 2026 Conference in Hamburg, Germany, Kubilius said Russia is expected to allocate €180 billion ($201 billion) to its 2027 military budget, about 3% more than this year.
“In purchasing power parity terms, Russia next year will spend the same amount, or even a little bit more, than all the EU member states,” he said.
Kubilius also said Russia was outpacing Europe in defense industrial production and rapidly developing military technologies, including drones.
He said that figure would amount to about 30,000 drones a day and argued that Russia was preparing for “a prolonged war and confrontation.”
“Our defense readiness has to speed up,” he said.
Kubilius stressed that Europe’s ability to deter aggression depends not only on higher defense spending and military procurement but also on the ability to move troops and equipment rapidly across the continent.
He said military mobility should be treated as an urgent operational requirement rather than a theoretical issue.
Kubilius called for an ambitious EU military mobility package that would effectively function as a “Military Schengen.”
He said the EU should replace its current patchwork of 27 national systems with a single European rulebook governing military transport.
Under the proposed system, a single European permit would be valid across the bloc and issued within a maximum of three days, Kubilius said.
For emergencies, he said the EU is proposing a new European Military Mobility Enhanced Response System that could be activated by the EU Council.

The approvals will enable the company to supply heat-treated wooden pallets, crates and dunnage for export shipments from its Gujarat facility.
                                    
                    
                    
                    
                                        Jay Wood Industry (JWI) has received ISPM-15 approvals for its Kosamba manufacturing facility in Gujarat, strengthening its heat-treatment infrastructure for export-compliant wooden packaging.
The approvals, issued under the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine & Storage (DPPQ&S), include IN-003 HT and IN-038 HT registrations, along with approval for the change of location of IN-707 HT to the Kosamba facility.
Kosamba facility to strengthen Gujarat export network
The ISPM-15 standard governs wood packaging material used in international trade. The approvals allow JWI to supply heat-treated wooden pallets, crates and dunnage that meet prescribed phytosanitary requirements for export markets, including the European Union and North America.
The company said the Kosamba facility will strengthen its operational footprint across Maharashtra and Gujarat and enable it to serve industrial clusters around Surat, Hazira, Vadodara, Vapi and Ahmedabad. Its network is positioned to support export corridors including Mundra, Hazira and Nhava Sheva.JWI said its ISPM-15-compliant packaging infrastructure targets export-oriented sectors including pharmaceuticals, chemicals, FMCG, auto components and heavy engineering.
Jay Shah, managing director and CEO of Jay Wood Industry, said the approvals would strengthen the company's compliant manufacturing infrastructure and its ability to support exporters with internationally compliant wooden packaging solutions.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘Judgment day’? Why death penalty crusade is bringing back firing squads - The Independent
articles.summary: Trump’s ‘Judgment day’? Why death penalty crusade is bringing back firing squads  The IndependentUS military will execute Fort Hood attacker by firing squad, a first in 60 years  BBCTrump orders firing squad execution for mass killer who shot 12 soldiers dead  Sky NewsArmy Sets Date for First Military Execution by Firing Squad Since 1945  The New York TimesTrump orders firing squad for gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
When Army Private Eddie Slovik faced a firing squad of 12 members from his own unit on Jan. 31, 1945, the riflemen aimed their M1 Garands at his heart from 20 paces away and fired on command.
Four shots were fatal, but he wasn’t immediately killed. Before the riflemen finished reloading, Slovik, 24, was dead.
Witness Nick Gozik later said the first and only U.S. military execution for desertion since 1864 was “traumatic” and “very unnerving.”
Donald Trump’s approval of the execution of Nidal Hasan will mark the military’s first execution by firing squad since Slovik’s killing in 1945, part of a renewed push by the president to restart federal executions — and turn to methods such as firing squads as well as nitrogen gas and electrocution to carry out sentences quicker.
“Judgment day for Hasan has finally come,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote on X.
“There is nothing Donald Trump loves more than the power to kill,” Death Penalty Action, a nonprofit group advocating for abolishing the death penalty, responded in a statement.
Public opinion polls have suggested that support for the death penalty has plummeted in recent decades, but Trump has pursued federal executions with unprecedented frequency.
During his first term, the federal government executed 13 people, the most under any president in more than 120 years, and a streak that resumed after a 17-year hiatus.
Before he left office, Joe Biden commuted the sentences of 37 people awaiting executions on federal death row, leaving death sentences in place for only three men. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the previous administration “failed in its duty to protect the American people” and took “extraordinary steps to weaken, delay, and dismantle the death penalty.”
Hours after returning to the White House last year, Trump signed an executive order directing the attorney general to seek the death penalty in future cases “for all crimes of a severity demanding its use.”
Earlier this year, the Justice Department unveiled a plan to “strengthen the death penalty” by directing the Bureau of Prisons to use pentobarbital for lethal injections and consider other execution methods — including firing squads and even electrocution — to expedite death sentences.
Trump also instructed the attorney general to “take all necessary and lawful action” to help states obtain lethal injection drugs to carry out more executions.
Bloody, public spectacles of deaths by firing squad began to disappear over the last century ago as states and the federal government moved towards what they considered more “humane” ways of killing people being closed doors through the expanded use of lethal gas, electrocution and drugs.
But, under pressure from anti-death penalty activists, pharmaceutical companies have refused to sell those drugs to states, diminishing their supplies and forcing them to turn to other killing methods to carry out executions for death row inmates.
Those methods have also included untested drug “cocktails” that have led to a wave of horrific botched executions. Some states have relied on compounding pharmacies, which make customized, non-FDA-approved versions of prescription drugs that are not subject to the same safety and efficacy reviews.
The Trump administration’s latest announcement followed the attempted execution of Christa Pike, who was scheduled to be executed by lethal injection with a single barbiturate — Tennessee’s first attempt to execute a woman in more than 200 years. But the execution failed. She survived two injections and was hospitalized and on a ventilator.
On Tuesday, her attorneys said she is now “conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care.”
Pike’s lawyers had previously asked state officials to consider an alternative to lethal injection, such as death by hanging or firing squad, after the state botched a different execution earlier this year.
Two dozen states do not carry out capital punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Deterrence is “one of the most commonly expressed reasons” for using the death penalty — but despite Trump’s claims, evidence shows that “states that impose the death penalty are not safer than states that do not use the death penalty,” according to the center.
At least five states allow firing squads as a method of execution. Last year, South Carolina carried out three killings by firing squad — the first in the state in 15 years.
In April 2025, a three-person firing squad in South Carolina shot Mikal Mahdi, who cried out as the bullets struck him. He groaned twice before taking one final breath.
An autopsy report later revealed two wounds on his chest, and none of the bullets directly hit his heart, which is where the gunmen are supposed to aim. Mahdi, 42, endured “excruciating conscious pain and suffering” for up to one minute and suffered a prolonged death, according to his attorneys.
Hasan killed 13 people and injured 32 others when he opened fire at Fort Hood’s Soldier Readiness Processing Center in 2009. He reportedly shouted out “Allahu akbar” — meaning “God is great” — before firing his handgun.
Acting as his own attorney, Hasan was convicted by a military jury on 45 counts of murder and sentenced to death in 2013. Hasan, who was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan at the end of 2009, admitted responsibility for the shooting and said he believed was on the wrong side of a war against Islam.
He was left partially paralyzed after he was shot by police during his arrest.
Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, a death sentence imposed by court-martial may not be carried out “until approved by the president.”
Trump gave that approval on Monday, according to chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared Parnell’s “judgment day” post, adding: “Justice.”
Still, Trump’s announcement “does not mean his execution is imminent,” Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told The Independent.
“Mr. Hasan may still pursue his habeas appeals and that would delay any execution date,” she said. “The Secretary of the Army will ultimately set the date, place and manner of execution.”
Army Secretary Adam Tell said Hasan’s execution will take place at 2 p.m. December 3.

articles.title: Soaring bond yields continue to hit new highs. Seven things driving the moves - investingLive
articles.summary: Soaring bond yields continue to hit new highs. Seven things driving the moves  investingLiveCOMMENTARY: Can Wall Street keep partying while bond markets burn?  ReutersMarket snapshot: AI overpowering other concerns  Interactive InvestorGlobal bond sell-off pushes U.S. Treasury yields to fresh 24-year highs  NBC NewsCNBC Daily Open: AI rally defies bond market rout  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Summary
- US 10-year yields up 8 basis points to 5.34%, long bonds to the highest since 2002
The Treasury market looks like it's determined to find the breaking point for risk assets. US long-dated yields have been rocketing higher since taking out the big 5% figure but that hasn't undermined stock markets yet, or even gold. At some point that will change as ever-higher yields compete with equities for capital.
Today, US 10s are up 8 bps to a high of 5.35%, which is narrowly below Monday's post-GFC high. Further out, US 30s are making a new 24-year high up 7.4 bps to 5.72%. A crack of 6% in long bonds would undoubtedly crack a few spots in the economy, especially housing (which is already badly struggling).
Recently, there was a brief respite in borrowing costs as economic data downshifted in the past 10 days with softer non-farm payrolls and the weak S&P Global services PMI but while that's curbed Fed rate hike bets, it hasn't stopped the rout in bonds. It's gotten so bad that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent put his tail between his legs and tried to walk back his 'I'm the house, bet against me if you want' talk.
Borrowing costs trickle down into everything but it's increasingly clear to me that something needs to change in a macro sense to arrest the move.
- 1) AI capex is extreme and that's soaking up available dollars. Today, SpaceX announced another $40 billion for Nvidia chips.
- 2) The US fiscal picture is nowhere close to sustainability and there are no credible Congressional voices pushing in that direction.
- 3) Trump's promise of $5000 checks isn't going anywhere but that kind of talk undermines any future pushes towards fiscal restraint, if anything, the opposite
- 4) US military adventurism is expensive
- 5) The Iran and Ukraine wars are in costly stalemates that will continue to push inflation higher until they end
- 6) The Fed appears to be determined to do the minimum it can to credibly fight inflation, which risks putting them behind the curve
- 7) The market may be seeing AI as inherently destabilizing fiscally and politically, opeing a pandora's box of costly social supports and creating turmoil.
The last one particularly frightens me because there is no reversing it, and the recent battle to slow it down has been seemingly abandoned. We are going full-speed towards wherever AI takes us and I strongly suspect it will be governments holding the bill in one way or another.

articles.title: State-Linked Yuyuantantian Signals Beijing’s Possible Approach to Breaking the China-EU Trade Deadlock - Geopolitechs
articles.summary: State-Linked Yuyuantantian Signals Beijing’s Possible Approach to Breaking the China-EU Trade Deadlock  Geopolitechs
articles.full_text:
Today, Yuyuantantian published a commentary on China-EU relations. The context behind the article is worth paying attention to: China and the EU are currently engaged in an intensive round of economic and trade consultations, while France and Germany, just ahead of a new round of ministerial talks, have proposed further strengthening the EU’s trade defence instruments.
In June, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao met with EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maroš Šefčovič in Brussels, where the two sides established a new China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism. They agreed to bring issues including the trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property and WTO reform into a single framework and to continue consultations at the ministerial level. At the time, the EU side stressed that it hoped to see some “concrete and measurable” outcomes by October.
The two sides have in fact remained in close discussions since then. On September 17, Wang and Šefčovič held another video call to take stock of progress since June and prepare for the second ministerial meeting in October. On September 23–24, Chinese Vice Minister of Commerce and Deputy China International Trade Representative Ling Ji held two days of talks in Beijing with senior officials from the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Trade. In other words, China and the EU have effectively developed a three-tier negotiating structure, with discussions moving forward simultaneously at the ministerial, deputy and working-group levels.
Against this backdrop, France and Germany proposed a new set of EU trade defence measures on October 5. These include not only a “diversification instrument” aimed at reducing supply-chain dependence on particular countries and companies, but also proposals allowing the EU to respond more rapidly to “systemic market distortions” in third countries. They are also considering the use of reverse qualified majority voting, which could make it easier for the EU to adopt restrictive measures. The shift in Germany’s position is somewhat surprising. France has long advocated stronger European trade defence measures, while Germany has traditionally been more cautious because of its deeper economic and trade ties with China. France and Germany now appear to be moving towards a more aligned position.
This makes the timing of another video call between the two sides’ deputies on October 6 particularly sensitive. Ling Ji and the Director-General of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Trade, Jørgensen, held a video consultation yesterday to make final preparations for the second ministerial meeting under the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism. Meanwhile, China’s Ministry of Commerce has publicly criticised the new measures proposed by France and Germany as protectionist.
What is particularly noteworthy is that Yuyuantantian’s article effectively puts forward, from a Chinese perspective, a possible negotiating approach for the upcoming Wang Wentao–Šefčovič meeting. Rather than fighting separate trade battles over electric vehicles, chemicals, foreign subsidies, medical devices, inverters and other individual issues, the article suggests placing trade balance, market access, investment, technology and supply chains within a broader negotiating framework.
Even though the commentary was never recognised as the official position of the Chinese government, the potential trade-off it outlines is relatively clear. Europe wants China to increase imports of European goods and services, improve market access for European companies, and address the rapid growth of exports in certain sectors. China, meanwhile, wants the EU to reduce discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies and provide a stable market environment for Chinese investment in Europe. If the two sides can address these issues as a package, there may be scope for a broader China-EU economic and trade arrangement.
Below is the full translation of the commentary:
On October 5, France and Germany submitted a non-paper to the European Commission, calling on the EU to strengthen its trade defence measures and introduce a number of new protectionist tools.
These tools are mainly aimed at several areas: restricting goods and companies from other countries from entering the European market, reducing so-called supply-chain dependencies, and preparing in advance for possible countermeasures taken by other countries.
At the same time, under the current proposal, the EU would be able to investigate another country’s overall policies. As long as the EU considers those policies to have undermined what it calls “fair market conditions,” it could take measures when deemed necessary.
China’s position on this is clear. If the European side insists on introducing discriminatory measures of this kind, China will respond resolutely to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries.
01 The European Side Needs to Answer Several Questions
In response to the efforts by France and Germany to push the EU to develop new trade-restriction tools, China could coordinate positions with potentially affected third countries within the framework of the World Trade Organization and jointly study possible countermeasures.
The tools currently available to China include anti-discrimination investigations, industrial and supply-chain security investigations, and investigations into the impact of foreign subsidies.
Zhou Mi of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce told Tan Zhu that these investigations can assess whether relevant overseas policies affect Chinese companies and create unfair competition, thereby safeguarding the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies and reducing the impact of unfair policies and their spillover effects on Chinese industries.
According to relevant disclosures, European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maroš Šefčovič will visit Beijing soon.
Attempting to introduce new restrictive tools at this particular juncture would, first of all, weaken the atmosphere for consultations between China and the EU. Moreover, the new tools could leave room for the European side to impose additional restrictions at any time. If this continues, it would not only further narrow the space for resolving problems through dialogue, but could also undermine the results already achieved through negotiations.
It should be remembered that in June this year, China and the EU established a trade and investment consultation mechanism, with four working areas: trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights, and WTO reform.
Therefore, the first question the European side needs to answer when it comes to the negotiating table is: Which of the issues currently under discussion are these new restrictive tools actually intended to resolve?
The concerns of both sides can already be put on the table.
One is the balance of trade and investment.
The European side hopes that China will further open its market and increase imports of European goods and services.
But Europe needs to understand that it will be difficult to achieve balanced trade if, on the one hand, it asks China to buy more European products while, on the other hand, attempting to impose restrictions on China in multiple areas.
The second is market access and corporate investment.
China has consistently supported Chinese companies investing in Europe and welcomes greater investment in China by European companies.
However, the EU is investigating Chinese companies in sectors such as wind power and security inspection equipment under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation. It is also continuously strengthening foreign investment screening, restricting Chinese companies and products from participating in public procurement for medical devices, and prohibiting financial support for projects that use Chinese inverters. These practices will only increase uncertainty.
Market access should be reciprocal.
After Chinese companies invest in Europe, whether they can receive stable, transparent and non-discriminatory treatment is a question to which the European side needs to provide a clear answer.
The third concerns critical items and intellectual property rights.
China and the EU are discussing how to balance trade, how to mutually open their markets, and how to maintain stable supply chains. Yet the new tools proposed by France and Germany are instead designed to address how the EU can impose restrictive measures more quickly and more easily.
Such an approach does nothing to resolve the issues already under discussion.
The European side therefore needs to answer a second question: Where are the boundaries for the application of these so-called trade tools?
The boundary between normal responses and so-called “economic coercion”
The new tools proposed by France and Germany could allow the EU to rapidly impose additional retaliatory measures.
This could easily create a problem: the EU could take measures first, and when another country responds, the EU could then treat that response as justification for further escalation.
Affected countries can still take corresponding measures within the WTO framework and in accordance with their own domestic laws. Every additional round of restrictions imposed by the EU would also entail higher costs for its own trade and industries.
The boundary between reducing dependency and creating discrimination
France and Germany have called for the establishment of a new “diversification instrument.” This instrument would examine the concentration of EU imports of goods from a particular country or company, as well as the global market share of the companies concerned.
This may sound like an effort to reduce risks.
But if it ultimately results in procurement quotas, investment thresholds or market-share restrictions based on the nationality of compa

articles.title: Ericsson to export India-made antennas to Europe; India has competitive edge for 6G: Executive - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Ericsson to export India-made antennas to Europe; India has competitive edge for 6G: Executive  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Ericsson said India’s 95% mid-band 5G population coverage and completed 5G standalone rollout give the country an edge in moving towards 6G and building AI-ready networks.
Speaking at the India Mobile Congress 2026, Andres Vicente, Senior Vice President and Head of Market Area South East Asia, Oceania, and India, Ericsson, said it is impressive that India's mid-band 5G coverage reaches 95 per cent of the population against 45 per cent globally.
India has a competitive advantage in order to take another step moving towards 6G because the difficult part, which is setting the right architecture, has already been done, he noted.
"Today, we are making the announcement that we will export to Europe all the capabilities and antennas that we are manufacturing here in India," Vicente said.
According to Vicente, India's transition to 5G standalone has been completed. As a result, its networks are cloud-driven and programmable and can offer differentiated connectivity, which he described as the ingredients needed to evolve to 6G.
Citing 5G adoption figures, Vicente said India has 430 million 5G mobile subscriptions, which make up 35 per cent of the country's total subscriptions. He said 43 per cent of mobile data traffic is carried on 5G.
"India is the country with the highest usage in the world per customer," he said, putting the figure at 35 gigabytes. He said usage is growing across categories, including video and gaming.
AI will reshape the telecom industry in two ways, he said, AI for networks and networks for AI. To prepare networks for AI, compute power will have to be introduced at many levels so that networks become more efficient, intelligent, intent-driven, and autonomous.
He said networks will also need significant investment in uplink experience and low latency to support AI use cases such as autonomous vehicles and drones. He described bringing AI compute and inference closer to the network as a key opportunity for telecom operators and for governments "in order to take control and sovereignty of this intelligence".

articles.title: India sets its chemical industry on a $1 trillion path by 2040 - Indiatimes
articles.summary: India sets its chemical industry on a $1 trillion path by 2040  Indiatimes
articles.full_text:
India is trying to turn chemicals from a supporting industry into a strategic growth pillar, with the government now openly linking the sector to batteries, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing. At the launch of India Chem 2026 in New Delhi, the Centre sketched an ambition that goes well beyond capacity addition: a $1 trillion chemicals industry by 2040 and a stronger role for India in global supply chains.
According to Indian Chemical News, Union minister of state for chemicals and fertilisers Anupriya Patel said the country’s next phase of industrial policy must align infrastructure, research and investment if India is to become a serious contender in speciality, battery and semiconductor chemicals. The broader message was clear: the chemicals sector is no longer being treated as a standalone manufacturing story, but as a platform for technology-led industrial expansion.
From manufacturing base to strategic supply chain linkCritical Mineral Mission, the Rare Earth Corridor, India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, the National Manufacturing Mission and foreign direct investment reforms. The intent, she said, is to position India as a global centre for battery chemicals, speciality chemicals and semiconductor chemicals by 2040.
That ambition matters because these segments sit at the intersection of energy storage, electronics and industrial competitiveness. Battery-grade inputs are increasingly central to electric mobility and grid storage, while semiconductor chemicals are crucial for chip fabrication and associated supply chains. If India can build scale in these categories, the sector could move from import dependence to export relevance in select niches.
The emphasis on chemical parks is significant because industrial clusters often determine whether India can cut logistics costs, improve utilities access and attract anchor investors. For a sector that competes on process efficiency and scale, plug-and-play infrastructure can be as important as tax incentives. The government’s pitch is that well-designed parks could lower entry barriers for new projects and help existing producers expand faster.
R&D spending moves to the centre of the policy debateDepartment of Chemicals and Petrochemicals is working with the Department of Science and Technology to have chemicals and petrochemicals recognised as a priority sector under the new Research Development Innovation scheme, which has an outlay of about ₹1 lakh crore.
Officials say cost competitiveness is the next frontierTejveer Singh, secretary in the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, described chemicals as the foundation of India’s economic growth and development. He said the proposed parks under the BHAVYA Rasayan Scheme are close to becoming reality and are expected to offer shared infrastructure that can improve efficiency and reduce production costs.Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade on import-substitution exercises across the chemicals and petrochemicals space. That suggests the policy focus is not only on exports, but also on replacing imported intermediates and reducing vulnerability in critical value chains.
Industry wants scale, capital and partnershipsDeepankar Aron, joint secretary in the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, said the 14th edition of India Chem is designed to draw investment and create business-to-business partnerships across the sector. The government-backed platform is being used as both a policy signal and a market-making exercise, bringing together producers, investors and technology stakeholders under one roof.Prabh Das, chairman of the FICCI National Petrochemicals and Plastics Committee and managing director and chief executive officer of HPCL-Mittal Energy Ltd, said India must increase production and that the government is backing that effort. S Ganeshkumar, co-chair of the FICCI Chemicals Committee and managing director of Chemplast Sanmar Ltd, said the sector can absorb large capital, attract foreign direct investment and emerge as one of the world’s most attractive chemical markets.Why the 2040 target matters for India’s industrial policyIndia Chem 2026 as a platform for the next phaseFederation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, will run in Mumbai from October 22 to 24. The three-day event will include an international exhibition and conference, along with sector-specific discussions on agrochemicals, petrochemicals and speciality chemicals.

articles.title: Kyiv Rocked by Repeated Russian Missile Attacks Overnight, 2 Killed After Zelensky’s ‘Massive Strike’ Warning - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: Kyiv Rocked by Repeated Russian Missile Attacks Overnight, 2 Killed After Zelensky’s ‘Massive Strike’ Warning  Kyiv PostKyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit  BBCRussian forces attack transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia  UkrinformZelenskyy says Ukraine will intensify oil refinery attacks as Kyiv bridges come under fire  DW.comRussian drone slams into Kyiv bridge in escalating campaign as Germany’s ch...
articles.full_text:
Multiple explosions rocked Kyiv in repeated waves in the early hours of Wednesday as Russia launched ballistic missiles toward the Ukrainian capital, with damage reported across several districts.
A Kyiv Post journalist in the capital reported several strong explosions after the Ukrainian Air Force warned that ballistic missiles were heading toward the city.
Several hours later, Kyiv was rocked by explosions for a second time. Ukrinform reported renewed blasts at around 5:12 a.m., shortly after the Air Force detected several more ballistic missiles heading toward the capital. The air raid alert remained in force.
The attacks came only hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned in his nightly address that Ukrainian intelligence had received updated information indicating Russia was preparing a “massive strike.” He urged residents to take missile alerts seriously and said Ukrainian forces were ready to respond “as much as our defenses allow.”
Ukraine’s Air Force warned of ballistic missiles heading toward Kyiv, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia after reporting a threat from Russia’s Bryansk region and from the south.
The overnight assault also included jet-powered drones moving across several regions. The Air Force tracked such drones over northern Kyiv region, while cruise missiles were later reported over the Kharkiv and Poltava regions.
Damage reported across Kyiv
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko and the Kyiv City Military Administration reported damage in several districts as the attack unfolded.
In the Obolonskyi district, a strike was recorded in an area of non-residential development.
In Podilskyi, warehouse facilities were hit and damaged.
In Darnytskyi, burning debris fell on an open area, while in the Shevchenkivskyi district another strike hit a non-residential area.
The Kyiv City Military Administration later reported further consequences of the attack in Darnytskyi, where damage was recorded on the territory of a garage cooperative.
Air defenses were operating over the capital as officials repeatedly urged residents to remain in shelters.
Kyiv hit again before dawn
The second round of explosions came several hours after the initial ballistic missile attack.
Shortly before the renewed blasts, the Ukrainian Air Force detected several ballistic missiles heading toward Kyiv.
The repeated explosions formed part of a broader overnight Russian assault in which missiles and fast-moving drones were tracked across multiple regions of Ukraine.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported in the morning that two people had been killed in the attack.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) said firefighters extinguished a fire covering 200 square meters at a garage cooperative in the Darnytskyi district. The bodies of two victims were found during the firefighting operation, while two other people were rescued.
Kyiv under mounting pressure
The latest attack comes as Kyiv faces an intensifying Russian air campaign approaching winter.
Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s energy and transport infrastructure, including railways, roads and bridges over the Dnipro.
The capital has also endured repeated daytime and nighttime drone attacks in recent days, while air raid sirens have sounded for prolonged periods and forced residents into shelters, basements and metro stations.
Scheduled power cuts had already plunged parts of Kyiv into darkness Tuesday evening in an effort to reduce strain on the damaged electricity grid.
Russian forces have also repeatedly struck Kyiv’s bridges in recent days, disrupting road and metro traffic across key crossings over the Dnipro.
Warning came hours before attack
Zelensky said Tuesday evening that Ukrainian intelligence had fresh information about Russian preparations for a large-scale attack.
“There is updated intelligence regarding Russia’s preparations for a massive strike,” he said, urging Ukrainians to respond to missile alerts.
He also stressed that Ukraine’s ability to repel incoming missiles remained dependent on continued weapons deliveries from allies.
The warning was followed later Tuesday by reports that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from the Belaya air base.
Hours later, ballistic missiles were heading toward Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities, followed by renewed explosions in the capital before dawn.
