articles.title: Why Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in Brazil’s election - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Why Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in Brazil’s election  Al JazeeraFlávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners  The GuardianBrazil is a right-wing country now  The EconomistBrazil’s markets surge as investors bet on Flávio Bolsonaro election win  Financial TimesWhy Bolsonarismo Won’t Die  Tribunemag.co.uk
articles.full_text:
With three weeks to go until Brazil’s presidential runoff, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva finds himself in a weaker position than he — or most pollsters — had expected.
A second round of voting was widely predicted. But most recent polls had Lula entering a runoff from first place, putting him about three percentage points ahead of rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Instead, Bolsonaro took about 47 percent of the vote on Sunday to Lula’s 45 percent, a reversal that surprised analysts and raised questions about what happened in the final days of the campaign, and what the polls may have missed.
What changed in the final days
Carlos Pereira, a political scientist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation think-tank in Brazil, believes part of the answer lies in a late shift among voters who had planned to support smaller right-wing candidates.
Bolsonaro himself had said he was banking on exactly that, telling reporters on election day that he expected a “protest vote” from people who might have otherwise backed another candidate but were united in their opposition to Lula.
“Usually, voters, they vote [sincerely] in the first round, and they vote strategically in the second round,” Pereira told Al Jazeera.
This time, he said, some voters who were planning to cast their ballot for candidates like the former governor of the central state of Goias, Ronaldo Caiado, and businessman and founder of the right-wing Free Brazil Movement, Renan Santos, appear to have made the strategic choice earlier.
“They thought, ‘Let’s try to resolve this election right now,’” Pereira said. “If you’re gonna vote for Flavio anyway in the second round, why not vote for him right now?”
That early consolidation could also matter in the runoff. Political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters news agency that some of the support Bolsonaro would have usually picked up only in a second round had already been “front-loaded,” potentially leaving him less room to expand his coalition.
Another factor, Pereira said, was the Banco Master scandal, a sprawling alleged banking fraud that rattled both campaigns in the final weeks, touching figures across the political spectrum.
Among them was Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case that sent Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, to prison. De Moraes was accused of improper ties to Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro after documents emerged appearing to show the banker seeking legal advice from him. De Moraes has denied the allegations.
Pereira believes that connection may have acted as a late “trigger” for some voters. Bolsonaro’s supporters have seen Moraes as a political ally of Lula, with Flavio making a direct link between the two on the campaign trail earlier this year, saying, “Anyone voting for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes.”
A September Datafolha poll found 34 percent of Brazilians associated the Banco Master scandal more with the left, compared with 27 percent who associated it more with the right.
Andre Pagliarini, a professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of Lula: A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, agreed the scandal may have hurt the president. A campaign dominated by “spectacular, unceasing scandal involving seemingly the entire political class”, he said, played to Bolsonaro’s strengths as an “anti-institutional insurgent”.
“The irony, of course, is that Flavio himself was directly implicated in the Banco Master scandal in a way that Lula is not,” he said in an email.
The younger Bolsonaro is under investigation over allegations that he sought money from Vorcaro to finance a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.
A broader shift to the right
Neither analyst saw the result as a wholesale failure of the polls.
For Pagliarini, the bigger surprise was the scale of support for the right, which extended well beyond the presidential race.
Bolsonaro won nearly four percentage points more than his father did in the first round in 2022, while his Liberal Party emerged with the largest bloc in Brazil’s Senate. The right also came out strong in gubernatorial races and made significant gains in the southeast of the country.
“There clearly was a powerful information environment around Flavio that allowed his campaign to keep its message in front of voters even as the mainstream press exposed scandal after scandal,” said Pagliarini. “If anything, the polls underestimated the commitment of voters already leaning right.”
But the results also point to a deeper challenge for Lula and the Brazilian left: a sense among many voters that the government is not delivering enough, particularly on the economy and public security.
On paper, Lula can point to a number of positive economic indicators, like record-low unemployment, falling inequality and easing inflation. But that hasn’t necessarily translated into a sense that life is getting easier, as Brazilians have continued to feel squeezed by high food prices and household debt.
A September Quaest poll found nearly half of those surveyed believed the economy had gotten worse over the previous year, compared with just 19 percent who thought it had improved.
“Voters can acknowledge that poverty is down and unemployment is low and still feel overworked, indebted, unsafe and fed up with political conflict,” Pagliarini said. “The right has figured out how to turn those frustrations into a very clear political identity.”
An uphill battle for Lula
Lula now has three weeks to close a gap of about 2.2 million votes. And there are millions potentially up for grabs.
About nine million votes went to other candidates in the first round, while more than 33.4 million Brazilians didn’t vote – 28 percent of registered voters.
“It’s possible, but the arithmetic is tough,” Pagliarini said.
For Lula to turn things around, he’d need to win voters who backed minor candidates, reach some of those who abstained and find more support in the northeast, which is already his strongest region.
His campaign is preparing a new communications team. Pargliarini said he’ll be watching the debates, where Lula could make a case directly against Bolsonaro rather than against his brand.
“The odds are steep, but Lula remains an extremely powerful communicator,” he said. “Going hard at Flavio in this round is his only hope.”

articles.title: 2012 nightmare returns to Eurozone as French spreads surge - Bankingnews
articles.summary: 2012 nightmare returns to Eurozone as French spreads surge  Bankingnews
articles.full_text:
The Eurozone is re-entering a trajectory of dangerous destabilization, as the surge in borrowing costs for France revives the nightmare of the 2012 sovereign debt crisis. Markets are reacting nervously to the French fiscal impasse, triggering a wave of sell-offs that threatens to sweep up sovereign bonds in Italy, Belgium, and Greece.
Confronted with the hazard of a systemic domino effect, Europe faces a renewed existential threat, with all eyes turning toward the resilience of the ECB.
Specifically, borrowing costs for France are rising abruptly, with investors worldwide waking up to the risk of a full-blown sovereign debt crisis in the EU's second-largest economy.
Turmoil across financial markets has begun spreading beyond national borders, intensifying anxieties that political dysfunction in France could ignite a wider, regional problem.
Memories of the sovereign debt crisis that jeopardized the survival of the single currency 15 years ago are beginning to resurface.
France has failed to post a balanced budget for over 30 years.
The debt burden of France is now so massive (and mounting so rapidly) that some are beginning to worry the country might not be able to repay it in full.
What happens if French woes deteriorate further?
Is Europe confronting another existential crisis?
Will the European Central Bank rush to the rescue through whatever means necessary? And will that be enough?
How serious is the situation?
Investor anxieties surrounding the fiscal and political deadlock in France have magnified.
However, following the pandemic and, more recently, after the disastrous political gamble taken by President Emmanuel Macron to call snap elections two years ago, the spread began widening: initially incrementally, and now sharply.
From 0.55 percentage points in mid-September, it had climbed to 1.45 by Monday morning.
It had not stood at such elevated levels since the debt crisis of 2012. In absolute metrics, the yield on the 10-year French bond is hovering near 5%, marking its highest level since 2008.
Concerns are acute enough that the Governor of the Bank of France, Emmanuel Moulin, warned that «everything possible must be done» to avert a debt crisis heading into the 2027 presidential elections.
Did you say the situation is spreading to the rest of Europe?
Well, that is beginning to unfold. France has been an outlier in Europe in recent weeks, yet sovereign bond yield spreads (the risk premiums investors demand for each sovereign) have likewise started widening for Italy, Belgium, and Greece.
The movements were abrupt, yet the risk premium remains at thresholds that would not yet be classified as full crisis levels.
The complication is that bond prices, which move inversely to yields, can decline rapidly when investors reassess risk.
The ownership profile of French sovereign debt could also amplify a mass liquidation.
Unlike Italy, where the bulk of public debt is held by domestic investors, more than half of French sovereign paper is in the hands of foreign institutional investors, who tend to head for the exits faster when volatility spikes.
Sumitomo Mitsui DS Asset Management, one of Japan's premier asset managers, announced over the weekend that it had liquidated its entire exposure to French sovereign debt.
In the event of an acceleration in selling (or worse, forced liquidations), the risk of contagion toward other member states of the Eurozone expands further.
Who you gonna call? The... spread busters
The widening of sovereign yield spreads across nations has stirred questions regarding whether and how the European Central Bank could arrest the deterioration.
The ECB's Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) enables the central bank to purchase sovereign debt on the secondary market to counter «unwarranted, disorderly» market dynamics, but strictly subject to established criteria.
Before the ECB can deploy it, it must judge that a member state pursues sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies. For France, this would mandate large-scale fiscal adjustments that would be politically impossible to execute heading into the 2027 electoral race.
«Assistance would likely demand a genuine commitment to stability via fiscal discipline, structural reforms, or both. Securing such backing will not prove politically easy», stated Christian Schulz, Chief Economist at Allianz Global Investors.
Stop (in the name of love for the euro)?
The ECB could also, theoretically, step in by utilizing its balance sheet. Over approximately the past two years, it has allowed bonds acquired during the Quantitative Easing (QE) era to run off gradually as they reach maturity. This has compelled governments to refinance maturing liabilities directly through open markets. This dynamic expands the net supply of paper on the market and exacerbates upward pressure on yields.
Carsten Brzeski, Global Head of Macro Research at ING, argued that the ECB could «temporarily pause Quantitative Tightening (QT) and reinvest maturing paper in its portfolio with flexibility, conveying a constructive signal to bond markets».
This option was also tabled on Monday in an op-ed by Lorenzo Bini Smaghi, former Italian member of the ECB Executive Board. It likewise lies at the core of the appeal made by Jean-Luc Melenchon, candidate of the French far left for the presidency, urging the ECB to place a portion of sovereign debt «in the deep freeze».
What about interest rates?
Should the turmoil affect the wider region, the ECB could also leverage its other primary and relatively blunt policy instrument (policy rates) to suppress borrowing costs, analysts argue.
«Action by the ECB still appears distant, yet an initial step would be to temper some of the interest rate hikes priced in by markets», analysts at Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG) recently wrote.
Markets have already markedly pared back expectations for subsequent rate increases, yet ECB President Christine Lagarde took care to leave the door open for further tightening during her latest press briefing. And with Eurozone inflation touching a three-year peak of 3.8% in September, there are limits to how accommodative Frankfurt can become.
What is the worst-case scenario?
As framed by Robin Brooks, Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution, in a recent post on Substack, the ECB cannot rush to bail out every single sovereign.
«There must be a waiting window, like a debutante at a ball playing hard to get», he argued. «That is the phase we are currently navigating».
Nonetheless, he added that if backstopping France is the sole path to preserving the integrity of the euro, that is precisely what the ECB will do, even at the cost of «sheer horror in Germany and the remainder of Northern Europe».
«I am as worried as Draghi», says outgoing EU financial chief
The EU risks descending into crisis unless the bloc succeeds in revitalizing its economy, which has essentially ceased expanding, warned the top economic official in Brussels following his departure from a four-decade career within the European Commission.
«I am as worried as Mario Draghi», stated John Berrigan in an interview, referring to the former President of the European Central Bank, who had previously warned that Europe would face a «slow agony» without massive capital expenditure of at least 800 billion euros annually to revamp its fractured economic engine.
The public finances of most sovereign administrations are far too constrained to shoulder the bulk of this burden, having deployed massive fiscal outlays to buffer European enterprises and households from the fallout of the pandemic and two consecutive energy shocks since 2022.
The increase in borrowing rates aimed at tackling elevated inflation has ratcheted up debt servicing costs, rendering debt rollover even more punitive for cash-strapped treasuries, let alone in the face of an additional crisis.
Without accelerated economic growth, highly indebted sovereigns will struggle to generate sufficient fiscal revenue to balance budgets without resorting to painful austerity, just as hard-right and eurosceptic factions gain electoral momentum.
«We are trapped in a low-growth equilibrium», Berrigan noted from the 10th floor of the Berlaymont building overlooking the European Quarter, where he has served since 1986.
«And that, at some juncture, will mutate into a stability concern on its own merit».
The Commission tasked Draghi with authoring a 400-page roadmap cataloging policies, initiatives, and structural reforms that the EU ought to enact to turn its stagnant economy into a unified engine capable of competing against economic titans like the United States and China. Two years following the unveiling of the Draghi report, the EU has implemented barely one out of four recommendations.
Concurrently, Brussels has embarked on an initiative to cut red tape and dismantle regulatory hurdles to help companies scale up.
Banks seek to participate, lobbying Brussels to lower capital buffer requirements that, they argue, constrain them from financing Europe's investment backlog.
However, Berrigan cautioned that seeking expansion through the dilution of lending standards could heighten the bloc's vulnerability.
«There is no impression that citizens are lining up outside credit institutions clamoring for access to credit», the 65-year-old stated. Diluting financial safety margins is particularly hazardous when treasuries hold negligible fiscal space to absorb another shock, he warned, because «if a shock punctures the system's resilience, it will propagate across the whole system. There will be no mechanism to soften the blow».
Berrigan, who retired last Wednesday after six years steering the Commission's Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union (FISMA), is no stranger to financial turmoil. articles.title: EU-China trade talks zero in on cars - POLITICO.eu
articles.summary: EU-China trade talks zero in on cars  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
BRUSSELS — Crunch negotiations between the European Commission and China are zeroing in on cars ahead of Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing this week, four people with knowledge of the situation told POLITICO.
Brussels is eyeing a commitment from Beijing on stemming exports of hybrid vehicles, one of the people said, making it a potential deliverable of Šefčovič’s two-day visit starting Thursday. The discussions mark the final round of a four-month-old push by Brussels to reduce the bloc’s €1-billion-a-day trade deficit with China.
Šefčovič will meet Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao with political backing from the EU’s biggest countries to take a tougher line toward Beijing.

articles.title: France offers to share energy expertise with Malaysia - Newswav
articles.summary: France offers to share energy expertise with Malaysia  Newswav
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: France is opening up its energy experience to Malaysia, particularly in hydropower, low-carbon, renewables, carbon capture, nuclear and other power resources already operational in France.
Deputy head of mission at the Embassy of France in Malaysia Olivier Sigaud said growing geostrategic uncertainties have affected the supply chain for oil, gas and fuel, through the cost of living for people and operating costs for companies.
“So, what can France do with Malaysia to address the challenge of energy transition? First, we can share our experience.
“Around 98% of France’s electricity is low-carbon, thanks largely to nuclear energy and hydropower. We have extensive hydropower experience and can share that expertise with Malaysia.
“We can also share our experience in developing a regulatory framework. As you know, the EU energy market is fully integrated. In Malaysia, as part of Asean, we are very interested in the Asean Power Grid because it is an important part of strengthening the resilience of the regional electricity network while also improving efficiency and cost effectiveness.
“That is another area where we can share our experience,” he told delegates at the Schneider Electric Innovation Day Kuala Lumpur 2026, held under the theme ‘Advancing Energy Tech for Malaysia’s Future’ today.
Sigaud said France can help connect French industry with the relevant players here in Malaysia.
“As you may know, France already has a significant footprint in Malaysia, with around 600 companies providing some 30,000 jobs. Companies such as Schneider Electric, which has been here for decades, have contributed significantly to this presence and helped build Malaysia’s industrial ecosystem,” he added.
Sigaud said France can bring a broad range of expertise, from power generation and traditional energy companies such as Électricité de France, a French multinational electric utility company owned by the French government, and TotalEnergies, to electricity and energy management, with flagship companies such as Schneider Electric.
“But we also have to think about the future, and that means investing in human capital, training and research and development.
“And I think Malaysia is one of the most promising countries in terms of its digital ecosystem. From the upstream, where you have a very vibrant semiconductor industry that is trying to move up the value chain and provide the chips and computing capacity needed for data centres, to very good data connectivity, including subsea communication cables,” Sigaud said.
Speaking on efforts to attract more investments, Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) deputy CEO (investment promotion and facilitation) Zalina Zainol said Malaysia is moving towards a more technology-intensive, sustainable and high-value economy.
Malaysia recorded RM218.5 billion in approved investments across 2,746 projects in the first half of this year, with more than 99,000 jobs expected to be created.
“But attracting investment is only part of the story. We also need to make sure these approvals translate into projects on the ground, create good jobs, provide opportunities for businesses and bring long-term value to the economy,” said Zalina.
She added that sectors such as data centres, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing were creating new opportunities for Malaysia, as the country sought to strengthen its position in higher-value industries.
In the first half of this year, data centre and cloud computing projects accounted for RM95.8 billion in approved investments, Zalina said. “Digital infrastructure is an important part of this transformation. It supports AI, cloud computing, automation and other advanced technologies.”
Digital infrastructure would support Malaysia’s ambition to develop 3,000 smart factories by 2030, she said. “But these investments need the right infrastructure. We need reliable energy and water, digital connectivity, skilled talent and sustainable solutions.”
Zalina said Malaysia has built strong foundations in these areas, but as investment needs evolve, its infrastructure must keep pace. “Investment readiness and infrastructure readiness have to move together.”
However, she added, the focus should not be limited to infrastructure, and more effort is needed to ensure Malaysian businesses and talent also participate in and benefit from the investments coming into the country.
Schneider Electric Innovation Day Kuala Lumpur 2026 brought together leaders from government, utilities, and industry to discuss how electricity demand, grid readiness, cooling, water availability, and decarbonization are becoming increasingly important considerations for investors, especially with the growth of AI technologies.
During panel discussions, industry stakeholders explored how Malaysia can further strengthen the infrastructure needed to support its continued growth.
The event also marked the formation of a partnership between Schneider Electric and Universiti Tenaga Nasional. The collaboration brings together Schneider Electric’s global energy technology expertise and the university’s research and talent development capabilities, strengthening France-Malaysia cooperation in areas that can help Malaysia prepare its energy systems and workforce for future growth.

articles.title: “Europe Must Defend Itself”: U.S. Prioritizes Homeland Defense and Countering China, Leaving Europe to Take the Lead in Deterring Russia - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: “Europe Must Defend Itself”: U.S. Prioritizes Homeland Defense and Countering China, Leaving Europe to Take the Lead in Deterring Russia  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
U.S. pressure for greater defense burden-sharing compounds fears of Russian provocations
Europe’s pursuit of defense self-reliance takes shape through force expansion and operational reforms
Preparations intensify, from drone and AI defense strategies to troop deployments near the border
The United States has renewed pressure on Europe to assume greater responsibility for its defense as it considers redeploying some U.S. forces stationed on the continent to the American homeland and Latin America. The proposal envisages European allies taking the lead in deterring Russia while Washington concentrates its military resources on homeland defense and countering China. Europe, which has been preparing for a reduced U.S. security role, is now focusing on strengthening its ability to respond in combat, building on increases in defense spending and joint arms procurement. Amid concerns over localized Russian provocations, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is refining defense strategies incorporating drones and artificial intelligence (AI), while Estonia is moving its main forces closer to the border to halt an enemy advance from the outset of an invasion.
Pentagon Expands Military Operations in Latin America
According to an October 6 report by The Hill, a U.S. news outlet covering Congress, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters in Colorado Springs, Colorado, on October 3 that “we are expanding our military presence and the scope of our activities in Latin America, including Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala and Panama,” adding that “partnerships with Latin America have opened up an entirely new set of economic and military options.” He continued: “We want Europe to shoulder more of the burden,” and said some forces could “return to bases we will build at home, or be redeployed in other configurations within the Western Hemisphere to counter designated terrorist organizations.” His remarks were interpreted as signaling a possible redeployment of U.S. forces from Europe and stronger action against Latin American drug cartels, while underscoring Europe’s responsibility to share the security burden. All dates are local.
The Pentagon is conducting a six-month review, due to conclude by the end of the year, of potential redeployments of U.S. troops in Europe. The review reportedly includes proposals to transfer responsibility for conventional defense to European allies. In a September 30 address on the state of U.S. military forces at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth also urged state governors to compete to host new military bases. This raises the possibility that relocating some Europe-based troops to the United States will also be considered.
Latin America is a region where China has expanded its foothold within Washington’s traditional sphere of influence through deeper economic cooperation with countries including Venezuela. Although the United States has no large military bases in South America, demand for troops in the region has increased as Washington has intensified military action against Latin American drug cartels since last fall. U.S. forces have attacked vessels suspected of involvement in drug trafficking in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. More recently, operations off Ecuador have involved intercepting large fishing vessels suspected of serving as “floating fuel stations,” removing their crews and then blowing up the vessels. Last week, approximately 50 U.S. military and law enforcement personnel also joined Ecuadorian police in a ground raid targeting suspected drug traffickers.
Washington Looks to Reallocate Military Resources as Europe Assumes Defense Responsibilities
Washington’s force deployment plans reflect a strategic judgment that military resources should be directed first toward homeland defense and countering China. This approach was also evident at the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting at NATO headquarters in February last year. At the time, Hegseth cited U.S. border security and the threat from China as he made clear that Washington’s role in European security had limits. He called on European allies to lead the region’s conventional defense and assume responsibility for a substantial share of assistance to Ukraine. The underlying calculation appears to be that greater European investment in its own defense would give the United States more capacity to meet military demands elsewhere.
Europe’s transformed security landscape since the end of the Cold War also appears to inform Washington’s demands for a redistribution of responsibilities. When the Soviet Union exerted influence over Eastern Europe, the military dividing line between the West and the Eastern bloc ran through a divided Germany. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary subsequently joined NATO in 1999, followed in 2004 by seven more countries, including the three Baltic states of Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia, extending the alliance’s defensive perimeter eastward. Washington’s view is that, with countries once within the Soviet sphere now incorporated into the Western collective defense system, Europe must develop defense capabilities commensurate with that expansion.
China’s growing presence in Latin America provides an additional incentive for Washington to reorganize the security architecture around its own territory. Since September last year, the Donald Trump administration has been considering ways to help U.S. and other Western companies acquire Chinese stakes in major ports around the world. Panama and the Caribbean were among the areas drawing U.S. officials’ attention, while Chinese investment in Jamaica’s Port of Kingston was also cited as a security concern. Officials within the Trump administration have also concluded that the United States lacks sufficient shipping capacity for wartime military logistics and is overly dependent on foreign vessels and ports. From Washington’s perspective, the greater China’s influence over maritime transport routes and logistics hubs connected to the U.S. homeland, the stronger the need to commit diplomatic and military resources to the Western Hemisphere.
Table 1. Europe’s Expanding Defense Responsibilities and Financing, Production and Procurement Challenges
| Category | Key Details | 
|---|---|
| Spending Target | NATO members to raise defense and security spending to 5% of GDP by 2035 | 
| Allocation by Sector | At least 3.5% of GDP for core defense requirements and up to 1.5% for security-related areas, including infrastructure protection and network defense | 
| Financing Burden | National governments must fund not only weapons purchases and personnel costs but also road and port upgrades for military transport | 
| Implementation Review | Annual spending plans required; the timetable for increases and the composition of spending to be reviewed in 2029 | 
| Production and Procurement Reform | Nationally fragmented defense industries and differing weapons systems constrain production growth and the efficiency of combined operations. Less duplication and greater joint procurement are needed | 
| EU Financial Support | Approximately $170.7 billion to support joint arms purchases and the expansion of critical defense capabilities | 
| Reconciling National Interests | Allocating production volumes and manufacturing sites for joint projects remains a challenge as governments prioritize their domestic defense industries | 
NATO to Raise Defense and Security Spending to 5% of GDP by 2035
Washington’s demands that Europe assume greater defense responsibilities are intensifying pressure on European governments to secure the funding for their own defense. At the summit in The Hague in June last year, NATO members agreed to increase defense and security-related spending to 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035. Specifically, at least 3.5% of GDP is to be allocated to core defense requirements, including personnel and weapons systems, and up to 1.5% to security-related areas such as critical infrastructure protection and network defense. National governments must therefore fund not only weapons acquisitions and force sustainment but also the roads and ports needed for military transport. To implement the agreement, members must submit annual plans for spending increases. In 2029, they will review the timetable and composition of those increases in light of the security environment and required military capabilities.
Ensuring that these funds translate efficiently into greater military capability also requires urgent reform of Europe’s fragmented weapons production and procurement systems. According to the Associated Press, nationally divided defense industries and disparate weapons systems have hampered efforts to expand production and improve the efficiency of combined operations. With Europe also needing to develop military equipment and intelligence capabilities for which it has relied on the United States, the case for reducing duplicate national investments and expanding joint procurement has become stronger. The EU has therefore decided to provide approximately $170.7 billion in financial support to help member states purchase weapons jointly and expand critical defense capabilities. However, with governments prioritizing their domestic defense manufacturers, negotiations over production volumes and manufacturing locations for joint projects are expected to prove difficult.
Developing a “Theory of Victory” Against a Russian Invasion
Europe’s debate over greater defense self-reliance is also driving changes to operational arrangements in preparation for reduced U.S. military support. This reflects a recognition that troops and equipment across the region must be closely integrated to ensure an effective initial response in a crisis. articles.title: EU Wants to Track Potential Rogue Efforts to Block Out Sun - Energy Connects
articles.summary: EU Wants to Track Potential Rogue Efforts to Block Out Sun  Energy Connects
articles.full_text:
(Bloomberg) -- The European Union has launched a €35 million ($39.4 million) tender to fund research and coordination on, among other things, detecting rogue efforts to alter the earth’s atmosphere by blocking out the sun.
The EU’s Horizon Europe arm, which funds research and innovation, launched the call for projects on Tuesday as part of an early stage effort to coordinate action on so-called Solar Radiation Modification, a nascent and controversial technology that could be used to cool the planet should temperatures rise to critical tipping points.
In a report last month, the UN warned that global temperatures are set to cross the key 1.5C threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years, and could climb as high as 2.6C without changes to current policies. The effects of climate change are already being felt with wildfires, droughts, hurricanes and severe floods happening increasingly frequently.
That’s led to concerns that governments or private actors could launch unsanctioned experiments to try and alter the climate at a regional or global level with potentially dangerous side effects. So far there is little in the way of international agreements to control or monitor such a move, and some scientists have called for an international non-use agreement on such solutions.
“This robust monitoring framework should be designed to detect and attribute outdoor experiments and deter potential unilateral deployments by private or state actors,” the tender published by the EU said. The tender makes clear that deployment and field experiments are out of the scope of the project.

articles.title: EU, China clash in Beijing talks over trade gap, PHEV curbs and rare earths - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: EU, China clash in Beijing talks over trade gap, PHEV curbs and rare earths - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
The European Union (EU) and China are locked in a tense war of nerves ahead of a high-level meeting in Beijing on the 8th–9th to discuss trade issues. As the EU pushes China to voluntarily restrict exports of some items and expand European corporations' access to the Chinese market to reduce its trade deficit with China, Beijing is rolling out countermeasures against what it calls EU protectionism. With the two sides clashing in particular over potential limits on exports of Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) to Europe, attention is on whether the talks will mark a turning point in the trade dispute.
According to Reuters on the 8th, Maroš Šefčovič, the European Union (EU) commissioner for trade and economic security, will meet with Wang Wentao, China's commerce minister, from that day to discuss trade imbalances and restrictions on exports of critical minerals. With a summit set for Oct. 15–16, the EU aims to secure concrete results at the talks that can reduce its trade deficit with China.
◇ EU unsheathes its sword over trade deficit… taking aim at Chinese PHEVs
The crux of this showdown is addressing the trade imbalance. The EU has long allowed broader market access for Chinese goods than the United States. As a result, the EU's trade deficit with China reached €360.6 billion (about 540 trillion won) in 2025, up 15% from the previous year. For the first half of this year, it is estimated to have risen 9% year over year. In response, the EU has been expanding anti-subsidy and anti-dumping investigations into Chinese products.
France and Germany on the 5th urged the European Commission to draw up rules that could restrict imports of Chinese goods. Germany, the EU's largest economy, had been reluctant to intervene in trade, but is said to have shifted to a tougher stance as competition with China has intensified difficulties for flagship German corporations such as Volkswagen. The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that if new rules are created, they are expected to function similarly to Section 301 of U.S. trade law.
The EU is particularly wary of the advance of Chinese automobiles into Europe. Reports say EU imports of electric vehicles rose 40% year over year in the past year. For plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), imports jumped 86% while prices fell 20%. More than half of the vehicles the EU imported were Chinese-made. While China still accounts for a large share of EU auto imports, PHEV imports in particular are rising rapidly.
This is attributed to tariff effects. Since Oct. 2024, the EU has imposed tariffs of up to 45.3% on Chinese electric vehicles, while PHEVs face only a 10% tariff, concentrating demand. The EU has therefore asked China to voluntarily limit PHEV exports. It is also reportedly preparing separate measures to curb imports of Chinese PHEVs. Bloomberg said, "If this measure succeeds, the EU could expand the same approach to other industries where it judges the trade imbalance to be severe."
◇ China counters EU protectionism… rare earths on the negotiating table
Beijing argues that the competitiveness of Chinese cars stems not only from government subsidies but also from technology, supply chain strength and market competition. It is pushing back that the EU's demand to curb exports on grounds of Chinese products' competitiveness is effectively a protectionist measure.
On the widening EU trade deficit with China, Beijing also argues that Europe's export restrictions on China and limits on market access are factors exacerbating the imbalance. The logic is that restricting Chinese corporations and products from entering the European market while demanding only China expand imports makes it difficult to achieve trade balance.
State-run Global Times warned in an editorial late the previous night that "the bill for protectionism will ultimately be paid by the party concerned (the EU)." The editorial claimed that sales of French cognac fell as a result of China's response to the EU's tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Citing the United States, it said, "The increase in output of protected domestic industries (from tariffs on China) was extremely limited," and argued the damage would ultimately fall on German manufacturing corporations, French wineries and European consumers.
Authorities warned of retaliation. China's Ministry of Commerce said on the 6th that if the EU adopts discriminatory restrictions on Chinese corporations or products, it will respond firmly. China has already launched an anti-dumping probe into EU-made para-nitrotoluene. On the 7th, "Weiyuantantian," a social media account under state-run China Central Television (CCTV), listed possible tools China could use if the EU adopts discriminatory measures against Chinese corporations or products, including anti-discrimination investigations, industrial and supply chain security reviews, and probes into the impact of overseas subsidies.
China is expected to use rare earths as a bargaining chip. The EU has raised concerns that Chinese controls on rare earth exports could expose European automakers and advanced manufacturers to supply chain uncertainty, and is asking for stable supply and predictability in export licensing procedures—an issue that has also been a key agenda item in a working group the two sides have operated since June.
Given the diverging interests over trade issues, pulling off a major agreement in the short term will not be easy. But because both China and the EU are experiencing trade frictions with the United States and would be burdened if their own clashes escalate into a full-blown trade conflict, they may use this meeting to seek compromises on some issues.
Weiyuantantian suggested several compromise options in a post on the 7th. Specifically: ▲ jointly monitor trade flows for hybrid cars and chemical products ▲ resolve the EV dispute through price undertakings ▲ expand European investment by Chinese corporations ▲ ensure a stable, non-discriminatory policy environment for Chinese corporations ▲ secure stable supplies of key materials (rare earths). Weiyuantantian said, "Because trade imbalances are structural problems formed over a long period, they are hard to solve with short-term restrictions alone. Both sides need to maintain strategic patience."

articles.title: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets - CNBC
articles.summary: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets  CNBCBritish Airways reveals all-new First, Club Suite, World Traveller Plus and World Traveller cabins as part of its multi-billion investment into customer experience  British Airways Media CentreThe A380 is back in fashion — here’s what you need to know  The TimesBritish Airways refurbishing A380s with ‘world’s largest’ business-class cabin  FlightGlobalBA wants to turn its A...
articles.full_text:
British Airways is building what it calls the “world’s largest” business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers.
The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub.
Here’s what’s changing:
- British Airways will outfit its Airbus A380, the world’s largest passenger plane, with a monster 106-seat business-class cabin, up from the current configuration of 97 business-class seats.
- First class will also be refreshed and will include 12 suites, down from the current A380 configuration of 14.
- Premium economy class will grow to 84 seats from 55.
- Standard economy seats will shrink to just 215 from 303.
British Airways said the 106 business-class suites, with sliding doors, will take up the entirety of the A380′s upper deck.
Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers’ appetite for more luxurious trips.
British Airways’ joint-venture partner, American Airlines, last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in a recent interview that customers are seeking high-end options on long flights, like its Perth-London nonstop.
“There is absolutely a customer who wants this and is prepared to pay a premium for it,” she said.
Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase.
The prices can be even higher if they’re selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights.
Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification.
British Airways’ overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane’s largest user, Emirates, in late 2021.

articles.title: EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request - The Guardian
articles.summary: EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request  The GuardianEuropean Union, Lithuania, United States Pressured by US, Brussels pulls out of Disinfo 2026 conference in Vilnius  Intelligence OnlineCanada yanks sponsorship of disinformation conference discussing U.S. as a threat  CBCUS lobbies allies to cut ties to anti-disinformation conference over panel critical of Washington, sources say  ReutersTrump administration pressure...
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands.
The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab.
Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website.
Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste.
Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference.
Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”. The document says Washington was “grateful” Lithuania supposedly found a panel framing the US as a foreign information threat “reprehensible and surprising” and welcomed its decision to limit involvement in the conference.
That panel – called “USA as a FIMI threat: adapt, acknowledge, push back”, with the acronym FIMI referring to “foreign information manipulation and interference” – took place Wednesday. It explored how Europe’s disinformation community could rebuild resilience without Washington, and is the first time the conference appears to have entertained the idea that the US could be a disinformation actor in Europe. Sources and the internal document indicate the state department was explicitly focused on this panel, which included three American speakers, among them a former CIA officer.
According to one person familiar with the deliberations, other communications appeared to originate from the office of Sarah B Rogers, the US undersecretary of state for public diplomacy.
Nina Jankowicz, a former US official and disinformation expert who in 2022 briefly headed the Biden administration’s Disinformation Governance Board, which Republicans assailed as a vehicle for policing Americans’ speech, said she understood that Washington had pressured Lithuania and Canada to withdraw from the conference. The Guardian understands that France was contacted as well.
“What this amounts to is a purported defender of free speech at the state department using the enormous power of the US government to try to pressure Americans from criticizing their government,” said Jankowicz.
In statements, Lithuania, Canada and the EU said the program of the conference did not align with their official views on the US role in disinformation – although that program had been in place for months before they withdrew their support, since June.
“Lithuania has cancelled its participation in ‘Disinfo 2026’ as several parts of the conference programme differ from the official position of the Government,” Lithuania’s foreign ministry wrote in a statement.
Global Affairs Canada “carefully assesses participation in, and sponsorship of, external events on a case-by-case basis,” GAC spokesperson Samantha Lafleur said. “Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference.”
Canadian officials are still participating in the conference, Lafleur added.
An EU spokesperson confirmed that the European External Action Service had decided to withdraw its support from the conference because “the organisers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU.”
EU officials, the Guardian understands, did not agree with the characterisation of the US as a disinformation actor.
Despite withdrawing its branding as an official supporter, the EU continues to fund the conference.
In its latest report on foreign information manipulation and interference threats, published in March, the EU’s diplomatic service named Russia and China as “threat actors” without any negative reference to the US.
A diplomatic source at France’s foreign ministry said “there’s absolutely no reason for us to change our commitments” when it came to supporting the conference.
“We stick to supporting civil society. It’s not just principled, it’s operational,” she said, adding that the conference was a “laboratory” that helped Europe develop key policy around disinformation.
The US state department has taken an increasingly interventionist posture towards free speech and civil society in Europe over the past year. The Guardian has revealed that the state department is awarding millions of dollars in non-competitive grants to organisations across the continent supportive of Trump’s agenda.
Lithuania’s withdrawal comes just after the prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevicius, said Lithuania would pay for a permanent US military base if the US agreed, a day after Trump said he would consider the request. Sinkevicius called a lasting American presence a critical guarantee of deterrence against Russia.
“They are great people, so we will certainly look at it,” the US president said on Monday.
Sinkevicius said he first proposed the idea in a meeting with Trump’s envoy John Coale, and called it a “critically important guarantee of deterrence and security.” Lithuania, a member of the EU and Nato, borders Russia and its close ally Belarus.
The US has kept a rotating armoured battalion of almost 1,000 troops in the country since 2019, the US Army has noted.

articles.title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK - BBC
articles.summary: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK  BBC
articles.full_text:
The UK needs to do more to back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.
Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.
Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market, are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.
The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.
'Take the handbrake off'
"If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss podcast.
"We need to take the handbrake off."
The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion.
Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries.
But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange, travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York.
'Stop throwing shade'
Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled.
Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised.
It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns.
"We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said.
There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added.
But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said.
"We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit."
However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks.
She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks.
She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016.
Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange.
It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow.
The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month.
"As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said.

articles.title: Artist unveils golden statue of a nude Donald Trump at European parliament building - The Art Newspaper
articles.summary: Artist unveils golden statue of a nude Donald Trump at European parliament building  The Art Newspaper‘King of Injustice’: Golden naked Trump statue installed at European Parliament  CNNNaked Trump statue goes on display in Strasbourg  DW.comNaked statue of Trump named ‘Orange Plague’ unveiled at European Parliament  The IndependentGolden naked Trump statue unveiled at European Parliament  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday (7 October), the artist Jens Galschiøt unveiled The Orange Plague, a 2.6m-tall sculpture depicting US President Donald Trump nude and perched atop the shoulders of a frail man, inside the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, France. Covered in 23-carat gold leaf, the Trump figure holds tiny scales of justice in one hand and a golf club in the other. A golf-ball-sized globe sits at the feet of the smaller, frail man below him, who is rendered in bronze.
The sculpture was installed on a plinth labelled with the work’s title and a caption that reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back.”
According to the artist, the work was inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes, a fairy tale in which an emperor is convinced to buy “invisible” clothing that is in fact non-existent. While people applaud the naked king, “a little boy says, ‘He has no clothes on,’ and then everyone begins to laugh at him”, Galschiøt tells The Art Newspaper. He adds that when he unveiled The Golden Plague, the sculpture was also met with laughter and applause.
The sculpture is the centrepiece of a three-day exhibition hosted by Per Clausen, a Danish member of the European Parliament (MEP). All visitors receive a 3D-printed miniature of the sculpture to take home. Galschiøt says he printed around 20,000 sculptures that he distributed not only to visitors but also to staff throughout the European Parliament. Galschiøt has also made the design files free for anyone who wants to print their own.
Galschiøt was inspired to distribute the miniatures by the Democracy Movement in Hong Kong, which 3D-scanned and printed hundreds of miniature versions of his 1997 sculpture The Pillar of Shame, which commemorates human rights violations including the Tiananmen Square massacre. These miniature pillars appeared across Hong Kong after the original sculpture was seized and disassembled.
“Normally I attack systems, but in this case, I will attack Trump personally,” Galschiøt says. His rendering was inspired by the president’s extensive gilding of the White House’s oval office and other properties he controls. “Now we put the gold on him,” the artist says, adding that the resulting image is “even more ridiculous than before”. “Trump is shining so much that nobody can see other people.”
The Orange Plague was previously displayed at the “hands off Greenland” demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier this year and the CopP30 UN Climate Summit in Belém, Brazil last year. After the present installation in Strasbourg, Galschiøt plans to exhibit The Orange Plague again at the Cop31 UN Climate Conference next month Antalya, Türkiye.
“Nations as well as NGOs are afraid to openly raise the subject [of] how to deal with Trump and his policies, fearing tariffs, fund-cuts, deportations or the like,” Galschiøt wrote on his website. “As an independent art workshop we are not restricted by such bonds. This sculpture has been made to address ‘the elephant in the room’ and start a necessary debate [about] how the US is destroying the world’s only chance to counter the climate catastrophe.”
A spokesperson for the European Parliament told CNN that the exhibition of Galschiøt's sculpture had been approved by the parliament's quaestors, a cross-party group of MEPs that handles administrative decisions. “Each MEP is entitled to sponsor two cultural events or exhibitions per parliamentary term in dedicated areas,” the spokesperson added.
Galschiøt’s work follows in a long line of protest art targeting Trump in the decade since he launched his 2016 presidential campaign, much of it brightly gilded, depicting him fully or nearly nude—and, occasionally, both.

articles.title: Defence spending hike a sign ‘Europe can awaken from long slumber’, says Rubio - Cotswold Journal
articles.summary: Defence spending hike a sign ‘Europe can awaken from long slumber’, says Rubio  Cotswold Journal
articles.full_text:
Increased military funding is a sign “Europe can awaken from its long slumber”, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said.
Speaking in Greece, America’s top diplomat highlighted the commitment made by the UK and other Nato members last year to hike defence spending to 5% of economic output by 2035 in the face of burgeoning threats from Russia and China, and demands by US President Donald Trump that allies make a bigger contribution to their own security.
The British Government is under pressure to set out how it will meet the target, amid reports Prime Minister Andy Burnham is looking at delaying an announcement on a key funding milestone.
Mr Rubio also said that while “passions” had strained ties between the US and Europe, they “must not be allowed to break them” as he highlighted the importance of a strong alliance in “confronting the threats of our age”.
And standing in front of the ruins of the Acropolis, Mr Rubio linked the values of ancient Greece to the US president’s “America First” agenda.
The former Republican senator has been tipped as a frontrunner for his party’s nomination in next year’s race for the White House.
Pointing out that the ancient Greeks understood that nations have interests, Mr Rubio said: “They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.
“This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump administration hopes to reclaim – reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilisation.
“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.
“There are already signs.
“Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift – skyrocketing defence spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programmes, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defence commitments made last year in The Hague.”
Mr Rubio added: “Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.
“Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age. And we can.
“Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum. Quite the opposite. Our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts.”
He highlighted the “unprecedented” agreement recently struck between the US, Denmark and Greenland over the Arctic territory.
Mr Rubio said: “All three partners in that deal emerged victorious. All of Europe, and Nato and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.
“We want to win together. We must win together.”
The secretary of state also warned that the West had come “to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional”.
He said: “We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world. Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt. We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness.
“The word ‘nationalism’ became a dirty word. And so we tore down our monuments, we condemned our own history. And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.
“In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay.”
In the meantime, rivals and adversaries had filled “the vacuum left behind by our weakness”, Mr Rubio said.
Arguing Western civilisation was “at a crossroads”, he said: “The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.
“Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice. We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power – to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialise our economy, to rebuild our defence, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future.”
Mr Rubio added: “It has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritising the global community over one’s own people.
“And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else.”
But in making the case for nationalism he also stressed the importance of partnerships in the face of war, terrorism and global competition.
Mr Rubio said: “And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together – understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them, it is to defend them.
“And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognise their common interests.”

articles.title: Maricarmen, symbol of Spain's housing protests, dies - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Maricarmen, symbol of Spain's housing protests, dies  Euronews.comSpanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies, union says  BBC87-year-old Maricarmen dies in hospital after infamous eviction ordeal  Euronews.comThe 87-year-old woman evicted from her home in Spain has died  Sky NewsMaría del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
The 87-year-old woman had withstood four eviction attempts in the past decade. In a final message from her hospital bed, she urged protesters: "Fight!"
Maricarmen Abascal, whose resistance to eviction from her flat in Madrid sparked a growing nationwide protest has died. Her plight brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets and ultimately brought forward a general election after mass demonstrations across the country.
The elderly woman, who had lived in her flat in Madrid’s Retiro district for 70 years, was eventually evicted at the fourth attempt under the gaze of the media, after she was unable to pay the increased rent. She was admitted to hospital, but she managed to force the property fund that expelled her from her home to back down and allow her to return, following an agreement with the authorities.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenant’s Union said in a statement Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”
Protesters who have been camped out in Madrid's iconic Sol square held a minute of silence after hearing news of her passing.
Pedro Sanchez expresses condolences after hearing of Maricarmens's passing
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has expressed his condolences in a post on X. "All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said, “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”
Meanwhile protester are gathering again in Madrid and unions are promoting a general strike. The UGT and CCOO unions urged the population to "mobilise for better salaries, for decent housing and for price controls in the face of inflation that undermines our purchasing power".
Pedro Sanchez's left-wing minority government last week suffered a bruising legislative defeat when right-wing opposition parties voted down emergency decrees to address the housing crisis.
A fresh round of protests turned violent in Barcelona on Monday night, just hours after Sánchez announced he was dissolving Parliament and calling early elections for Nov. 29.
Spain’s government on Tuesday approved urgent measures to tackle the housing crisis, similar to those Parliament rejected last week.
Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. The protesters have been demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud, and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable.

articles.title: EU-Canada Pact Heralds Bloc’s Enlargement Again - Carolina Political Review
articles.summary: EU-Canada Pact Heralds Bloc’s Enlargement Again  Carolina Political Review
articles.full_text:
Both sides of the Atlantic welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s invitation for Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union during the annual European Parliament’s State of the Union address with open arms. Though Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney received a standing ovation, the other side of the Atlantic has more questions than answers, as current candidate countries Montenegro, Albania, or Ukraine were rarely mentioned.
Von der Leyen’s call to elevate the EU’s relationship with Canada to “the highest level possible” accompanied a sense of urgency to reimagine partnerships amid looming economic, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity threats. Chief among all concerns, though, was gratitude for their shared values, in part due to their cooperation across defense in Ukraine, climate change, artificial intelligence, and supply chains. Von der Leyen said, “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world.” Carney similarly repeated the same idea at the Toronto International Film Festival, as analysts wonder if this is to justify their unusual transatlantic alliance to critics, who may argue this is simply to pressure the President of the United States away from economic aggression.
The EU and Canada may argue this is a natural next step for their relationship as they already share a provisional Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), Canada’s biggest bilateral initiative since the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which was dissolved in June 2020. Although not fully in force, it eliminated duties on 99 percent of all tariff lines for European goods exported to Canada; however, full implementation requires ratification by the national parliaments of all EU member states.
However, European Parliamentarians may see the CETA’s progression toward an “Alliance for the Future” as Von der Leyen stepping on member states’ toes to accelerate the alliance. National capitals report never being consulted on Canada’s associate membership before the address, and diplomats granted anonymity labelled the secrecy as “dangerous” and “unwise”, according to Politico. The European Commission President has already received criticism from Parliamentarians over her centralized and hierarchical leadership in a failed no-confidence vote. Manon Aubry, a French member of the European Parliament, added to increasing discontent and questioned Von der Leyen’s democratic and popular mandate for Canada’s membership in the EU.
Additional members of the European Parliament may raise eyebrows, as Politico reported that earlier drafts of the State of the Union address did not feature the Canadian initiative. The Parliament’s polarisation could mean there are more differences between the 27 member states over the Union’s expansion and Von der Leyen’s authority that may need to be resolved before another member could be added.
Discussions of what benefits associate membership may entail are already underway. Membership may reflect the European Economic Area’s access to the EU’s single market, built around the free movement of goods, services, capital and people throughout the 27-member bloc. If “associate membership” reflects the benefits that full members of the EU have, Canadians could also be privy to living, studying, working, and retiring anywhere in the EU, on top of access to EU funding, agricultural subsidies, and recourse to the European Court of Justice. However, Canada may need to fulfill supranational obligations, including adopting the acquis, the complete acceptance and implementation of the entire body of existing EU law and treaties. These could also include contributing to the EU budget and adopting the euro currency, if Canada chooses to integrate deeper into the eurozone under the Economic and Monetary Union.
For Europe, the ‘associate membership’ offer appears to be another throwback, reminiscent of the bloc’s 2004 “Big Bang” enlargement, which added twelve countries before other rapid changes, including the adoption of the Lisbon Treaty and the widespread circulation of the euro. The 27-nation bloc has since faced various challenges, including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, sovereign debt, and migration crises. Meanwhile, candidate countries such as Ukraine, Montenegro, and Albania are still waiting to join the EU after more than two decades of negotiations. They face significant roadblocks, like pro-Russian member states blocking Ukraine’s membership or the EU’s concerns over democratic backsliding for both Georgia and Serbia. Although Montenegro has been named a “front-runner” among applicant states, it is not expected to achieve full membership until 2028 at the earliest. Yet, it has been thirteen years since the last country joined the Union, and more than twenty years since the EU promised accession to the Western Balkans at the 2003 Thessaloniki summit. Frustration amongst the Western Balkans may stifle Canadian ambitions for a quick entry.
As European Parliamentarians and critics alike race to quell candidate countries’ anxieties, non-candidate countries are also reassessing their ties to the bloc. Norway, Liechtenstein and Iceland are part of the EU’s internal market in the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). However, they are not part of the EU’s customs union, trade policy framework, or judicial participation. Similarly, Switzerland, another non-candidate country, supports bilateral agreement packages with the EU and participates in the Schengen Area, while also contributing financially to the post-2004 member states. None of these nations have full decision-making power within the bloc, offering a preview of what Canadian membership in the EU could entail in the absence of a defined framework.
Other non-EU member states, especially Türkiye, have had more public and seemingly harried stances over recent EU changes in the UN General Assembly. Despite the EU’s reliance on Turkish regional security and migration management, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan warned that he may review relations with the bloc. Türkiye's forty-year-long application has repeatedly stalled as EU officials cite human rights concerns and democratic backsliding. Nevertheless, the two entities share a 217 billion euros customs union, heavily dependent on arms and defence given its position in the Corridor. This surpasses the EU-Canada trade relationship, worth a mere 92 billion euros.
Multiple non-members have similarly been attracted by the prospect of EU integration before being swayed by eurosceptic worries. Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Greenland have also held unsuccessful referendums, and Greenland swiftly exited the EU’s predecessor, the European Economic Community, in 1985. But eurosceptic anxieties over loss of regulatory autonomy and economic governance under the EU seem to still be potent after the eurozone crisis. Greece’s bailout referendum in 2015 even inspired Citigroup to label their eurosceptic ambitions as “Grexit” during the eurozone crisis, before Brexit happened a year later.
The EU sustained political goodwill, but the Troika’s structural adjustment policies during the eurozone crisis caused long-lasting political damage, which far-right and anti-EU figures such as Dutch Member of the House of Representatives Geert Wilders and Marine Le Pen in France have capitalized on. Furthermore, the financial burden of enlargement extends beyond political cost, as expenses to current member states rise to more than 256 billion euros should they expand to the nine candidate countries, excluding Canada.
Ex-EU members have also weighed in on Von der Leyen’s offer to Canada as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham continued lobbying for the UK’s inclusion in “Made in Europe” laws during the UN General Assembly, but associate membership remains off the table. He said, “The European Union made it clear that that wasn’t open to us.” British diplomats may view this as favoritism towards Canada, given that the EU Chief Brexit Negotiator previously said no nation can have a relationship with the EU where they can be “half in and half out” of the single market. Under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the UK still enjoys tariff-free, quota-free trade in qualifying goods with the EU, though frictionless trade remains far from reality. British politicians may yield that the UK failed to reach a post-Brexit deal that could have mirrored the potential perks of associate EU membership now presented to Carney. As former Bank of England governor, he had warned about Brexit’s recession impacts despite calls that he breached his impartiality mandate, but his fears of lower economic growth, business investment and a weaker pound came to fruition regardless. Meanwhile, other British Commonwealth of Nations countries, like Australia, seem to take great interest in Canada’s approach in deepening their ties to the EU.
Debates over integrating more member states into the European Union will intensify in the coming weeks amid the excitement that Canadians could enjoy the benefits of EU membership. However, they may have to first wait for the potentially hefty financial contributions and regulatory burdens that associate membership may come with, if it even comes at all. As always, candidate countries will continue to reflect on their own statuses, and non-members will try to seek an answer to the age-old question of whether deepening their partnership with the EU is worth it. Europe and the transatlantic community will grapple with what it means to be in the EU if associate membership allows Canadians to enjoy access privileges, such as subsidized university education in Brussels, that remain out of reach for Ukrainians. After waves of EU expansion, many European citizens in applicant countries may still wonder whether the “ever closer union” will ever be that close for them.
