articles.title: Far-right surge threatens Europe’s drive to rearm - POLITICO.eu
articles.summary: Far-right surge threatens Europe’s drive to rearm  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
The growing popularity of far-right parties across Europe is sparking worries in NATO that they could weaken public support for rearmament and military aid to Ukraine as risks grow of a confrontation with Russia.
In France, Italy, Belgium, Germany, Poland and Romania, these parties are looking to turn voters’ cost-of-living concerns into opposition to aid for Kyiv, and rejection of higher national defense budgets and a greater role for the EU in defense — although each party has often sharply diverging views on those issues.
France’s National Rally leader Marine Le Pen last month called for limiting aid to Ukraine, saying: “financially, we can’t do it anymore.”

articles.title: Russia: Doubling down in Ukraine – and against the West - Lowy Institute
articles.summary: Russia: Doubling down in Ukraine – and against the West  Lowy Institute
articles.full_text:
Russia is intensifying aerial onslaughts against Ukrainian cities, particularly the capital Kyiv (Mladen Antonov/AFP via Getty Images)
Russia: Doubling down in Ukraine – and against the West
Peace talks continue in name only, as Moscow counts on exhaustion to secure gains it cannot win on the battlefield.
Hopes turned out misplaced that Kyiv’s long-range drone attacks on Russian energy and other infrastructure over the summer heralded a turning of the tide in Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. As winter approaches, Ukraine finds itself under relentless, widespread and damaging Russian missile and drone assaults.
Russia’s strategy seems clear: sustain maximum battlefield pressure on Ukraine; intensify aerial onslaughts against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure; step up hybrid attacks on Kyiv’s European allies; all the while engaging performatively in US efforts to secure a negotiated settlement to end the war.
Russia has been unable so far to seize the key “fortress” cities of Slovyansk, Kramatorsk and Kostyantynivka. This war of attrition, with the battlefield dominated by drones, has offered Moscow little scope for dramatic advances (although an innovative Ukrainian counter-offensive (Opens in new window) has recently made targeted gains).
Russia continues to sustain heavy casualties, requiring it to recruit at least 30,000 new troops monthly. This has been getting harder via voluntary recruitment, prompting speculation (Opens in new window) that Moscow might engage in a creeping mobilisation – something the Kremlin would prefer to avoid for political and economic reasons. However, Ukraine too is suffering substantial losses (Opens in new window), and faces a growing deficit in personnel and munitions, relative to its much larger adversary.
Vladimir Putin still thinks time is on Russia’s side – and that it can outlast both Kyiv and its European supporters.
Moscow wants to undermine civilian morale by making life intolerable, especially in Kyiv, thereby bringing the city to its knees.
Facing stalemate on the battlefield, Moscow has stepped up its aerial assault on Ukraine. With the introduction of jet-propelled drones and ballistic missiles, Russia has sharply ramped up the frequency, volume and range of targets of its attacks in recent weeks. And made them even more deadly and damaging.
Ukraine’s efforts to counter these attacks have been hampered by insufficient air defences – especially Patriot systems. As colder winter conditions set in over coming months, Russia will intensify its missile and drone attacks, seeking to destroy key energy and logistic infrastructure. Moscow wants to undermine civilian morale by making life intolerable, especially in Kyiv, thereby bringing the city to its knees.
Ukraine faces other problems, too. The economy is floundering (Opens in new window), with its vital but besieged steel industry at a standstill, and grain exports cut off through Black Sea ports. Kyiv is also running out of money, and has sought an advance on EU (Opens in new window) and IMF (Opens in new window) funding for 2027.
Signs are growing of disunity within the Ukrainian political elite, not helped by missteps (Opens in new window) from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Moscow will doubtless seek to foment such dissension, seeking to distract and undermine Kyiv’s war effort.
Further afield, Russia will step up efforts to influence opinion and weaken support for Ukraine in Europe – as European leaders have warned recently.
This may include social media manipulation, political interference, cyber-attacks, and sabotage. Such “grey-zone” malign actions are calibrated not to provoke a collective response under NATO’s Article V but aim to unsettle public opinion and discourage European support (military, economic and political) for Ukraine.
So far, European support has held firm. But the rise of populist parties on the right and left, challenging traditional centrist governments, especially in France and Germany, suggests European support may come under greater pressure next year.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy meeting with troops in Kupyansk in December (President of Ukraine/Flickr)
Meanwhile, Russia will doubtless affect a continuing interest in US efforts to negotiate an end to the fighting in Ukraine. But, unless such a settlement meets Moscow’s key interests and objectives, its engagement will be essentially performative.
Moscow will aim to keep the Trump administration on side, while driving a wedge between Washington and its European allies. Moscow is reportedly (Opens in new window) offering Washington bilateral commercial advantages, presumably to persuade it to pressure Kyiv into accepting a deal.
But there’s no real sign that Moscow is seriously interested yet in ending the fighting.
Grumbling (Opens in new window) in the Russian elite and wider population about tiring of the war (Opens in new window) is hardly surprising. Economic strains from the burden of war are growing. But in Russia, public opinion can be managed (and if necessary, dissent repressed), while the economic problems are not of an order to constrain Putin’s determination to continue the fighting until the Kremlin’s objectives are achieved.
Nor does Moscow consider itself isolated in the world. In recent weeks, Putin has engaged with its BRICS and Shanghai Cooperation Organisation partners, including China and India, while also portraying itself as a leader of the “Global Majority”, contesting (Opens in new window) Western domination of traditional multilateral institutions.
Recent statements by Putin (Opens in new window) and Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov (Opens in new window) indicate that Moscow remains committed to achieving its core objectives – control over all of Donbas, pliant government in Kyiv, and Ukrainian neutrality – such as would draw Ukraine back into Russia’s sphere of influence.
And it’s not just Ukraine.
In his speech (Opens in new window) last week to the Valdai Discussion Club, Putin reiterated that Moscow considered the Ukraine war a proxy conflict, with Kyiv merely a puppet acting at the behest of Western governments intent on undermining Russia.
Reflecting that Russia sees itself pitched in long-term confrontation with the West, Moscow’s 2027 budget projects a 27% rise in defence spending (Opens in new window). The cost will be borne by reduced spending on health and education, and a rising budget deficit.
The Kremlin, then, remains determined to achieve its goals in Ukraine, while pursuing its wider ambition to build Russia’s military capabilities to bolster Russia’s standing and influence in the emerging multipolar world.

Dublin, Oct. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- "USA Semiconductor Foundry Market - Strategic Insights and Forecasts (2026-2031)" has been added to ResearchAndMarkets.com's offering.
The US Semiconductor Foundry Market is projected to grow from USD 16.4 billion in 2026 to USD 23.9 billion by 2031, representing a CAGR of 7.8%. Market expansion is being supported by rising investments in domestic semiconductor manufacturing, federal and state-level incentives, supply chain security priorities, and increasing chip demand across artificial intelligence, automotive electronics, data centers, telecommunications, industrial automation, and defense systems.
The United States continues to expand fabrication infrastructure to reduce dependence on overseas manufacturing and improve access to critical semiconductor technologies. Public funding, tax incentives, and private capital commitments are accelerating the construction and modernization of fabrication facilities. These investments are expected to strengthen domestic production capacity, encourage process innovation, and support long-term technology leadership.
Key Market Drivers
Government policy remains a central growth driver for the US Semiconductor Foundry Market. Funding programs and tax incentives reduce financial exposure associated with large-scale fabrication projects and encourage investment in advanced process technologies, specialty manufacturing, and domestic supply networks.
Demand from high-growth industries is also shaping foundry investment strategies. Automotive electrification, advanced driver assistance systems, power electronics, and connected vehicle platforms require high-voltage, radio-frequency, analog, mixed-signal, and power semiconductor technologies. Mature and mid-range process nodes, including the 65 nm to 200 nm range, remain important for automotive, industrial, communications, and defense applications.
Artificial intelligence and high-performance computing are creating additional opportunities for advanced nodes, specialized chip architectures, and advanced packaging. Continued growth in cloud computing and data center infrastructure is increasing demand for high-performance processors, accelerators, and associated semiconductor components. Telecommunications and industrial automation further support the need for reliable domestic foundry capacity.
Market Challenges
High capital requirements and lengthy construction schedules remain significant constraints. Semiconductor fabs require specialized equipment, complex commissioning processes, dependable utility infrastructure, and highly skilled engineering talent. These requirements can delay the transition from announced investment to commercial production.
Domestic manufacturers also remain connected to a global network of semiconductor equipment suppliers, specialty chemical producers, material providers, and component manufacturers. Supply disruptions, equipment lead times, raw material shortages, and rising operating costs may affect production schedules. Workforce availability is another strategic concern as companies compete for experienced engineers, technicians, and manufacturing specialists.
Technology and Application Outlook
The market includes advanced and mature technology nodes supporting logic, analog, mixed-signal, power, and specialty semiconductor production. Advanced nodes are expected to remain critical for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing, while mature technologies will continue serving automotive electronics, industrial equipment, communications infrastructure, consumer electronics, and defense applications.
Both integrated device manufacturer foundries and pure-play foundries are investing in capacity, process development, advanced packaging, and specialty manufacturing capabilities. Automotive and industrial electronics are expected to remain prominent end-use segments as vehicles, factories, energy systems, and connected equipment incorporate more semiconductor-based controls.
Competitive and Strategic Outlook
Competition is centered on fabrication scale, process capability, production reliability, advanced packaging, customer access, and the ability to support specialized applications. Semiconductor manufacturers are forming strategic collaborations with equipment suppliers, research institutions, technology companies, and government agencies to accelerate research and development, improve workforce training, and strengthen domestic supply chains.
The long-term outlook remains positive, supported by policy initiatives, industrial investment, and sustained semiconductor demand. Although capital intensity, talent shortages, and global supply dependencies may limit the pace of expansion, coordinated public and private investment is expected to improve US semiconductor manufacturing resilience through 2031.

articles.summary: Western Pharmaceutical Supply Vulnerabilities Exposed in Deepening China Reliance  azat.tv
articles.full_text:
The Upstream Chokepoint in Global Medicine Supply
Decades of cost containment in Western health systems have left the United States and Europe deeply vulnerable to Chinese pharmaceutical dominance, according to a report published by the Council on Foreign Relations. While public attention often focuses on finished drugs, the most critical risk sits further upstream in active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and the basic chemical building blocks required to manufacture them.
For essential medications such as metformin, a widely prescribed diabetes drug, roughly one-third of the supply relies on Chinese ingredients. However, when tracing the chemical precursors back to their earliest stages, exposure surpasses four-fifths. Antibiotics including amoxicillin and cefpodoxime follow a similar trajectory, exposing a structural chokepoint that neither transatlantic tariffs nor unilateral onshoring efforts have resolved.
Transatlantic Pressures and the Tariff Dilemma
The strategic challenge escalated when Washington introduced tariffs of up to 100 percent on imported patented medicines and their core ingredients, capping European products at 15 percent. Generic drugs remain temporarily exempt pending a crucial review. According to the analysis, these unilateral measures risk backfiring by raising production costs for allied manufacturers and eroding political backing in European capitals for coordinated supply chain security.
Despite these pressures, Europe retains critical manufacturing assets that North America lacks. Austria hosts the Western world’s last large-scale, fully integrated penicillin production facility, while the United States maintains no domestic capacity for penicillin ingredients or core precursors. Consequently, European regulators approach Washington not as supplicants, but as potential co-suppliers of strategic health security.
Practical Steps for Transatlantic Resilience
Experts argue that transatlantic partners should bypass contentious tariff negotiations and begin with measures that require minimal political trust. Initial priorities include joint mapping of upstream supply flows through bodies like the European Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority alongside U.S. counterparts. Additionally, NATO should incorporate demand stress-testing for antibiotics, analgesics, and anesthetics under mobilization conditions into its core resilience framework.
Long-term security will ultimately require coordinated demand—such as long-term purchase commitments that help western manufacturers bridge the 40 percent price gap with Chinese alternatives. However, analysts warn that Europe must safeguard its regulatory and pricing autonomy rather than trading one dependency for another under mounting trade pressures.

articles.title: UK airports introduce major border change from today for all passport holders - Manchester Evening News
articles.summary: UK airports introduce major border change from today for all passport holders  Manchester Evening NewsRoll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates  BBCAirports to go contactless in major boost for UK passengers  GOV.UKThe five new air travel rules every British holidaymaker needs to know  The i PaperNew technology will see UK passengers able to pass through airport gates without showing passports  The Independent
articles.full_text:
Airport security is going contactless - but passengers will still need their passports with them
East Midlands Airport will be the first UK airport to introduce a major change to the way people get through security. From October 6, eGates at UK airports will gradually switch to the new contactless technology, with every eGate set to be upgraded by early 2027.
Under the new system, passengers will approach an eGate and have their photo taken, the system checks this live image against verified immigration, travel and passport information and then the eGate opens automatically once these checks are complete.
The technology was successfully trialled for three weeks at Manchester Airport in October last year, The Times reports. According to the Home Office, passengers typically passed through the gates faster and had a better experience.
Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter
The phased rollout will start at East Midlands Airport, initially for British citizens, before it will be expanded to more airports and other nationalities already eligible for eGates over the coming months.
All e-gates, which are in operation at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted airports, will have the upgraded system by early next year.
The Government has stressed that passengers will still need to travel with their passport, as they will need it to check in and board the plane.
Phil Douglas, Director General of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country. By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK’s robust border security.
"Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families."
Karen Dee, chief executive of AirportsUK, the trade body for UK airports, said: "This will be excellent news for the passenger and demonstrates how UK airports continue to be at the forefront of new technologies to keep our borders safe, while improving the travelling experience.
"It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout."
Steve Griffiths, Managing Director of East Midlands Airport, said: "We’re delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless eGates introduced by Border Force. As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers’ journeys smoother, swifter and simpler.
"This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area."

Chris Wilson, Head of Terminal & Capacity Planning at Birmingham Airport, said: "We’re pleased to be one of the first airports in the UK to introduce UK Border Force’s contactless eGates. Working closely with our industry partners and government agencies, we have actively supported the rollout of the new UK Border Force system here at Birmingham Airport."

articles.title: Euro falls against dollar: are we heading for a new debt crisis ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - Opinions - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: Euro falls against dollar: are we heading for a new debt crisis ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - Opinions  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
The euro fell to a 17-month low against the US dollar. This will increase inflation in the EU, where political worries and concerns about French debt are already worrying investors. Is a new fiscal crisis looming?
The euro's exchange rate against the dollar has collapsed to values not seen in 17 months. This is happening against the background of growing risks related to debts, especially in France, concerns about government bond yields and rising fuel prices.
The euro has been falling against the dollar for most of 2026, having lost about 5% of its value since the beginning of the year. On Monday, it reached $1.12, its lowest level since early 2025.
France has serious fiscal problems
Ricardo Amaro, an economist at “Oxford Economics", told DW that the overall decline could be due to a change in investors' expectations about the US Federal Reserve's interest rate policy. However, he pointed out that the latest depreciation of the euro was probably caused by concerns about France.
Paris has long had severe fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron took office in May 2017, public spending has increased while he introduced significant tax breaks. As a result, the country's public debt has increased by more than 1 trillion euros.
The country's debt-to-gross domestic product ratio is currently almost 118%. Budgets are out of balance, and deficits regularly exceed 5 percent. Concerns about low growth in the eurozone and a surge in energy prices have led many investors to look again at France's problems, while many have turned to safer options such as German government bonds.
The spread between the yields on 10-year French and German government bonds hit its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week. It is a closely watched indicator of financial stability in the EU.
Will the European Central Bank intervene?
The pressure on the euro and on European government bond markets, including Italy, has led to calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent anxiety from turning into panic. Jim Reid of „Deutsche Bank“ said on Monday that at one point last week the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" had set in.
Economist Ricardo Amaro believes this will be a challenge for the ECB to act in a way that doesn't make the situation worse. He expects policymakers to continue to monitor currency trends between the US dollar and the euro but to refrain from trying to influence the market.
In recent years, France has been gripped by political crises, with the adoption of annual budgets becoming a serious test of the government's stability. Although the 2027 budget, which has been approved, includes reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, Marine Le Pen's far-right party continues to lead in the polls for the 2027 presidential election.
Inflation further complicates the situation
The prospect of a Le Pen victory is scaring investors, as is the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany party in the Federal Republic. Much of the political instability is due to voter dissatisfaction with the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called early elections after measures to tackle the country's housing crisis were rejected in parliament.
According to Amaro, the weakening of the euro could deepen the inflation problem. “A sharper weakening of the euro would amplify the inflation shock, and inflation is already expected to remain high into 2027,” he said. A weaker euro would raise the price of imported goods, especially those denominated in U.S. dollars. The prices of global commodities such as oil and gas are determined in dollars, meaning that the surge in energy prices is likely to continue, as are those for U.S. imports.
Memories of the EU debt crisis have many observers worried that the signals from France could lead to a similar development. Some economists are skeptical, but Amaro warns that the expected rise in interest rates from the ECB and inflation mean the situation needs to be watched closely.

articles.title: Three risks weigh on Europe's growth - Times of Oman
articles.summary: Three risks weigh on Europe's growth  Times of Oman
articles.full_text:
Brussels: Costly energy, rising inflation and higher borrowing costs together threaten to weaken Europe's economic recovery by squeezing household spending and business investment.
The euro area economy has proved more resilient than expected, prompting the European Central Bank (ECB) to raise its 2026 and 2027 growth forecasts in September.
Emergency fuel releases may ease the immediate supply strain, but reliance on imports leaves Europe exposed to further disruptions. The ECB must balance inflation risks against weakening demand, while governments face pressure from rising costs as they seek to cushion the energy shock.
A coordinated release of emergency reserves may ease Europe's diesel shortage, but declining domestic refining capacity leaves the region dependent on imports.
On Oct. 2, leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over four months through the International Energy Agency, including substantial diesel supplies within the first 20 days. They also pledged to avoid export restrictions among member countries and called for coordinated refinery maintenance and higher utilisation rates where feasible.
The agreement followed US pressure on European governments to release emergency diesel stocks. Later that day, US President Donald Trump said the United States would not impose a diesel export ban, easing concerns about a potential disruption to European supplies.
Releasing stocks may buy time, but can not solve insufficient production capacity. FuelsEurope, an association representing European fuel manufacturers, said that 35 European refineries had closed since 2009, reducing capacity by 20 percent. It said Europe's dependence on imported diesel and jet fuel could deepen and extend to other products without corrective action.
Additional crude supplies cannot fully relieve a diesel shortage if refineries lack the capacity to process them. The G7's focus on refinery operations alongside reserve releases reflects that problem.
Gas supplies pose another risk ahead of winter. Joachim Nagel, president of Germany's central bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank, said on Monday that low storage levels may force Europe to purchase substantially larger volumes during the heating season, leaving gas prices vulnerable.
High energy costs squeeze business profits and may prompt companies to raise prices. Higher fuel and heating bills also reduce households' spending power, weakening demand for other goods and services.
Philip R. Lane, a member of the ECB's executive board, said companies may have to pay higher energy and input bills before they can adjust production or selling prices, increasing their need for short-term financing.
Annual inflation in the euro area rose to an estimated 3.8 percent in September from 3.2 percent in August, according to Eurostat's flash estimate. Energy prices rose 18.8 percent from a year earlier, up from 14.3 percent in August.
Underlying price pressures remained more contained. Inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco edged up to 2.5 percent from 2.4 percent. Services inflation rose to 3.2 percent, while inflation in non-energy industrial goods eased to 1.1 percent.
The figures highlight the ECB's challenge: determining whether the energy shock will spread to other prices and wages or weaken demand enough to curb inflation.
"There are so far no clear signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting," Nagel said. Longer-term inflation expectations remained consistent with the ECB's 2 percent target, he added.
A prolonged shock, however, could encourage companies to pass on costs and workers to seek compensation for lost purchasing power.
The ECB raised its key interest rates by 25 basis points in both June and September, bringing its deposit facility rate to 2.5 percent. It said further rate decisions will depend on incoming data and assessments at each meeting.
On Monday, Lane said higher energy costs could weaken activity and reduce household incomes and business profits. Those effects, together with tighter financial conditions, could limit the monetary policy adjustment needed to bring inflation back to target.
Concerns about government finances are adding to borrowing costs.
France remains a focus of investor concern. The spread between French and German 10-year government bond yields widened by about 5 basis points to 145.5 basis points in Monday early trading. Investors questioned France's ability to rein in its budget deficit amid political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Borrowing costs can rise even without another ECB rate increase. Investors may demand greater compensation for fiscal risk, while higher government bond yields can feed into financing costs across the economy.
Global developments also matter. Lane said the worldwide artificial intelligence investment boom was plausibly contributing to higher long-term interest rates. "Especially since the scale of the European AI boom is not of the same order as the global AI boom, the increase in long-term interest rates constitutes a material tightening of financial conditions for the euro area," he said.
Governments face a difficult trade-off. Subsidies can cushion households and companies against energy costs, but financing them through additional borrowing can intensify investors' concerns about public finances.
Europe's resilience will depend partly on whether fuel supplies improve before expensive energy and credit force businesses to cut investment and households to curb spending. Emergency reserves can ease the immediate squeeze, but they cannot resolve the import dependence and capacity constraints that leave the region exposed to further shocks.

articles.title: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vapers - BBC
articles.summary: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vapers  BBCSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
More than a million people who say they have never smoked are now vapers, latest data for 2025 reveals - up from around 940,000 in 2024.
People aged 25-34 are vaping more than any others, overtaking 16 to 24-year-olds, with 16.4% using e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.
For the second year in a row, more over-16s in Great Britain are using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Meanwhile, the number of smokers in the UK continues to fall to nearly one in 10 adults, or 4.9 million people, down from 5.3 million in 2024, with more over-16s now vaping than smoking at 5.4 million.
Vaping has overtaken smoking
Experts say the popularity of cigarette smoking has decreased as the harmful effects of tobacco have encouraged many to quit.
Vaping is less harmful than smoking, although the long-term effects are not yet clear, says the NHS.
It says non-smokers and people aged 17 and under should never vape.
The ONS figures show the percentage of people who had never used an e-cigarette continued to decrease in 2025 (83.0%) compared with 2024 (83.4%).
Twenty-five to 34-year-olds are now more likely to use vapes than 16 to 24-year-olds.
David Mais, from the ONS, said vapers were getting older and that "may reflect existing users getting older, growing popularity among this age group, or a combination of both".
Smoke-free generation
New legislation in the UK, taking affect in the new year, will permanently ban the legal sale of tobacco to anyone born on or after January 1, 2009 to create a "smoke-free" generation.
Hazel Cheeseman, from the charity Action on Smoking and Health, said the latest statics showed encouraging progress in cutting smoking rates.
She added: "Smoking has fallen enormously over recent decades, but it remains the biggest driver of preventable death in the UK. Now is the time to finish the job."
According to the ONS, men were more likely to smoke than women in 2025, similar to previous years.
And people aged 45-54 had the highest proportion of current smokers (12.4%).
Young adults aged 18 to 24 years have seen the largest drop in smoking among all age groups.
Of the people who currently smoked in 2025, half said they intended to quit. Some 7.2% of people reported having used an e-cigarette, up from 6.6% in 2024.
Kruti Shrotri from Cancer Research UK said: "While a continued fall in smoking rates is encouraging, tobacco remains the leading cause of cancer in the UK.
"Although we don't know the long-term risks of vaping, evidence so far shows that legal vapes are less harmful than tobacco and an effective tool to stop smoking."
The vaping data includes people aged 16 and over in Great Britain, while the smoking statistics cover adults in the whole of the UK.

articles.title: European shares gain as Genmab jumps, bond yields retreat - WTVB
articles.summary: European shares gain as Genmab jumps, bond yields retreat  WTVB
articles.full_text:
By Sudeshna Ghoshal
Oct 6 (Reuters) – European shares rose towards one-week highs on Tuesday, buoyed by gains in healthcare stocks after Genmab’s upbeat drug-trial results, while euro zone bond yields took a breather after rallying on fiscal and inflation concerns.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index was up 0.8% to 638.67 points by 0835 GMT, poised for a third straight session of gains.
Genmab climbed 7.7% to a three-year high after the Danish biotech firm and US drugmaker AbbVie’s combination treatment for patients newly diagnosed with a type of lymphoma reduced the risk of disease progression or death in a late-stage study.
The broader healthcare index was up 1.4%, leading sectoral gains in Europe.
Attention now turns to euro zone retail sales data due later, which could offer clues about the region’s consumer spending.
Data also showed UK construction activity fell in September, but the decline was the smallest since January.
The euro hovered near a 17-month low, weighed down by worries over France’s high debt burden and a political gridlock. Political uncertainty in the region deepened after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election on Monday.
“A new 2027 budget now looks unlikely, meaning Spain may again roll over its previous budget, keeping fiscal policy broadly steady and debt-to-GDP on a declining path,” Danske Bank analysts said in a note.
“We do not expect a near-term impact on growth or public finances, supported by strong employment and consumption, though tighter immigration policy could weigh on medium-term potential growth.”
Euro zone bond yields eased, having touched multi-decade highs last week. The spread between French and German 10-year yields narrowed further from its peak of last Friday as investors assessed whether the recent surge in France’s risk premium had gone too far, too quickly.[GVD/EUR]
Persistently high rates raise borrowing costs for companies and mortgage holders, while increasing governments’ interest burdens.
MARKETS SCALE BACK ECB TIGHTENING BETS
The recent turmoil in bond markets have prompted investors to dial back their expectations for interest rate hikes from the European Central Bank.
Markets are now pricing in an 80% chance of another rate hike by the end of the year. They had been pricing in at least three more hikes by the March meeting but now are just fully pricing in one hike and around an 80% chance of a second.
Among other stocks, Italy’s Technoprobe gained 4.5% after J.P.Morgan initiated coverage on the stock with an “overweight” rating.
Spain’s property developer Neinor Homes advanced 4.2% after raising its 2026-2027 outlook, unveiling 2028 targets and announcing a planned €200- €250 million ($225-$281 million) dividend for 2028.
(Reporting by Sudeshna Ghoshal in Bengaluru; Editing by Mrigank Dhaniwala and Tasim Zahid)

articles.summary: ECB’s Rehn: High long-term rates contributing to a slowdown in growth  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The comments from European Central Bank (ECB) official and Finnish Central Bank Governor Olli Rehn released during the European trading session on Tuesday signal economic warnings due to higher long-term interest rates.
Comments
High long-term rates contributing to a slowdown in growth and reduces pass-through of energy prices to other prices and to wages.
We have not seen inflation spread to non-energy prices or wages.
Market Reaction
There seems to be no impact of ECB Rehn's comments on the Euro (EUR). At press time, EUR/USD trades 0.12% higher to near 1.1233 due to some correction in the US Dollar (USD).
ECB FAQs
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.
Author
Sagar Dua is associated with the financial markets from his college days. Along with pursuing post-graduation in Commerce in 2014, he started his markets training with chart analysis.

articles.title: German orders plummet by 10.6%, euro under pressure amid political uncertainty and debt concerns - Moomoo
articles.summary: German orders plummet by 10.6%, euro under pressure amid political uncertainty and debt concerns  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
On Tuesday, October 6, during the European session, the euro continued to weaken against the U.S. dollar as the greenback remained firm, with mounting political uncertainty and a deteriorating fiscal outlook reigniting concerns about contagion in the eurozone debt market. Weak German factory orders failed to provide meaningful support, and after the pair was capped below 1.1230 in the Asian session, attempts at a rebound proved futile, pushing it further toward the 1.1200 area.
German factory orders plunged 10.6%, with transport equipment orders plummeting 61%.
German factory orders were the immediate catalyst for the euro's decline on Tuesday. According to data from the Federal Statistical Office, factory orders plunged 10.6% month-on-month in August, compared with a 3.2% increase in July—far exceeding the market's expectation of a 1% drop. Year-on-year growth also slumped sharply, from 14% to 2.7%.
The report notes that a 61% decline in sales of transportation equipment—such as aircraft, ships, trains, and military vehicles—was the primary drag on August's figures, after having doubled in July. Excluding large‑value orders, sales across all other categories fell by just 0.1%.
This detail suggests that the sharp plunge in August was driven primarily by volatility in large orders, rather than a broad-based collapse in industrial demand. Even so, the 10.6% decline was enough to weigh on euro sentiment, as it heightened market concerns about the German economy's momentum.
Debt Concerns and Political Uncertainty: The Spread Between French OATs and German Bunds Widens to Its Broadest Level Since 2009
The euro remains under pressure from concerns about public finances. The yield spread between French OATs and German Bunds has reached levels not seen since the 2009 financial crisis. France is also grappling with political gridlock, with any major austerity measures put on hold—at least until the 2027 presidential election.
Even worse, Spanish Prime Minister Sánchez announced that general elections will be held ahead of schedule in November. Coupled with the fragility of Germany's Merz-led cabinet, investors are confronted with a highly uncertain political landscape, prompting them to steer clear of the euro.
This combination of political and fiscal factors lies at the heart of the euro's weakness. France's debt woes, Spain's snap general election, and the fragility of Germany's governing coalition—when taken together—have pushed sovereign risk premiums in the eurozone higher, prompting capital to flow into safe-haven assets such as the U.S. dollar. The yield spread between French OATs and German bunds has widened to its widest level since 2009, a direct market reflection of this heightened risk.
The decline in oil prices has provided some relief, but the U.S.-Iran conflict remains in a gray area.
Oil prices are another key driver of the euro's weakness, but they have recently retreated from their recent highs, with Brent crude now trading below the critical $100-per-barrel threshold, providing some relief to the euro.
Middle East reports indicate that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have risen significantly, yet prices remain more than 25% above their August lows. Meanwhile, U.S.-Iran tensions persist in a gray zone, and the prospect of a peace agreement remains distant.
The decline in oil prices has a dual implication for the euro: on the one hand, falling energy prices have eased inflationary pressures in the eurozone, reducing the need for the European Central Bank to tighten monetary policy further; on the other hand, oil prices remain well above their August lows, meaning that energy costs continue to weigh on the eurozone economy without being fundamentally alleviated.
The gray zone of U.S.-Iran tensions means that oil prices could resume their upward trajectory at any time should the situation escalate, and this risk premium will continue to weigh on the euro.
The European Central Bank faces a dilemma: tightening could exacerbate bond sell-offs, while inflation remains well above target.
The European Central Bank remains in a difficult position, needing to fine-tune its monetary policy. Further monetary tightening could exacerbate the sell-off in government bonds. On the other hand, inflation is running well above the 2% target and, unless the situation in the Middle East improves substantially, it is unlikely to ease, adding another layer of uncertainty to the eurozone's economic outlook.
This predicament implies that the European Central Bank's policy space is constrained by fiscal risks. If the ECB raises interest rates to combat inflation, it could exacerbate debt pressures in countries like France, widen yield spreads, and thereby weigh on the euro; conversely, if the ECB holds steady, inflation may remain persistently high, leaving real interest rates negative—also a drag on the euro. This dilemma leaves the euro without clear policy support.
On the U.S. dollar front: The ISM Services PMI has slowed, but Treasury yields have hit multi-decade highs.
In the United States, the ISM Services PMI released on Monday showed that business activity in September slowed more than expected, with firms reporting higher input prices and demand remaining robust.
However, the U.S. dollar continues to be supported by elevated U.S. Treasury yields, which have reached multi-decade highs.
This yield advantage is the core factor underpinning the U.S. dollar's strength and the key external driver of ongoing downward pressure on the euro-dollar exchange rate.
Summary
On Tuesday, the euro fell further against the U.S. dollar to around 1.1200, with Germany's August factory orders plunging 10.6% serving as the immediate catalyst; a sharp 61% drop in transportation equipment orders was the primary drag.
However, deeper pressures stem from political uncertainty and debt concerns: the yield spread between French OATs and German bunds has widened to its widest level since 2009, Spain has called early elections, and Germany's governing coalition remains fragile. The combined effect of these factors has pushed investors away from the euro. While a pullback in oil prices has provided some relief, U.S.-Iran tensions remain unresolved, leaving the drag on the eurozone from energy costs largely unaddressed.
The European Central Bank finds itself in a dilemma: tightening could fuel further bond sell-offs, while holding steady risks prolonging inflation. The U.S. dollar is finding support as Treasury yields hit multi-decade highs. Amid political risks, fiscal concerns, and policy trade-offs, the euro remains under downward pressure in the near term, with the 1.1200 level serving as a critical battleground between bulls and bears.
(EUR/USD daily chart, source: EasyForex)
At 15:06 Beijing time, the euro was trading at 1.1209/10 against the U.S. dollar.

articles.title: Italy Approves $3.7 Billion Silicon Box Chip Plant to Strengthen Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain- Expert View by Spherical Insights - Spherical Insights
articles.summary: Italy Approves $3.7 Billion Silicon Box Chip Plant to Strengthen Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain- Expert View by Spherical Insights  Spherical Insights
articles.full_text:
Italy is backing Silicon Box to strengthen semiconductor capabilities, attract high-tech investment, create jobs, reduce supply-chain vulnerabilities and establish Italy as a strategic European hub for advanced digital manufacturing.
Italy has cleared the financing framework for Silicon Box’s planned semiconductor manufacturing facility in Novara, marking a major step in the country’s strategy to strengthen its position in Europe’s semiconductor industry. The project, known as the Vulcan Project, involves a total investment of €3.2 billion, equivalent to roughly $3.7 billion, with the Italian government providing €1.3 billion (US$1.45 billion) in public support through the semiconductor sector fund established under the European Chips Act.
The project will establish Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing facility and is expected to focus on the back-end stages of semiconductor production, particularly chiplet integration, advanced packaging and testing. According to Italy’s Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, the Novara facility would be the first of its kind in Europe, introducing advanced chiplet and packaging capabilities that are currently not available at this scale within the European Union.

Call +1 303 800 4326 or Send us a message for a personalized consultation.
A strategic investment in semiconductor manufacturing
The Silicon Box investment in Novara, Italy, represents a €3.2 billion strategic project aimed at strengthening Europe’s semiconductor supply chain. In October 2026, Italy’s investment agency Invitalia approved €1.3 billion in public support, equivalent to roughly 41% of the total investment. The facility is expected to become Silicon Box’s first European manufacturing site and is projected to create around 1,600 direct jobs at full capacity.
The project focuses on advanced chiplet integration, packaging and testing, technologies increasingly important for artificial intelligence, data centres, electric and autonomous vehicles, telecommunications and high-performance computing. The European Commission granted the facility Open EU Foundry status in March 2026, with full production capacity expected by 2033.
For Italy, the investment supports a broader semiconductor strategy. The country has a multibillion-euro Chips Fund, more than €1 billion committed to EU microelectronics IPCEI projects, and a €225 million (US$252 billion) semiconductor-design centre in Pavia. Italy also ranks second in the EU by number of companies in electronic components and boards.
The project aligns with the EU Chips Act, which aims to mobilise over €100 billion (US$112.1 billion) in policy-driven investment and raise Europe’s semiconductor market share from about 10% to 20% by 2030.
Focus on advanced packaging and chiplets
Silicon Box’s Novara project is significant because it targets the “back-end” of semiconductor production, an area increasingly important as conventional chip scaling becomes more difficult. Instead of producing one large chip, chiplet architecture divides computing functions into smaller components that can be integrated within a single package. This enables manufacturers to combine different technologies and potentially reduce design and production costs.
The technology is particularly relevant to the rapid growth of AI and data-centre computing. The Semiconductor Industry Association estimates that the HBM market alone could reach $21 billion in 2025, reflecting the growing need for advanced memory and packaging solutions in AI systems.
The investment is also notable because Italy identified €4 billion in resources for its national microelectronics strategy, covering investment attraction, research and industrial development. Consequently, Novara could support Europe in developing capabilities beyond traditional wafer fabrication, particularly for AI, high-performance computing and next-generation automotive electronics.
Market Stats
- The Italian semiconductor market was valued at US$5.02 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach approximately US$8.76 billion by 2035, expanding at a CAGR of 5.70%.
- AI market: Italy’s AI market reached €1.8 billion (~$2.0B) in 2025, growing 50% year-on-year.
- AI adoption: 71% of large Italian companies had launched at least one AI project in 2025.
- AI ecosystem: Italy has 1,010 companies offering AI solutions and 135 AI startups funded over the past five years.
- Semiconductor market: Italy’s semiconductor sector is expected to generate approximately $2.3 billion in revenue in 2025, with STMicroelectronics as the dominant national player. Electronic components: Italy’s electronic-components market reached approximately $12.8 billion in 2025, with imports accounting for 68.4% of market size.
- Data centres: Italy had 513 MW of installed data-centre IT capacity in 2024, up 17% year-on-year. More than €10 billion (US$11.2 billion) of investment was expected for 2025-26.
Strengthening Europe’s Semiconductor Supply Chain
Silicon Box’s planned facility in Novara can be viewed as part of Europe’s broader effort to reduce vulnerabilities in a semiconductor industry still heavily concentrated outside the region. The European Commission estimates that East Asia accounts for 56% of global front-end wafer-fabrication capacity, while Europe represents only 9%. More broadly, Europe has around 10% of the global semiconductor market, despite having strong capabilities in research, equipment, automotive and industrial chips.

This imbalance matters because semiconductor disruptions can affect entire manufacturing industries. The European Commission notes that some European countries experienced car-production declines of up to one-third during the 2020-22 chip shortage. At the same time, automotive and industrial applications are particularly important to Europe: automotive chips account for 37% of European semiconductor demand, while industrial applications represent another 28%.
Its importance therefore extends beyond Italy. By adding capacity in a previously limited segment of Europe’s semiconductor value chain, the project could diversify sourcing, strengthen links between chip designers and manufacturers, and support European demand for AI, high-performance computing and electric-vehicle technologies. This complements the EU Chips Act’s target of increasing Europe’s global semiconductor share from 10% to 20% by 2030.
Why Italy is backing the investment
The primary purpose of the investment is to strengthen Italy’s domestic semiconductor capabilities, attract high-tech manufacturing, reduce vulnerabilities in critical supply chains and support Europe’s technological independence.
Italy is also seeking to position itself as a production platform for the wider digital economy. Italian Industry Minister Adolfo Urso described the project as reinforcing the country's role as a productive platform for the digital economy.
The government has also designated Silicon Box's investment as a project of strategic national interest. Italy has developed mechanisms to accelerate major strategic investments, particularly those involving foreign companies and technologies considered important to national industrial competitiveness.
For Silicon Box, establishing a European manufacturing base provides access to one of the world's largest industrial markets while allowing the company to develop advanced packaging capabilities closer to European customers.
Italy’s Government AI Policy
Italy has developed a national AI policy focused on innovation, competitiveness and responsible use. Its Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024-2026 concentrates on four areas: research, public administration, businesses and education/training. The strategy aims to strengthen domestic AI research, encourage companies to adopt AI and improve government services through digital technologies.
In September 2025, Italy approved its national AI law, establishing a framework aligned with the EU AI Act. The legislation emphasises human oversight, transparency, cybersecurity, privacy and accountability, with rules covering healthcare, employment, education, justice and public administration. AgID and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) were designated as key national AI authorities.
A major economic component is a €1 billion (US$1.12 billion) investment programme supporting AI, cybersecurity and related emerging technologies, particularly startups and SMEs. Digital Transformation Department
Overall, Italy’s approach combines regulation with industrial policy, seeking to develop domestic AI capabilities while ensuring that adoption remains secure, transparent and human-centred. MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has finally done something the far right approves of — calling a snap election on Nov. 29 that the anti-immigrant Vox party is hailing as “Spain’s last chance to be Spain again.”
Polling third in the race, Vox is Spain’s leading nationalist, euroskeptic force and it sees next month’s contest as its prime opportunity to remold the country after eight years of Sánchez’s socialist premiership by getting its people into top ministerial jobs.
Party leader Santiago Abascal greeted Monday’s election announcement as “excellent news.” His delight is hardly surprising given that polls suggest Vox is on track to make the biggest gains of any major party.

articles.title: Huge solar farm approved near Bath as government says green belt is actually 'grey' - Somerset Live
articles.summary: Huge solar farm approved near Bath as government says green belt is actually 'grey'  Somerset LivePACE wins appeal for 49.5MW solar plant  Solar Power Portal‘Inspector overturns council’s refusal of 28ha grey belt solar farm’  Planning ResourceBurnett solar farm plan approved on appeal  Keynsham VoicePathfinder wins consent for 49.5-MW solar park in UK after appeal  Renewables Now
articles.full_text:
The 28 hectare solar farm will generate enough electricity to power 5,500 home
A solar farm blocked by local councillors can now go ahead, as the fields it would be built on have been ruled to be “grey belt”.
Bath and North East Somerset Council’s planning committee had voted to refuse planning permission for the 28 hectare solar farm in September 2025. People from the neighbouring village of Burnett warned it would spoil their “rural idyll” and councillors agreed that it would be an inappropriate development in the green belt.
But now it has been approved after an appeal to the government’s planning inspectorate, which ruled that the fields were “grey belt” and not green belt after all. The idea of grey belt was introduced by Labour as a way to ensure that developments on low quality areas, such as former car parks, were not blocked just because they lay inside the green belt.
These fields have never been previously developed and lie in the open North East Somerset countryside, just across the brow of a hill from Keynsham. But the planning inspectorate said that it was precisely because they were not next to the town that they could be classed as grey belt, as it was not contributing to the purpose of the green belt.
Planning inspector R. E. Jones said: “Whilst the appeal site appears large when viewed at a local level, it nevertheless occupies a very small proportion of the intervening green belt land between Keynsham and Bath. Its development as a solar farm would not therefore result in a loss of visual separation between these towns.”
The inspector said that the plan would “industrialise a sizeable part of the local countryside” and harm the landscape character, but warned this had to be balanced against the positive impacts. The solar farm would generate up to 22 gigawatt hours of clean electricity a year, enough to power 5,574 homes.
The planning committee’s decision to block the solar farm, despite the council having declared a climate emergency, was controversial at the time. As councillors voted in September 2025, planning committee member John Leach (Walcot, Liberal Democrat) rejected the idea the site would be an “eyesore.”
He said at the time: “I don’t see it as an eyesore and I think future generations will be even more likely not to see this as an eyesore but to see it as a possible sign of our efforts to deal with a crisis as a crisis.”

articles.summary: Kier lands £115m Manchester Airport station upgrade  Construction Enquirer£115m investment takes flight at Manchester Airport station  Network Rail media centreManchester Airport rail station to get £115m upgrade for more trains  BBCMajor UK airport to SHUT station for 24 hours as £115million upgrade begins  The SunDecember start for £115m Manchester Airport station upgrade  Place North West
articles.full_text:
Network Rail and Kier will deliver the programme through to 2028 as part of the wider Manchester Rail Upgrade.
The job will extend platforms 1, 2 and 3 to accommodate longer trains, remodel the station approach tracks and modernise signalling to support more frequent and reliable services.
Engineers will tackle the first major milestone on 6 December, closing the station for one day to install a utility bridge carrying electrical cables across the railway.
This will pave the way for an existing bridge used by Manchester Airport Group to be removed at Easter 2027, with a replacement built later that year.
The programme aims to unlock capacity for future passenger growth and strengthen rail links to one of Britain’s busiest transport hubs.
Simon Daly, Network Rail senior sponsor, said: “This £115m investment represents a major commitment to improving one of the country’s most important transport interchanges.
“Manchester Airport station plays a vital role in connecting people across the country so these improvements will create more capacity for passengers, allow longer trains to serve the station and improve the reliability of services for years to come.”

articles.title: Zelensky Warns of Massive Russian Strike as 3 Tu-160 Bombers Take Off - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: Zelensky Warns of Massive Russian Strike as 3 Tu-160 Bombers Take Off  Kyiv PostUkraine war briefing: Kyiv claims half of Russia’s oil refining capacity destroyed  The GuardianUkrainian forces hit two oil facilities, training range in Russia – Zelensky  UkrinformDefense Forces Strike Samara Oil Facility as Large Fire Breaks Out  MilitarnyiHuge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged Ukrainian citizens to take shelter when air raid alerts sound, citing updated intelligence reports about a massive strike planned by Moscow.
Ukrainian emergency services and the Air Force are ready to respond, Zelensky said in his evening address on Tuesday, Oct. 6, but the scale of their response depends on the air defense capabilities available to the country.
“A lot depends on our partners – every leader and every country in the world that has the defensive capabilities we need and can provide them to us,” Zelensky said, urging allies to continue supplying Kyiv as the war nears its fifth winter.
Bombers took off from Siberia
Hours later, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported that three Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers had taken off from Belaya airbase in Russia’s Siberian Irkutsk region.
In case the aircraft fire cruise missiles, the missiles could likely cross into Ukrainian airspace sometime after 3 a.m. local time, the Air Force said, urging citizens not to ignore air raid alerts and to stay in shelters.
Earlier warning
The evening address followed an initial warning Zelensky issued on Tuesday afternoon.
He announced the warning after a coordination meeting with government officials, military commanders and emergency services. According to the president, Kyiv was also preparing countermeasures.
At that meeting, the defense minister and the Air Force commander briefed the president on how air defense assets were being distributed and how protection was organized around key facilities.
Zelensky said the government and regional authorities had also prepared additional logistics measures in response to what he called a Russian operation against Ukraine’s logistics. Deadlines were set for many of the tasks, and the most urgent ones were already underway.
Separately on Tuesday, Zelensky chaired a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.
According to the president, electronic warfare systems neutralize a significant share of Russia’s Shahed drones, and the most effective approaches will be scaled up.
The meeting also set priorities for supplying Ukrainian forces with long-range drones next year, with the main goal of giving Ukraine the ability to respond in kind to Russian strikes.

articles.title: Belfast’s £100m ‘Factory of the Future’ opens with pledge to create 1,500 jobs - The Irish News
articles.summary: Belfast’s £100m ‘Factory of the Future’ opens with pledge to create 1,500 jobs  The Irish NewsQueen’s University unveils ‘factory of the future’ that’s tipped to create up to 1,500 jobs  Belfast TelegraphMinister for Northern Ireland champions Northern Ireland economic growth, exports and innovation  GOV.UKOpening of AMIC a key driver for investment and advanced technology – Kearney  sinnfein.ieMagherafelt firm celebrates major success at CEF Awards &...
articles.full_text:
Belfast’s new £100 million Advanced Manufacturing Innovation Centre (AMIC), which promises to bridge the gap between ground-breaking academic research and real-world commercial application, has been officially opened.
Located at Global Point in Newtownabbey, the so-called ‘Factory of the Future’ is expected to create up to 1,500 jobs, contribute £1.3 billion to the north’s economy, and support the training of 300 apprentices by 2050.
The research, development and industrial‑innovation hub is led by Queen’s University Belfast, with support from Invest NI and Belfast Region City Deal partners.
It is designed to be Northern Ireland’s flagship centre for advanced manufacturing, helping local firms adopt cutting‑edge technologies, improve productivity, and accelerate innovation.
Although the facility has been operational since April, it was officially opened by Sarah Owen MP, deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly, economy minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald, finance minister John O’Dowd, South Antrim MP Robin Swann and Antrim and Newtownabbey mayor Henry Cushinan.
The investment in AMIC includes £78m from the UK Government, £10m from Antrim and Newtownabbey Borough Council, £8m from Queen’s University and £1.3m from Ulster University.
It has been designed in response to the needs of the north’s burgeoning advanced manufacturing sector, with businesses and industry partners helping to shape its capabilities.
Sarah Owen MP said: “AMIC is a beacon for innovation which reinforces Northern Ireland’s reputation as an ideal hub for global investment and is key to an exciting future for manufacturing in Northern Ireland.
“This world-class centre brings together Queen’s University Belfast, Ulster University and industry partners under one roof.
“The centre will supercharge business competitiveness, drive decarbonisation, invest in local talent and create high-value jobs.”
Economy minister Caoimhe Archibald added: “This flagship investment demonstrates the power of partnership between central and local government, industry and our universities to drive economic transformation.
“The state-of-the-art facility will help businesses innovate, boost productivity and seize new opportunities in global markets.
“The benefits of this will be felt across the north through stronger businesses, higher-value jobs and enhanced skills for future generations, helping to ensure long-term prosperity for communities and industry alike.”
AMIC’s expert engineering team supports businesses to explore and adopt technologies that may not otherwise be available to them in-house, helping them address future technology, skills and sustainability challenges.
Engineers are already deploying technologies atAMIC including robotics and automation, advanced materials, digital twins, artificial intelligence, advanced metrology and machining to improve productivity, efficiency and industry competitiveness.
Among major projects currently under way is the £9.5m Project 4WARD, which is focused on advancing welding automation in partnership with Hyster-Yale, Terex, 4DNI, Nugent Trailers and Datum Tool Design, with support from Invest NI.
Alongside digitalisation and automation, the Factory of the Future team is tackling some of the biggest challenges facing manufacturers - from energy efficiency and renewable energy to circularity and resource use.
And it says that by developing and applying these technologies, its work is helping businesses move towards a more productive, competitive and low-carbon future.
